poets.name: Ben Jonson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ben Jonson — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ben Jonson (1572-1637) was an English poet and playwright, the dominant literary figure of the Jacobean stage and a rival and friend of Shakespeare.

Beyond his comedies and tragedies, he wrote a substantial body of lyric and occasional verse, including epigrams and elegies collected here from a posthumous volume of his poems and prose "Discoveries."

poets.name: Sir Philip Sidney
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Philip Sidney · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Philip Sidney (1554–1586) was an English poet, courtier, and soldier, killed at the Battle of Zutphen at thirty-one.
His sonnet sequence Astrophel and Stella (1591) is the first great sequence in English, chronicling an unrequited, thinly-veiled autobiographical love.

poets.name: Fulke Greville
poets.credit: Unknown artist, c. 1620 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Fulke Greville, Lord Brooke (1554–1628), was an English poet and statesman, the close friend and biographer of Philip Sidney.
His philosophical sequences, published posthumously as Certaine Learned and Elegant Workes, weigh monarchy, religion, and human frailty in dense, difficult verse.

poets.name: Samuel Daniel
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Samuel Daniel (1562–1619) was an English poet and historian, admired for the plain, measured elegance of his style.
His sonnet sequence Delia and the narrative poem The Complaint of Rosamond made his early reputation.

poets.name: Michael Drayton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Michael Drayton (1563–1631) was an English poet whose vast body of work spans the sonnet sequence Idea, historical verse, and the topographical epic Poly-Olbion.
His Barons' Wars retells the civil strife of Edward II's reign in stately ottava rima.

poets.name: Thomas Heywood
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Heywood was an English actor and a prolific dramatist. His dates of birth and death are uncertain.
Palgrave includes his song "Pack, clouds, away, and welcome day".

poets.name: John White
poets.credit: No known portrait · text from Davids Psalms in Metre (1655), EEBO-TCP A76568 (CC0)
bio: John White (1575–1648) was an English Puritan clergyman, rector of Holy Trinity, Dorchester, in Dorset, where his long ministry earned him the nickname the ‘Patriarch of Dorchester’. He took a close interest in the colonisation of New England and was instrumental in organising the Dorchester Company and in the founding of the Massachusetts Bay Company.

His metrical version of the Psalms, made for congregational singing in common tunes, was left in the care of his son and printed posthumously in 1655 as Davids Psalms in Metre, with a preface by his successor Stanley Gower. The Psalms here are the 1655 text, with its original spelling. Fourteen psalms whose source pages are damaged or illegible are omitted.

poets.name: William Barton
poets.credit: No known portrait — text from The Book of Psalms in Metre (1644), EEBO-TCP A27789 (CC0)
bio: William Barton (1598?–1678) was an English hymnodist and metrical psalmist. His versification of the Psalms was offered to Parliament as a replacement for the older version of Sternhold and Hopkins.

The Psalms here are the 1644 text of The Book of Psalms in Metre, with its original spelling. All 150 psalms are included, none omitted. Psalms made up of several parts, such as Psalm 119, are given as a single poem, and the printed musical notation, tune directions, argument and marginal notes are left out. A bullet (•) marks a letter that is illegible in the digitised source.

poets.name: John Fletcher
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Fletcher was an English dramatist who collaborated with Francis Beaumont and later with Shakespeare. Songs scattered through his plays are admired for their lyric grace.
Palgrave includes his song "Melancholy".

poets.name: Henry Peacham
poets.credit: Title page of The Compleat Gentleman (1622) by Henry Peacham, not a portrait (no authenticated likeness is used here) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Peacham was an English emblem writer, schoolmaster and author, best known for The Compleat Gentleman (1622), a guide to the education and accomplishments of a gentleman. He was educated at Cambridge, taught school, and travelled on the Continent; the dates usually given for his birth and death (about 1576 and about 1643) are uncertain, and some sources place his birth in 1578.

Minerva Britanna, or a Garden of Heroical Devices (1612), dedicated to Henry, Prince of Wales, is a book of emblems, each a woodcut or engraving with a Latin motto, English verses and Latin glosses, addressed to patrons, friends and public figures. Only the English verses are given here, under the Latin mottoes that head each emblem.

poets.name: George Sandys
poets.credit: Portrait of George Sandys (engraving), reproduced by Robert Alonzo Brock and Virgil Anson Lewis · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Sandys (1578–1644) was an English traveller, colonist and poet. In 1610 he journeyed through the Ottoman Empire, Egypt and the Holy Land, and published an account of it as A Relation of a Journey (1615), one of the most widely read travel books of its day. From 1621 he was in Virginia as treasurer of the Virginia Company, and there he worked on his English translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses, published in full in 1632.

Back in England he turned to sacred verse: A Paraphrase upon the Psalms of David (1636) and A Paraphrase upon the Divine Poems (1638), which added Job, Ecclesiastes, Lamentations and the scriptural songs, with musical settings by Henry Lawes. The 1638 volume is the source of the poems here, given in the original spelling.

poets.name: William Alexander, Earl of Stirling
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Alexander, later Earl of Stirling, was a Scottish courtier and poet who served James VI and I. He published the sonnet sequence Aurora in 1604 and a set of verse tragedies, the Monarchicke Tragedies.
Palgrave includes one poem by him, the song "To Aurora".

poets.name: John Webster
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Webster was an English dramatist, author of The White Devil and The Duchess of Malfi. His birth date is unknown.
Palgrave includes "A Land Dirge", a song from The White Devil.

poets.name: John Taylor
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of John Taylor, the Water Poet, by Thomas Cockson, from All the Workes of John Taylor (1630) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Taylor (1580–1653), known as “the Water Poet”, was a Thames waterman who made himself a prolific pamphleteer and verse-writer. He worked the river as a ferryman and sculler, served the navy in his youth, and later enjoyed the notice of the court of James I.

The Sculler (1612) and The Nipping and Snipping of Abuses (1614), both gathered here, are early miscellanies of satires, epigrams, sonnets and anagrams. They mix anti-Catholic invective, jibes at the manners of the city, and verses of compliment to patrons and fellow writers.

poets.name: Sir John Beaumont
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir John Beaumont (1583–1627), 1st Baronet, was born at Grace-Dieu in Leicestershire, the elder brother of the dramatist Francis Beaumont, whose death he mourns in one of the epitaphs printed here. He was a country gentleman and a baronet rather than a professional writer, and his poems circulated among friends and were not collected in his lifetime.

His verse appeared posthumously in Bosworth-field, with a Taste of the Variety of Other Poems (1629), set forth by his son. The book joins a long historical poem on the battle that ended the Wars of the Roses with devotional pieces, verses to the Stuart court and the Duke of Buckingham, elegies and epitaphs, and translations from Virgil, Horace, Persius, Juvenal, Ausonius, Claudian and Prudentius. His easy, balanced couplets are often seen as a forerunner of the polished heroic couplet of later in the century. The 1629 text is damaged in the EEBO-TCP transcription, so lost letters and words are shown in square brackets; two pages of the book (181 and 182), following the epitaph on Lord Wriothesley, are missing from that transcription altogether.

poets.name: Phineas Fletcher
poets.credit: No authentic portrait is known.
bio: Phineas Fletcher (1582–1650), the elder son of Giles Fletcher the elder and brother of the poet Giles Fletcher the younger, was educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge. He took holy orders, and from 1621 until his death he was rector of Hilgay in Norfolk. He is generally regarded as the leading Spenserian poet of his generation.

His chief work, The Purple Island, or The Isle of Man, an allegorical poem in twelve cantos on the human body and soul, was printed at Cambridge in 1633 together with Piscatorie Eclogs and Poeticall Miscellanies. Those two shorter collections are given here: seven eclogues in which fishermen take the place of shepherds, and a miscellany of occasional verses, epigrams, translations from Boethius, psalm paraphrases and hymns. The Purple Island itself is not part of this selection.

poets.name: William Drummond of Hawthornden
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Drummond of Hawthornden (1585–1649) was the first considerable Scottish poet to write in English rather than Scots.
His polished sonnets and elegies were shaped by his wide reading in French and Italian verse.

poets.name: John Donne
poets.credit: Portrait of John Donne by Isaac Oliver · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Donne (1572–1631) was an English poet and cleric, the foremost of the metaphysical poets.
His verse — by turns erotic, witty, and devout — moved from the love poems of his youth to the religious sonnets of his years as Dean of St Paul's.

poets.name: Francis Beaumont
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Francis Beaumont was an English dramatist, best known for his plays written in collaboration with John Fletcher. His own poems were collected and published after his death.
Palgrave includes his lines on the tombs in Westminster Abbey.

poets.name: George Herbert
poets.credit: Portrait of George Herbert · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Herbert (1593–1633) was a Welsh-born English poet and priest, a central figure of the metaphysical school.
His single collection, The Temple (1633), published just after his death, gathers the devotional lyrics for which he is loved.

poets.name: Thomas Carew
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait of Carew survives.
bio: Thomas Carew (1595–1640) was an English Cavalier poet at the court of Charles I, admired for the polish of his amorous lyrics.
His Poems (1640) circulated widely and shaped the courtly style later followed by Lovelace and Suckling.

poets.name: James Shirley
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Shirley was an English dramatist of the reign of Charles I, one of the last playwrights of the Jacobean and Caroline stage.
Palgrave includes two of his lyrics, "The Last Conqueror" and "Death the Leveller".

poets.name: Sir John Suckling
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir John Suckling (1609–1641) was an English Cavalier poet and courtier, famed for his wit and his invention of the card game cribbage.
His collected verse, Fragmenta Aurea (1646), mixes light, conversational love lyrics with plays and prose.

poets.name: Nathaniel Whiting
poets.credit: No portrait of Whiting is known.
bio: Nathaniel Whiting was a Cambridge-educated poet and later a Puritan minister. He took his B.A. at Queens' College, Cambridge, in 1631 and his M.A. in 1635, and in 1637 published, under the initials N. W., the long verse romance Le Hore di Recreatione, or The Pleasant History of Albino and Bellama. He later became minister of Aldwincle in Northamptonshire and was deprived of the living at the Restoration.

Albino and Bellama, printed with the dream-poem Il Insonio Insonnadado that defends poetry against its critics, is written in an odd, inventive diction. The text here follows George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921).

poets.name: Thomas Jordan
poets.credit: No portrait is known; none sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Jordan (c. 1612–1685) was an English actor, dramatist and poet. He began as a player in London before the theatres were closed in 1642, and published his verse in small, miscellaneous volumes through the Civil War, the Interregnum and the Restoration.

His Divine Raptures (1646) turns everyday sights — a weathercock, a windmill, a ship — into pious meditations; the later volumes gathered here, Divinity and Morality in Robes of Poetry and The Muses Melody, both printed undated, mix moral epigrams, elegies, acrostics and occasional verse with amorous and satirical pieces.

poets.name: Sir William Davenant
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir William Davenant · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir William Davenant (1606–1668) was an English poet and playwright who served as Poet Laureate from 1638. A bridge between the ages of Shakespeare and Dryden, he helped reopen and reshape the English theatre after the Restoration.
His most ambitious work is the unfinished heroic poem Gondibert (1651); the collection Madagascar; with Other Poems (1638) gathers his courtly and occasional verse.

poets.name: Sir William Killigrew
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir William Killigrew by Anthony van Dyck, 1638 (Tate Britain) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir William Killigrew (1606–1695), of Kempton Park, Middlesex, was an English court official who served under both Charles I and Charles II. He was the brother of the dramatist Thomas Killigrew, and Anthony van Dyck painted his portrait in 1638.

In old age he published Mid-night and Daily Thoughts, in Prose and Verse (1694), a book of short devotional meditations, each followed or replaced by a rhymed poem on a Christian theme: repentance, faith, time, the Christian festivals and the fear of death. The poems collected here are the verse of that book.

poets.name: Henry King
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry King (1592–1669) was an English poet and Bishop of Chichester.
He is remembered above all for ‘The Exequy,’ his elegy for his young wife — one of the great grief poems of the century.

poets.name: John Milton
poets.credit: Portrait, Christ’s College, Cambridge · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and polemicist, author of the epic Paradise Lost. He went blind in mid-life and composed his greatest work by dictation.
Though he predates the Romantic movement, his blank verse and his figure of Satan shaped nearly every English poet who followed.

poets.name: Sir Aston Cokain
poets.credit: Engraving of Sir Aston Cokain, published 1796 (after an earlier print) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Aston Cokain (also spelt Cokayne or Cockayne, 1608–1684) was a Derbyshire gentleman, Royalist and minor poet and dramatist, born at Ashbourne Hall. He was educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and travelled in France and Italy before settling into the life of a country squire. He was created a baronet in 1642 and sided with the King in the Civil War, after which his estates were much reduced.

Cokain moved in literary circles and was a friend and admirer of Philip Massinger and John Fletcher, on whose shared grave in Southwark he wrote an epitaph, and a kinsman of Charles Cotton. His chief book, A Chain of Golden Poems (1658), gathers epigrams, love and funeral elegies, songs, eclogues, verse letters and a satire, together with two comedies, The Obstinate Lady and Trappolin Suppos'd a Prince. It is a lively record of Cavalier manners and of the Derbyshire gentry around him.

poets.name: Anne Bradstreet
poets.credit: Title page of The Tenth Muse (London, 1650); no authentic portrait of Bradstreet survives · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anne Bradstreet (c. 1612–1672), born Anne Dudley in Northampton, England, emigrated to Massachusetts in 1630 with her husband Simon Bradstreet and her parents, Thomas and Dorothy Dudley. She raised eight children and is regarded as the first English-language poet of the American colonies, writing amid the work of a household in the new settlements, and she died at North Andover.

Her brother-in-law took a manuscript to London, where it appeared without her knowledge as The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America (1650). A revised and enlarged edition, Several Poems, was printed in Boston in 1678, six years after her death, and is the source of this selection; it holds her long quaternions and historical poems alongside the shorter personal poems, 'Contemplations' and the verses to her husband and children.

poets.name: Richard Crashaw
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait of Crashaw survives.
bio: Richard Crashaw (1613–1649) was an English metaphysical poet known for the ecstatic, ornate devotion of his sacred verse.
A convert to Catholicism, he collected his poems as Steps to the Temple (1646), consciously following George Herbert.

poets.name: John Cleveland
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of John Cleveland, frontispiece to his Works (1687) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Cleveland (1613–1658) was an English Royalist poet and satirist, a fellow of St John's College, Cambridge, who lost his post when the Civil War came and served the King's cause with his pen. He is best known for his sharp political satires against Scots, Parliament men and Puritans, and for love poems in the most extravagant 'strong-lined' conceited style.

Cleveland's verse was enormously popular in the 1650s and was reprinted many times, though the collections that carry his name also contain pieces by other hands. The text here follows George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921), using the poems he prints as Cleveland's and leaving out those he marks as disputed.

poets.name: William Hammond
poets.credit: No known portrait · Text from EEBO-TCP A87057 (Poems. By W. H., London, 1655)
bio: William Hammond is a Royalist-period lyric poet known from a single book, Poems, published in London by Thomas Dring in 1655. Its title page gives only the initials "W. H."; the attribution to William Hammond, born in 1614, comes from the library catalogue record of the volume.

The book gathers love lyrics, pastoral dialogues, verse letters, elegies and English versions of Horace. Many of the poems are addressed to a close family circle: his kinsman T. S., a brother, H. S., mourned as drowned, a sister, Mrs. S., and an uncle, Mr. G. Sandys. Little else about his life can be stated from the book itself.

poets.name: Richard Baxter
poets.credit: After Robert White, engraving, c. 1670 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Baxter (1615–1691) was an English Puritan minister, theologian and controversialist, long associated with Kidderminster in Worcestershire. A prolific author of devotional prose, he was a leading Nonconformist voice after the Restoration and suffered fines and imprisonment for his beliefs.

His metrical Paraphrase on the Psalms of David was published in 1692, the year after his death, 'left fitted for the press by his own hand', together with a handful of hymns. In it he marks his own additions to the biblical text in square brackets. Several psalms are followed by alternative versions, including one by George Herbert.

poets.name: Abraham Cowley
poets.credit: Portrait of Abraham Cowley by Sir Peter Lely · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Abraham Cowley (1618–1667) was among the most celebrated English poets of his century, a child prodigy admired for his metaphysical wit.
His 1656 Poems gathers odes, elegies, and the love sequence The Mistress.

poets.name: Richard Lovelace
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait of this collection's engraving survives in the public record used here.
bio: Richard Lovelace (1617–1657) was an English Cavalier poet who fought and was imprisoned for the Royalist cause.
Best remembered for ‘To Althea, from Prison’ and ‘To Lucasta, Going to the Wars,’ his posthumous Lucasta volumes appeared in 1659.

poets.name: William Habington
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Habington (1605–1654) was an English poet whose single collection, Castara (1634), celebrates — unusually for the age — his courtship and marriage to one woman.

poets.name: Sir John Denham
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir John Denham (1615–1669) was an English poet best known for Cooper's Hill (1642), a landscape meditation that founded the English topographical poem.
His couplets were much admired by Dryden and Pope for their balance and control.

poets.name: Thomas Randolph
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Randolph · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Randolph (1605–1635) was an English poet and dramatist, a celebrated wit at Cambridge and an adopted ‘son’ of Ben Jonson.
He died at twenty-nine; his collected Poems appeared three years later.

poets.name: Edmund Waller
poets.credit: Portrait of Edmund Waller · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edmund Waller (1606–1687) was an English poet and politician whose smooth, regular couplets influenced the coming Augustan style.
He wrote equally fluent verse for both sides of the Civil War, a flexibility that shadowed his reputation.

poets.name: Sir Charles Sedley
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Charles Sedley (1639–1701) was an English Restoration poet, playwright, and courtier known for his wit and libertine reputation at the court of Charles II.

poets.name: George Wither
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Wither (1588–1667) was a prolific English poet and pamphleteer whose early verse, collected as Juvenilia, made him one of the most popular poets of his generation before his turn to satire and religious controversy.

poets.name: Richard Brathwaite
poets.credit: Richard Brathwaite, engraving by Charles Pye after George Clint (1823), from a print by Robert Vaughan prefixed to The English Gentleman · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Brathwaite (also spelled Brathwait, c. 1588-1673) was an English poet and prose writer from Westmorland, in the north of England. He studied at Oxford and Cambridge, spent most of his life in the north, and wrote a long run of conduct books, moral treatises and verse, among them The English Gentleman (1630).

The poems here come from two early volumes. A Strappado for the Divell (1615) mixes satirical epigrams, verse addresses to the townsfolk of Kendal, and the Ovidian tale of Pyramus and Thisbe. Natures Embassie (1621) gathers satires, funeral elegies, pastoral eclogues and the bird poems that give the book its name. Poems too badly damaged in the digital transcription of the printed text have been left out.

poets.name: William Browne of Tavistock
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Browne of Tavistock (1590–1645) was an English pastoral poet from Devon, educated at Exeter College, Oxford, and the Inner Temple. A follower of Spenser, he is best known for Britannia's Pastorals (1613–16), a long poem of the Devon countryside, and for The Shepherd's Pipe (1614), to which his friend George Wither also contributed.

He also wrote the masque of the Inner Temple, the sonnet sequences gathered here under Cælia and Visions, and a celebrated epitaph on Mary Sidney, Countess of Pembroke. His verse is prized for its close, affectionate observation of birds, flowers, rivers and rural customs.

poets.name: Robert Herrick
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Herrick · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Herrick (1591–1674) was an English poet and clergyman, the most prolific of the Cavalier poets.
His single vast collection, Hesperides (1648), moves between pagan celebration, courtly love, and country ritual — over a thousand short poems in one book.

poets.name: Francis Quarles
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Quarles (engraving, c. 1640) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Quarles (1592–1644) was an English poet and prose writer, born in Essex and educated at Christ's College, Cambridge, and Lincoln's Inn. He served as cupbearer to Elizabeth of Bohemia, the daughter of James I, and later as secretary to James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, in Ireland. In 1639 he was appointed chronologer of the City of London, and he remained a committed royalist during the Civil War.

Quarles was among the most widely read devotional writers of the seventeenth century. His Divine Fancies (1633) gathers epigrams, meditations and observations in verse; his best-known work, Emblemes (1635), pairs engraved emblems with sacred poems, and was followed by Hieroglyphikes of the Life of Man (1638). His popularity endured for generations among readers of plain, pointed religious verse.

poets.name: Thomas Bancroft
poets.credit: No known portrait
bio: Thomas Bancroft (fl. 1633–1658) was an English epigrammatist and verse satirist. Little is securely recorded of his life; his poems are addressed to gentry and neighbours of the English Midlands, and he published two books of epigrams and epitaphs in London in 1639.

Two Bookes of Epigrammes, and Epitaphs was dedicated to Sir Charles Shirley, Baronet, and William Davenport, Esquire, and printed by I. Okes for Matthew Walbancke. The first book is largely satirical and occasional, mixing portraits of types and named acquaintances with epitaphs; the second turns often to scriptural and devotional themes. A later volume, Time's out of Tune, appeared in 1658.

poets.name: Andrew Marvell
poets.credit: Portrait of Andrew Marvell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Andrew Marvell (1621–1678) was an English metaphysical poet and politician.
Celebrated for lyrics such as ‘To His Coy Mistress’ and ‘The Garden,’ most of his poems appeared posthumously in the Miscellaneous Poems of 1681.

poets.name: Jean de La Fontaine
poets.credit: Portrait of Jean de La Fontaine by Hyacinthe Rigaud, 1690 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jean de La Fontaine (1621–1695) was a French poet born at Château-Thierry in Champagne. After an unsettled early career in law and the administration of forests and waters, he found patrons in Paris, among them Nicolas Fouquet and later Madame de La Sablière, and became one of the glories of the age of Louis XIV; he was elected to the Académie française in 1684.

His Fables, published in collected books between 1668 and 1694, retell the stories of Aesop, Phaedrus and the Indian tradition in supple, irregular verse of great wit and economy. Under the guise of animals they observe the manners, vanities and cruelties of court and town. This selection follows the English verse translation by Walter Thornbury (London, 1886), printed with Gustave Doré's illustrations.

poets.name: Henry Vaughan
poets.credit: Title-page emblem from Silex Scintillans (1650) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Vaughan (1621–1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet and physician who styled himself ‘the Silurist.’
He is best known for the sacred poems of Silex Scintillans (1650), written under the deep influence of George Herbert.

poets.name: Thomas Stanley
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Stanley, 1660 · Public domain (Wikipedia)
bio: Thomas Stanley (1625–1678) was an English poet, translator and scholar, remembered for his History of Philosophy (1655–62) and for his edition of Aeschylus. Educated at Cambridge, he lived in London and moved among Royalist writers such as Shirley and Fanshawe.

His own poems, first printed in 1647 and reprinted in 1651 and 1656, are polished, graceful love lyrics addressed mostly to a lady called Chariessa or Celia. This selection takes his original poems from George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921) and leaves out the pieces that Stanley translated from other poets.

poets.name: Charles Cotton
poets.credit: Charles Cotton, British (English) School, 17th century (National Trust) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Cotton (1630–1687) was an English poet and translator from Beresford Hall in Staffordshire, on the river Dove. He was the friend and adopted "son" of Izaak Walton, and wrote the second part of The Compleat Angler (1676), the treatise on fly-fishing added to Walton's book. His translation of Montaigne's Essays (1685) remained the standard English version for generations.

His burlesques, Scarronides (a travesty of Virgil, 1664) and A Voyage to Ireland in Burlesque, made him a leading comic poet of the Restoration, while his love lyrics, odes and "quatrains" of the countryside show a quieter, more personal voice. Poems on Several Occasions appeared posthumously in 1689; the text here follows that edition (EEBO-TCP), including its closing section of translations from Horace, Martial, Catullus, Johannes Secundus and French and Italian poets, and leaving out the commendatory verses by another hand.

poets.name: Katherine Philips
poets.credit: Portrait of Katherine Philips · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Katherine Philips (1632–1664), called ‘the Matchless Orinda,’ was an English poet and translator.
She was admired above all for her poems of female friendship; her collected Poems appeared in 1664 and 1667.

poets.name: John Dryden
poets.credit: Portrait of John Dryden by an unknown artist, after Sir Godfrey Kneller · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Dryden (1631–1700) was England’s dominant literary figure of the later 17th century — poet, satirist, playwright, and critic — and was made the first official Poet Laureate in 1668.
His satires — Absalom and Achitophel, Mac Flecknoe, The Medal — and his public odes set the model for Augustan verse that Pope and Swift would inherit.

poets.name: Samuel Pordage
bio: Samuel Pordage (1633–1691?) was an English poet and dramatist, the son of the Behmenist mystic John Pordage. His dates are uncertain; the year of his death is given only as a probable one.

His Poems upon Several Occasions appeared in 1660, signed “S. P. Gent.”, and includes panegyrics on Monck and on Charles II. He is also remembered as the author of Azaria and Hushai (1682), a reply to Dryden’s Absalom and Achitophel.

poets.name: Thomas Flatman
poets.credit: Thomas Flatman, self-portrait miniature · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Flatman (1635–1688) was an English poet and miniature painter, born in London, educated at Winchester and New College, Oxford, and called to the bar at the Inner Temple. He became a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1668 and was admired for his portrait miniatures as much as for his verse.

His Poems and Songs went through four editions between 1674 and 1686. They range from Pindaric odes on the deaths of public figures, through devotional pieces such as the Hymn for the Morning, to witty songs and satires. The text here follows George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921), leaving out his Latin pieces and his translations and paraphrases of Horace, Ovid and others.

poets.name: Thomas Shipman
poets.credit: No portrait known · text from Carolina, or Loyal Poems (1683), EEBO-TCP A59967 (CC0)
bio: Thomas Shipman (1632–1680) was a Royalist gentleman-poet of Nottinghamshire. He wrote steadily from the last years of the Commonwealth through the Restoration, and his verse is largely occasional: elegies for friends and for Charles I, verse-letters and thank-you poems to neighbouring gentry, drinking songs in praise of Canary wine, and prologues written for players. Many of the poems carry the year of composition in their titles.

Almost nothing of his verse was printed in his lifetime. Carolina, or Loyal Poems appeared in 1683, three years after his death, published by friends. It opens with poems on the execution of Charles I and the Restoration and closes with a long Pindaric poem on Belvoir Castle, the seat of the Earls of Rutland. The Resolute Courtier is the poem by which he is most often anthologised.

poets.name: Robert Heath
poets.credit: No known portrait · text from Clarastella (1650), EEBO-TCP A86166 (CC0)
bio: Robert Heath, styled Esquire on his title page, was an English poet of the Caroline and Interregnum years. Very little is securely known of his life, and he is remembered almost entirely for a single printed volume, which gives its name to a wider circle of friends and patrons named only by their initials in his dedications and elegies.

Clarastella, together with Poems Occasional, Elegies, Epigrams, Satyrs was printed in London in 1650 for Humphrey Moseley. It opens with a sequence of love poems addressed to the fictional Clarastella, then turns to occasional verse, elegies for friends and for Royalist casualties of the Civil War, two books of short satirical epigrams, and four longer verse satires on the follies of the age.

poets.name: Samuel Woodford
poets.credit: Thomas Flatman, Samuel Woodforde DD (1661) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Woodford (1636-1700) was an Anglican clergyman and poet, born in London and educated at St Paul's School and Wadham College, Oxford. He studied at the Inner Temple, where his chamber-fellow was the poet Thomas Flatman, and was elected to the Royal Society in 1664. He took holy orders in 1669 and held livings and canonries in Hampshire, Chichester and Winchester, taking his D.D. in 1677.

He is best known for his verse paraphrases of scripture: a Paraphrase upon the Psalms (1667) and A Paraphrase upon the Canticles (1679), the latter gathering the Song of Solomon, hymns and psalms from the New and Old Testaments, and occasional odes and sonnets, among them poems to Izaak Walton and Sir John Denham. He drew his inspiration from Abraham Cowley, and wrote in the irregular, Pindaric stanzas of the Cowleyan ode.

poets.name: Philip Ayres
poets.credit: No known portrait · text from Lyric Poems (1687), EEBO-TCP A26293 (CC0)
bio: Philip Ayres (1638–1712) was an English poet and translator, born at Cottingham and educated at Westminster and St John's College, Oxford. He became tutor in the family of Montague Garrard Drake of Amersham, Buckinghamshire, and lived with them until his death on 1 December 1712.

His chief work is Lyric Poems, Made in Imitation of the Italians (1687), a collection of sonnets, songs and original pieces together with many translations from Italian, Spanish, Latin and Greek poets. One copy of verses is addressed to his friend John Dryden.

poets.name: Aphra Behn
poets.credit: Portrait of Aphra Behn by Sir Peter Lely (c. 1670) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Aphra Behn (1640–1689) was among the first Englishwomen to earn a living by her pen. Little is certain about her early life; she is said to have spent time in Surinam, and in 1666 she was sent to Antwerp as a spy for Charles II, writing under the code name Astrea. Back in London she turned to the stage, and from The Forc’d Marriage (1670) to The Rover (1677) and beyond she became one of the most successful playwrights of the Restoration, later adding prose fiction such as Oroonoko (1688). She was buried in the cloisters of Westminster Abbey.

Her verse was published in Poems upon Several Occasions (1684) and in A Miscellany (1685), and further pieces appeared after her death. It ranges from songs written for her plays, Pindaric odes and pastoral dialogues to satires, epistles to friends and patrons, and elegies for Rochester and Waller. This selection takes her own short and occasional poems from the sixth volume of Montague Summers’s edition (1915); her translations from Tallemant, A Voyage to the Isle of Love and Lycidus, are left out.

poets.name: Köroğlu
bio: Köroğlu (Kurroglou in older English spellings) is the legendary bandit-poet of Turkish and Turkic folklore. He robbed the caravans on the road between Persia and the Ottoman lands, and is remembered above all for the improvised songs he is said to have sung. He is the hero of a large cycle of tales and songs carried by wandering minstrels among the Turkic peoples of Anatolia, Azerbaijan and Central Asia.

The cycle is traditional, and its authorship is not known: no single author can be named, and the songs were passed on orally and changed with each telling. The English version used here is from Alexander Chodzko's Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842), which places the hero in northern Khorasan in the second half of the seventeenth century. Chodzko's versions are set within his prose narrative, so the songs are given as paragraphs rather than as verse lines.

poets.name: Benjamin Keach
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Benjamin Keach, 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Benjamin Keach (1640–1704) was an English Baptist preacher, born at Stoke Hammond in Buckinghamshire. He was imprisoned and put in the pillory in 1664 for his children's primer 'The Child's Instructor', and from 1668 he served as pastor of a Baptist congregation in Southwark, London, which later met at Horsleydown.

Keach wrote prolifically in prose and verse. 'Spiritual Melody, containing near three hundred sacred hymns' (1691) was among the first collections of hymns written for congregational singing in English Baptist worship, a move that was controversial in his own day. The hymns, plain in diction and built on scriptural images, are set out in nine parts.

poets.name: John Mason
bio: John Mason (1646?–1694) was an English clergyman, rector of Water Stratford in Buckinghamshire. He is remembered for his Spiritual Songs, first published in 1683, which were among the first English hymns written for congregational singing.

The collection pairs thirty-three Songs of Praise (thirty are given here, three being too damaged in the source) on the great occasions of Christian life with a verse rendering and a paraphrase of the Song of Songs, which Mason reads as a dialogue between Christ and his Church. The text here is the sixth edition of 1699, five years after his death.

poets.name: John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester
poets.credit: Portrait of John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester, attributed to Peter Lely (17th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Wilmot, second Earl of Rochester (1647–1680), was an English courtier and poet at the court of Charles II, and the most celebrated of the Restoration 'Court Wits'. Famed for his libertine life, he wrote satires, songs, lyrics and verse epistles, and died at thirty-three.
Texts and attributions follow The Works of the Right Honourable John, Earl of Rochester (London, 1718); some pieces in that collection are of disputed authorship.

poets.name: Jane Barker
bio: Jane Barker (1652–1732) was an English poet and novelist, born at Blatherwycke in Northamptonshire and later associated with Wilsthorpe in Lincolnshire. She was a Catholic and a Jacobite, and followed the exiled James II to the court at Saint-Germain in France after 1688, returning to England in the early eighteenth century.

Her first printed verse appeared as Part I of Poetical Recreations (1688), a miscellany of epistles, songs, odes and elegies, several of them addressed to friends and to her brother, with a second part by other hands. She later published further poems and the prose fictions Love Intrigues (1713), Exilius (1715) and A Patch-Work Screen for the Ladies (1723).

poets.name: John Oldham
poets.credit: Portrait of John Oldham, engraved (after William Dobson?) by Scheneker, in The Biographical Mirrour (1795) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Oldham (1653–1683) was an English satirist, the son of a Nonconformist minister in Gloucestershire. After St Edmund Hall, Oxford, he worked as an usher (assistant schoolmaster) at a school in Croydon. His Satyrs upon the Jesuits (1681), written in the vein of Juvenal, made his name, and he followed it with imitations and paraphrases of Latin and French poets, among them Juvenal, Horace, Boileau, Catullus and Anacreon.

The 1683 volume from which these poems are taken, Poems, and Translations, is anonymous on its title page (‘by the author of the Satyrs upon the Jesuits’); the author is identified as John Oldham by the TCP/ESTC catalogue record. He died of smallpox at the age of thirty. Dryden, who admired his work, wrote the elegy ‘To the Memory of Mr. Oldham’, and the archive also holds Gould’s elegy on him.

poets.name: Robert Gould
bio: Robert Gould (died about 1709) was an English poet and satirist of the Restoration. Little is securely known of his early life; he is generally said to have risen from domestic service in a noble household, and to have won the patronage of the Earl of Dorset and other grandees, several of whom he addresses in his verse.

He made his name with Love Given O'er (1682), a savage satire on women that provoked printed replies, followed by The Play-House (1685) and A Satyr upon Man. His collected Poems, chiefly consisting of Satyrs and Satyrical Epistles (1689) joined these to love songs, verse letters, funeral elegies and pindarick odes. He also wrote plays, and a posthumous Works appeared in 1709.

poets.name: Thomas D'Urfey
poets.credit: Thomas D'Urfey, engraving by Edward Gouge, c. 1819 (National Portrait Gallery, London) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas D'Urfey (1653-1723) was an English songwriter, poet and playwright, born in Exeter of Huguenot descent. He came to London to study law but turned to the stage and wrote some thirty plays, among them Madam Fickle (1676) and The Comical History of Don Quixote (1694-96). He was a familiar figure at the courts of Charles II, James II, William III and Anne, and was known above all as a writer and singer of comic and bawdy songs.

New Poems, consisting of Satyrs, Elegies and Odes, together with a Choice Collection of the Newest Court Songs (1690), from which this selection is drawn, mixes verse satires, prologues and epilogues, epithalamia and elegies with songs, several of them set by Henry Purcell and John Blow. D'Urfey later gathered songs, his own and others', into Wit and Mirth: or Pills to Purge Melancholy (1698-1720), the best-known song collection of its age.

poets.name: Sir Richard Blackmore
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Richard Blackmore (engraving, artist unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Richard Blackmore (1654–1729) was an English physician and poet. He practised medicine in London, became a Fellow of the College of Physicians, and served as physician in ordinary to William III, who knighted him in 1697. He is best known for his heavily moralising epics Prince Arthur (1695) and King Arthur (1697), and for the philosophical poem Creation (1712).

His verse was a favourite target of Dryden and Pope, and he became a byword for dull ambition in the satirical tradition. The poems here come from A Paraphrase on the Book of Job (1700), which turns the chapters of Job, with the songs of Moses and Deborah, David's lament for Saul and Jonathan, four psalms, five chapters of Isaiah and the third chapter of Habakkuk, into rhymed English verse. The text follows the 1700 printing, with its original spelling.

poets.name: John Dennis
poets.credit: John Vandergucht, line engraving, 1734 (National Portrait Gallery, London) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Dennis (1657–1734) was an English critic and dramatist, educated at Harrow and Cambridge. He wrote tragedies and comedies and a body of critical prose, and became notorious as the longtime antagonist of Alexander Pope, who satirised him in print.

His Miscellanies in Verse and Prose (1693) is an early volume of his verse: a Pindaric ode on William III, occasional and amatory pieces, burlesque fables with their morals, and versions of Horace, Boileau and Juvenal.

poets.name: Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea
bio: Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea (1661–1720), née Kingsmill, was a maid of honour to Mary of Modena and married Heneage Finch in 1684. After the Revolution of 1688 the couple retired to the country, where she wrote most of her poems. She published Miscellany Poems, on Several Occasions in 1713 and often called herself Ardelia in her verse.

Her ‘Nocturnal Reverie’ was singled out by Wordsworth as a rare piece of fresh nature description in its century, and her ode ‘The Spleen’ is among the earliest English poems on melancholy as a condition. She also wrote fables, satires, songs and religious poems.

poets.name: Sir Samuel Garth
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Samuel Garth by Sir Godfrey Kneller (Kit-Cat Club series) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Samuel Garth (1661–1719) was an English physician and poet, a leading member of the Whig Kit-Cat Club and a friend of Addison, Pope and Dryden, whose funeral oration he delivered in 1700. He was knighted in 1714 on the accession of George I.

His mock-heroic poem The Dispensary (1699) satirised the 1690s quarrel between the College of Physicians, who backed a free dispensary for the poor, and the apothecaries who opposed it, and became one of the most admired English burlesque epics of its day.

poets.name: Samuel Wesley
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: Maggots, or Poems on Several Subjects (1685), EEBO-TCP A65464 (CC0).
bio: Samuel Wesley (1662–1735) was an English clergyman and poet, born in Dorset and educated at Oxford. He became rector of Epworth in Lincolnshire in 1696 and held the living until his death. He is best remembered as the father of John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, and of the hymn-writer Charles Wesley.

Before his long career in the Church he published Maggots, or Poems on Several Subjects (1685), a book of comic verse written in his youth. Its mock-heroic and burlesque poems on trifling subjects, a hog's grunting, a cheese, a tobacco pipe, a louse, are the playful side of a man later known for pious and learned writing.

poets.name: Matthew Prior
bio: Matthew Prior (1664–1721) was the son of a joiner, educated at Westminster School and Cambridge, and made his career as a diplomat. He served as secretary to the embassy at The Hague and in Paris, and took part in the negotiations that led to the Treaty of Utrecht, and was imprisoned for a time after the Whig ministry came to power in 1715.

As a poet he was admired for his light, polished verse: songs and epigrams addressed to Cloe, tales and fables, and longer poems such as Alma and Solomon. His Poems on Several Occasions was published by subscription in 1718.

poets.name: Alexander Brome
poets.credit: No portrait available · monogram tile
bio: Alexander Brome (1620 – 30 June 1666) was an English poet and attorney, a staunch Royalist who made his name with satirical ballads, drinking songs and love lyrics written during the Civil War and the Interregnum, many of which circulated in manuscript and print against the Parliamentary cause.

Songs and Other Poems appeared in 1661 and in an enlarged second edition in 1664, the text used here. It gathers his songs, ballads, verse epistles to friends, and a section of epigrams translated from the classical tradition, together with pieces on the Restoration of Charles II in 1660.

poets.name: Jonathan Swift
poets.credit: Portrait of Jonathan Swift by Charles Jervas, c. 1718 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jonathan Swift (1667–1745), Dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin, is remembered above all for his prose satires, but his verse — plain-spoken, often savage, sometimes tender — was equally his own invention.

Poems like A Description of a City Shower and The Lady’s Dressing-Room turned unflinching, unglamorous observation into satire, while Cadenus and Vanessa and the Stella poems show a gentler, more private side of a famously guarded man.

poets.name: Colley Cibber
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Colley Cibber was an English actor-manager and playwright who became Poet Laureate in 1730. His stage comedies and his autobiography, An Apology for the Life of Mr. Colley Cibber, are better known than his verse.
Palgrave includes his song "The Blind Boy".

poets.name: Nedim
bio: Ahmed Nedim was one of the most celebrated Ottoman poets of the early 18th century, the age later called the Tulip Era, a period of peace, luxury and garden-pavilion culture in Istanbul. He wrote the courtly ghazel and became librarian and boon-companion of the Grand Vezir Ibrahim Pasha.

He died in October 1730, when the palace was stormed in the uprising that overthrew Sultan Ahmed III. E. J. W. Gibb, whose History of Ottoman Poetry gives the first sustained English account of him, warned that Nedim's delicate verbal music could scarcely survive translation. The poems below are Gibb's renderings of ghazels from the fourth volume of that history.

poets.name: Charles Goodall
poets.credit: No known portrait · text from Poems and Translations (1689), EEBO-TCP A41430 (CC0)
bio: Charles Goodall (1671–1689) is known only through one posthumous-looking book, Poems and Translations, Written upon Several Occasions, and to Several Persons (1689), whose title page says merely that it is "by a late Scholar of Eaton". The attribution to Goodall, and his dates of 1671 to 1689, come from the catalogue record of the EEBO-TCP transcription, not from the printed book; on those dates he died at about eighteen.

The volume carries a prose dedication to the Countess of Clarendon and a verse dedication to Mr. Roderick, Upper-Master of Eaton-School. Its contents are schoolboy and undergraduate-age verse: love poems and epigrams to a Hemiera and an Idera, verse letters to friends and to his brother, an elegy on Oldham, and versions of Anacreon, Bion, Theocritus, Catullus, Ovid, Seneca and Juvenal, with Greek epigrams in English. The spelling of the 1689 print is kept here.

poets.name: Ambrose Philips
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ambrose Philips was an English poet best known for his Pastorals (1709). Henry Carey gave his light verses to children the nickname "namby-pamby".
Palgrave includes his lines "To Charlotte Pulteney".

poets.name: Isaac Watts
poets.credit: Portrait of Isaac Watts, from the National Portrait Gallery, London (c. 1727) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Isaac Watts (1674–1748), born in Southampton, was an English Congregationalist minister, theologian and hymn-writer, often called the father of English hymnody. The son of a Nonconformist who was imprisoned for his beliefs, he was educated at the Dissenting academy in Stoke Newington and from 1702 served as pastor of the Independent congregation at Mark Lane, London. Poor health limited his preaching, and from 1712 he lived under the protection of the Abney family at Theobalds and Stoke Newington.

His Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707–09) broke with the English habit of singing only metrical psalms, and The Psalms of David Imitated in the Language of the New Testament (1719) recast the Psalter for Christian worship; it gave English-speaking churches such hymns as “O God, Our Help in Ages Past” and “Joy to the World.” His Divine Songs Attempted in Easy Language for the Use of Children (1715) became one of the most widely read children’s books of the eighteenth century, and a famous parody of its “How doth the little busy bee” appears in Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.

poets.name: George Sewell
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Sewell was an English physician and miscellaneous writer who died in 1726.
Palgrave includes his poem "The Dying Man in His Garden".

poets.name: John Hopkins
poets.credit: No portrait is known; none sourced for this archive.
bio: John Hopkins (fl. 1700) was an English poet of the turn of the eighteenth century, remembered for a single large work, Amasia, or, The Works of the Muses, published in London in 1700 in three volumes. Little is recorded of his life, and the catalogue gives only a floruit.

Amasia gathers love poems and verse epistles addressed to a lady under that name, together with occasional pieces, Ovidian tales in the manner of the day, and poems to friends. He should not be confused with John Hopkins, the sixteenth-century psalmist, or with Gerard Manley Hopkins.

poets.name: Thomas Parnell
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Thomas Parnell, artist unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Parnell (1679–1718) was an Anglo-Irish poet and clergyman, born in Dublin and educated at Trinity College, who became Archdeacon of Clogher in 1706. He was a friend of Swift, Pope, Gay and Arbuthnot, took part in the Scriblerus Club, and wrote the essay on Homer prefixed to Pope's Iliad.

He died at Chester in 1718, on a journey to Ireland. Pope edited his Poems on Several Occasions (1722). A Night-Piece on Death is often seen as an early forerunner of Gray's Elegy, and The Hermit, a moral tale in couplets, was widely reprinted through the eighteenth century.

poets.name: Edward Young
bio: Edward Young (1683–1765) was born in Hampshire and educated at Oxford, where he became a fellow of All Souls. He made his name with a poem on the Last Judgment, a series of satires called The Love of Fame, and some tragedies, and took holy orders in middle age, becoming rector of Welwyn in Hertfordshire in 1730.

His blank-verse The Complaint, or Night Thoughts (1742–1745), a long meditation in nine Nights on life, death and immortality, was one of the most widely read poems in Europe in the later eighteenth century. William Blake made a famous series of designs for it.

poets.name: John Gay
bio: John Gay (1685–1732) was an English poet and dramatist, born in Barnstaple, Devon. A friend of Pope, Swift and Arbuthnot, he wrote Trivia, a mock-georgic on walking the streets of London, and The Beggar’s Opera (1728), a ballad opera that was a great popular success.

His Fables, published in two series in 1727 and 1738, are short verse stories in which animals speak and act as foils to human folly. They were widely read for generations and are the part of his verse that still has readers.

poets.name: Henry Carey
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry Carey was an English poet, songwriter and musician who wrote the words and often the music of popular ballads and stage pieces. He died in 1743.
His best-known song is "Sally in Our Alley", which Palgrave includes.

poets.name: Alexander Pope
poets.credit: Portrait of Alexander Pope by Michael Dahl, c. 1727 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alexander Pope (1688–1744) was the foremost English poet of the early 18th century, master of the heroic couplet and the sharpest satirist of his age.

Barred by his Catholicism and ill health from university or public office, he made a career (and a fortune) from his verse and his acclaimed translation of Homer; The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Man remain his best-loved works.

poets.name: Richard Savage
bio: Richard Savage (1697/8–1743) was an English poet and satirist whose year of birth is contested: he himself claimed to be the illegitimate son of the Countess of Macclesfield and Earl Rivers, and the dates given for his birth vary, so 1697 or 1698 is only an approximation. He lived by his pen and by patrons, was condemned to death for a tavern killing in 1727 and pardoned, and died in Bristol's Newgate debtors' prison in 1743.

The Wanderer (1729), dedicated to Lord Tyrconnel, is his best-known poem, a visionary meditation in five cantos in heroic couplets that sets the still life against the active. His friend Samuel Johnson told his story in the Life of Mr Richard Savage (1744), which shaped his later reputation and from which much of what is told about his origins derives.

poets.name: Robert Blair
bio: Robert Blair (1699–1746) was a Scottish minister and poet, born in Edinburgh and for many years parish minister of Athelstaneford in East Lothian. He wrote little verse that survives.

His blank-verse poem The Grave (1743) is a gloomy meditation on death and the churchyard in the manner of the so-called graveyard poets, and was often reprinted, notably with William Blake’s designs in 1808.

poets.name: James Thomson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Thomson was a Scottish poet who made his name with The Seasons (1726-30), a landmark of eighteenth-century nature poetry.
Palgrave includes "Rule Britannia", written for the masque Alfred, and a short love song.

poets.name: Stephen Duck
bio: Stephen Duck (1705–1756) was an English poet, born in Wiltshire and working as an agricultural labourer when he began to write verse. His poem The Thresher's Labour, which describes the farm worker's year of toil, became known beyond his village and brought him to the notice of Queen Caroline, who gave him a pension and a place at court.

He later took holy orders and served as a clergyman and as keeper of the Queen's library at Richmond. Poems on Several Occasions (1736), the collection drawn on here, gathers his verse, including The Thresher's Labour, longer narrative poems such as Avaro and Amanda, and imitations of Horace.

poets.name: Philip Doddridge
poets.credit: Engraving by George Vertue, 1751 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Philip Doddridge (1702-1751) was an English Nonconformist minister, teacher and writer. Born in London, he became pastor of the Independent congregation at Northampton in 1729 and ran an academy there for training ministers. His best-known prose works include The Family Expositor and The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul.

He wrote many hymns, usually composed to accompany the conclusion of his Sunday sermons, and they circulated in manuscript and in print among Dissenting congregations. The present collection of 370 hymns was published after his death in 1755 from his manuscript by his friend Job Orton. Several of its hymns, such as O God of Bethel, by whose hand, remained in common use.

poets.name: Mather Byles
poets.credit: Mezzotint of Mather Byles by Peter Pelham (18th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mather Byles (1707–1788) was a Congregational minister in Boston and the best-known American poet of his generation. A nephew of Cotton Mather, he corresponded with Alexander Pope and others in England, and his Poems on Several Occasions was published in Boston in 1744.
Celebrated in Boston for his wit and his punning, he served the Hollis Street Church for decades. He remained loyal to the Crown during the Revolution and was dismissed from his pulpit in 1776.

poets.name: Samuel Johnson
poets.credit: Portrait of Samuel Johnson by Sir Joshua Reynolds, c. 1772 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Johnson (1709–1784) — lexicographer, essayist, critic, and the dominant literary figure of mid-18th-century England — also wrote poetry of severe, weighty moral force.
London and The Vanity of Human Wishes, both close imitations of Juvenal’s satires, and his plain elegy for his friend Robert Levet, show the same unflinching realism that marks his prose.

poets.name: George Alexander Stevens
poets.credit: George Alexander Stevens (with Mrs Paul Sandby), by Paul Sandby · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Alexander Stevens (1710–1784) was an English actor, dramatist and songwriter, born in London. After years as a strolling player he made his name on the London stage and, above all, as a solo entertainer: his comic monologue 'A Lecture upon Heads' (1764) was a long-running success in Britain and abroad.

His convivial and topical songs were performed at taverns, clubs and his own entertainments, and he gathered them in 'Songs, Comic and Satyrical' (1772). They mock fashion, politics, quackery and fashionable folly in the broad manner of the Augustan ballad, and many were set to popular tunes of the day.

poets.name: Mikhail Lomonosov
poets.credit: Portrait of Mikhail Lomonosov, engraving by L. Miropolsky (1787) after Georg Caspar Prenner · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mikhail Vasilyevich Lomonosov (1711–1765) was born near Kholmogory in the far north of Russia, the son of a fisherman. He studied in Moscow and in Germany, became a professor at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, took part in founding Moscow University (1755), and worked as both scientist and poet. He helped fix the rules of Russian versification and the literary language, and his solemn odes made him the leading Russian poet of the mid-eighteenth century.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: William Shenstone
poets.credit: Portrait of William Shenstone by Edward Alcock, 1760 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Shenstone (1714–1763) was an English poet and landscape gardener, born at Halesowen in Shropshire (now the West Midlands) and educated at Pembroke College, Oxford. He is remembered for The School-Mistress (1742), a gently comic imitation of Spenser, and for his Elegies, Odes, Songs and Ballads, which were widely admired in the middle of the eighteenth century.

From 1745 he lived on his family estate, The Leasowes, near Halesowen, which he laid out as a ferme ornee, a working farm shaped into a landscape of walks, cascades and inscriptions. Visitors came from across Britain to see it, and it helped shape the English taste for the picturesque garden. His Works in Verse and Prose appeared after his death, and the poems here follow the two-volume Poetical Works of 1778.

poets.name: Thomas Gray
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Gray by John Giles Eccardt, 1747-48 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Gray (1716–1771) was a reclusive Cambridge scholar who published only a handful of poems in his lifetime, yet his Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard became one of the most quoted poems in the English language.
His Pindaric odes The Progress of Poesy and The Bard helped carry English verse from Augustan restraint toward the Romantic sublime.

poets.name: Tobias Smollett
poets.credit: Portrait of Tobias Smollett by Nathaniel Dance-Holland, c. 1770 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Tobias Smollett (1721–1771) was a Scottish surgeon and writer, born at Dalquhurn in Dunbartonshire and trained in Glasgow. He served as a naval surgeon's mate, settled in London, and made his name with the picaresque novels Roderick Random (1748), Peregrine Pickle (1751) and Humphry Clinker (1771).

His verse is the smaller part of his work: the satires Advice and Reproof, The Tears of Scotland, written after Culloden in 1746, and the Ode to Independence, published after his death. He died near Livorno in Italy in 1771.

poets.name: Mark Akenside
bio: Mark Akenside (1721–1770) was born in Newcastle upon Tyne, the son of a butcher, and studied at Edinburgh and Leiden before practising as a physician in London. He was lame from a boyhood accident.

His blank-verse The Pleasures of Imagination (1744), a philosophical poem on the sources of aesthetic pleasure, made him famous when he was in his early twenties, and he later reworked it at length. His Odes and Hymn to the Naiads share its classical models and its enthusiasm for liberty.

poets.name: William Collins
bio: William Collins (1721–1759) was born in Chichester and educated at Winchester and Oxford. He went to London to live by his pen, and his small output of odes, published in 1746, made little stir at first but is now ranked among the finest lyric poetry of the century.

His odes to Evening, Fear and Simplicity, and ‘How sleep the brave,’ are often seen as turning eighteenth-century verse toward feeling and imagination. His mind failed in his later years and he died in Chichester at thirty-seven.

poets.name: Mary Leapor
poets.credit: Engraved frontispiece portrait of Mary Leapor, from Poems upon Several Occasions (1748) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Leapor (1722–1746) was an English poet, the daughter of a gardener at Marston St Lawrence, Northamptonshire, who worked as a kitchen-maid in the household at Weldon and later at Brackley, where she wrote verse in the margins of her duties. She taught herself to read and write, and modelled her heroic couplets on Pope, Dryden and Gay. She died of measles at the age of twenty-four, before her work could appear.

Her Poems upon Several Occasions was published by subscription in 1748, after her death, and a second volume followed in 1751. Her verse mixes satire on vanity and marriage, pastoral, fables, biblical paraphrase and sharp reflections on class and women's lot; the poems about 'Mira', such as 'Mira's Will', are generally read as self-portraits of the poet.

poets.name: Christopher Smart
bio: Christopher Smart (1722–1771) was born in Kent and educated at Cambridge, where he became a fellow of Pembroke Hall. He lived in London as a hack writer and was confined for mental illness between 1756 and 1763. He died in a debtors’ prison.

His A Song to David (1763) is the poem by which he is chiefly remembered; its ecstatic language was thought a sign of his madness and it was little read for a century. His Hymns for the Amusement of Children appeared in 1771, and Jubilate Agno, written in confinement, was not published until the twentieth century.

poets.name: Jane Elliot
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Jane Elliot was a Scottish poet of the eighteenth century, remembered for one famous lament.
Palgrave includes her "Lament for Flodden", a version of "The Flowers of the Forest".

poets.name: John Newton
poets.credit: After John Russell's portrait of John Newton (1788) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Newton (1725–1807) was an English clergyman and hymn-writer. The son of a merchant sea captain, he went to sea as a boy and later served on slave ships, including as a captain; after a near-fatal storm in 1748 he underwent a religious conversion, and he left the slave trade in 1754. He was ordained in the Church of England in 1764 and served as curate of Olney, Buckinghamshire, until 1780, then as rector of St Mary Woolnoth in London. In later life he spoke publicly against the slave trade and supported William Wilberforce's campaign for abolition.

At Olney he befriended the poet William Cowper, and together they compiled Olney Hymns (1779), in three books, for use in Newton's parish meetings. Newton wrote the great majority of the 348 hymns and Cowper 67 of them; Newton's include 'Amazing Grace' and 'Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken'. The Olney Hymns remained a staple of English-language evangelical worship.

poets.name: Oliver Goldsmith
poets.credit: Portrait of Oliver Goldsmith after Sir Joshua Reynolds · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oliver Goldsmith (1728–1774) was an Irish-born writer of extraordinary range — poet, playwright, and novelist — whose warmth and clarity made him one of the best-loved authors of his age.
The Deserted Village, his elegy for a vanishing rural England, and Retaliation, his affectionate mock-epitaphs on his own dinner-table friends, remain his most-read poems.

poets.name: William Cowper
poets.credit: Portrait of William Cowper by Lemuel Francis Abbott, 1792 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Cowper (1731–1800) wrote from a life shadowed by recurring breakdowns and religious despair, retired to the Buckinghamshire village of Olney under the care of friends.

His comic ballad John Gilpin made him briefly famous, but his lasting achievement is The Task, a long meditative poem on rural retirement, and the Olney Hymns he wrote with John Newton, including “God Moves in a Mysterious Way.”

poets.name: Vasily Petrov
bio: Vasily Petrovich Petrov (1736–1799), born in Moscow, was a court poet under Catherine II. He wrote ceremonial odes on Russian victories and translated Virgil’s Aeneid into Russian verse.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: William Julius Mickle
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Julius Mickle was a Scottish poet who translated the Lusiad of Camoens into English verse in 1775.
Palgrave includes "The Sailor's Wife", the song also known by the words "There's nae luck about the house".

poets.name: Robert Graham of Gartmore
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Graham of Gartmore was a Scottish landowner and politician who also wrote verse.
Palgrave signs his song "If doughty deeds my lady please" with the name Graham of Gartmore.

poets.name: Anna Seward
poets.credit: Portrait of Anna Seward by Tilly Kettle (1762) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anna Seward (1742–1809), born at Eyam in Derbyshire and raised in Lichfield, where her father was a canon of the cathedral, was known in her own day as the “Swan of Lichfield”. She was educated at home on progressive lines and became a prominent figure in the literary society of the Midlands, publishing an elegy on Captain Cook, a monody on Major André and the poetical novel Louisa (1784).

Her Original Sonnets on Various Subjects, and Odes Paraphrased from Horace appeared in 1799. The hundred sonnets, many in the Petrarchan and Miltonic manner and some of them nature poems or elegies, helped to revive the English sonnet in the years before Wordsworth, and the Horatian paraphrases freely expand their originals. Her letters were published posthumously in 1811.

poets.name: Ippolit Bogdanovich
bio: Ippolit Fyodorovich Bogdanovich (1743–1803), of Ukrainian origin, served as a state official and wrote light, graceful verse. His best-known work is Dushenka (1783), a free adaptation of La Fontaine’s tale of Psyche, which earned him Bowring’s title of “the Russian Anacreon”.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Anna Laetitia Barbauld
bio: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825), née Aikin, was born in Leicestershire, the daughter of a Dissenting minister and schoolmaster, and grew up at Warrington Academy. Her Poems (1773) went through several editions within a year, and she went on to write hymns, children’s books and essays and to teach at a school she ran with her husband.

Her later work includes the long political poem Eighteen Hundred and Eleven (1812), which looks forward to the decline of Britain and the rise of America. She was a friend of Joseph Priestley and a figure in the Dissenting and literary circles of her day.

poets.name: Gavrila Derzhavin
poets.credit: Portrait of Gavrila Derzhavin by Vladimir Borovikovsky (1811) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gavrila Romanovich Derzhavin (1743–1816), born near Kazan, served as a soldier and then as a state official: secretary to Catherine II, governor of provinces, and later Minister of Justice. His odes “Felitsa” (1782) and “God” (1784) brought him fame, and he is usually counted the greatest Russian poet before Pushkin. “God” was translated into many languages, and Bowring’s version of it is among the best known in English.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Ivan Khemnitser
bio: Ivan Ivanovich Khemnitser (1745–1784), of German descent, was a mining engineer and later a Russian consul in Smyrna, where he died. He is remembered for his fables, first published in 1779, whose plain, humorous style set an example for Krylov.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: John Logan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Logan was a Scottish minister and poet. He published a volume of poems in 1781.
Palgrave gives him "The Braes of Yarrow", a poem whose authorship has been disputed.

poets.name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
poets.credit: Portrait of Goethe by Joseph Karl Stieler (1828) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832) was born in Frankfurt am Main and studied law before the success of his novel The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774) made him famous across Europe. In 1775 he moved to Weimar at the invitation of Duke Karl August, where he served as a minister of state and director of the court theatre, and from 1794 he was the close friend and collaborator of Friedrich Schiller.

Best known for the drama Faust, he wrote lyrics, ballads, odes, elegies and epigrams throughout his life, from the early songs and the Roman Elegies and Venetian Epigrams of his Italian years to the West-Eastern Divan (1819), inspired by the Persian poet Hafiz. The English versions here are from Edgar Alfred Bowring’s 1853 The Poems of Goethe, translated in the original metres; it is a selection from his shorter verse.

poets.name: Charlotte Smith
poets.credit: Portrait of Charlotte Smith by George Romney (1792) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charlotte Smith (1749–1806) was an English poet and novelist, born Charlotte Turner and raised in Sussex and Surrey. Married young to a spendthrift husband who was imprisoned for debt in 1783, she turned to writing to support her many children.

Her Elegiac Sonnets (1784), expanded through many editions, is often credited with reviving the English sonnet as a form for personal feeling, and its melancholy landscapes of the Sussex downs and coast lie behind much Romantic poetry. She was also a successful novelist, and her long blank-verse poem Beachy Head appeared after her death in 1807.

poets.name: Lady Anne Lindsay
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Lady Anne Lindsay, later Lady Anne Barnard, was a Scottish writer. She wrote the ballad "Auld Robin Gray" in 1771.
Palgrave includes "Auld Robin Gray", her best-known poem.

poets.name: Phillis Wheatley
bio: Phillis Wheatley (c. 1753–1784) was born in West Africa, kidnapped and brought to Boston as a child in 1761, and purchased by the merchant John Wheatley. Taught to read and write in his household, she began publishing verse as a teenager.

Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773) was the first book of poems published by an African American. A group of Boston notables attested in its front matter that she had written the poems; she was freed shortly after the book appeared.

poets.name: John Philpot Curran
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Philpot Curran was an Irish barrister, orator and politician, born in Newmarket, County Cork. He defended many of the United Irishmen and served as Master of the Rolls in Ireland from 1806 to 1814.
His best-known song, "The Deserter's Meditation", is included in W. B. Yeats's A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: John Trumbull
poets.credit: Portrait of the poet by his cousin, the painter John Trumbull, 1793 (Detroit Institute of Arts) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Trumbull (1750–1831) was an American poet and lawyer, born in Watertown, Connecticut. He entered Yale as a child prodigy, later became a tutor there, and was a leading member of the Connecticut Wits. He trained in law under John Adams and practised in Hartford, serving also as a state judge.

His best-known work, M'Fingal (first part 1775, complete 1782), is a Hudibrastic mock-epic satirising a Tory squire in revolutionary Massachusetts. It was among the most widely read American poems of its age and went through dozens of editions.

poets.name: Richard Brinsley Sheridan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Brinsley Sheridan was born in Dublin and became one of the leading English-language dramatists of his century, the author of The Rivals and The School for Scandal. He was also manager of the Drury Lane Theatre and a Whig Member of Parliament.
The song "Thou canst not boast" is included in W. B. Yeats's A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Thomas Chatterton
bio: Thomas Chatterton (1752–1770) was born in Bristol, the posthumous son of a schoolmaster and church official, and was writing remarkable verse before he was in his teens. He invented a fifteenth-century Bristol priest named Thomas Rowley and wrote a body of poems in an imitation medieval English, passing them off as Rowley's recovered manuscripts.

He went to London in 1770 hoping to live by his pen and died there in August of that year, aged seventeen. The question whether the Rowley poems were genuine was argued for decades, but they are now known to be his own. Wordsworth called him ‘the marvellous Boy,’ and Keats dedicated Endymion to his memory.

poets.name: Yury Neledinsky-Meletsky
bio: Yury Aleksandrovich Neledinsky-Meletsky (1752–1828) was a court official who served under Catherine II and Paul I. He is remembered for songs written in the manner of Russian folk lyrics, many of which were set to music and sung widely.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Philip Freneau
poets.credit: Engraving of Philip Freneau by Frederick Halpin (1901) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Philip Freneau (1752–1832) was an American poet and journalist, born in New York City. He studied at Princeton alongside James Madison and became known as the “Poet of the American Revolution” for his satires on the British and his patriotic verse.
He later edited the National Gazette in Philadelphia. His nature lyrics, such as “The Wild Honey Suckle” (1786), are often seen as early signs of Romanticism in American poetry.

poets.name: George Crabbe
bio: George Crabbe (1754–1832) was born at Aldeburgh on the Suffolk coast, trained as a surgeon and apothecary, and went to London in 1780 to try his fortune as a poet. Edmund Burke took him up, and he afterward became a clergyman. The Village (1783), which Samuel Johnson read in manuscript, set out to show the real life of the rural poor against the conventions of pastoral.

His later narrative poems, The Parish Register, The Borough and the Tales, tell the lives of ordinary people in plain, exact couplets and were widely read in his day. Peter Grimes, from The Borough, is the source of Benjamin Britten’s opera.

poets.name: Yermil Kostrov
