bio: Yermil Ivanovich Kostrov (1755–1796) studied at Moscow University and made a name as a translator. He rendered part of Homer’s Iliad into Russian verse and worked on a version of Ossian, which, as Bowring notes, was completed after his early death by Gnedich.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: William Blake
poets.credit: Portrait by Thomas Phillips (1807) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Blake (1757–1827) was an English poet, painter, and printmaker, largely unrecognised in his lifetime and now seen as a seminal figure of the Romantic age.
He engraved and hand-coloured his own illuminated books, most famously Songs of Innocence and of Experience, where word and image are inseparable.

poets.name: Mikhail Muravyov
bio: Mikhail Nikitich Muravyov (1757–1807) was a poet and teacher who served as tutor to the future Alexander I and later as a curator of Moscow University. His gentle, personal verse looked forward to the sentimental school of Karamzin and Zhukovsky.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Vasily Kapnist
bio: Vasily Vasilyevich Kapnist (1758–1823), of Greek-Ukrainian family, wrote odes, songs and the satirical comedy Chicane (1798). Bowring notes that he wrote “on a variety of subjects”.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Robert Burns
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Burns by Alexander Nasmyth, 1787 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Burns (1759–1796), Scotland’s national poet, turned the everyday life and speech of Ayrshire farming folk into poetry of remarkable warmth, wit, and force.

Writing in Scots and English by turns, he ranged from the comic terror of Tam O’ Shanter to the tenderness of A Red, Red Rose and the satire of Holy Willie’s Prayer; his spelling is kept exactly as printed here.

poets.name: Ivan Dmitriev
bio: Ivan Ivanovich Dmitriev (1760–1837), born in the Simbirsk province, was a poet of the sentimental school and a close friend of Karamzin. He is best known for his songs and fables, and later served as Minister of Justice (1810–1814).

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Semyon Bobrov
bio: Semyon Sergeyevich Bobrov (c. 1763–1810) was a poet and official. His long poem Khersonida (1804), set in the Crimea, is the source of the three pieces given here; Bowring calls it “an oriental epic poem”. His writing is known for its obscure, ornate style.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: James Nugent Reynolds
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Nugent Reynolds was an Irish writer who died in 1802. He is remembered chiefly as the author of the ballad "Kathleen O'More".
Yeats includes the ballad in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Ivan Dolgorukov
bio: Prince Ivan Mikhailovich Dolgorukov (1764–1823) was a courtier, poet and memoirist. Bowring includes his poem “The Legacy” in the second part of the Specimens.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Şeyh Galip
bio: Mehmed Esad, known as Şeyh Galip or Galib Dede (1757–1799), was a Mevlevi dervish and sheikh of the Galata convent in Istanbul, and one of the foremost poets of the late Ottoman Romantic school. Sultan Selim III conferred on him the office of sheikh.

His masterpiece is the mystical romance Husn ü Aşk ('Beauty and Love'), from which two passages are given here. E. J. W. Gibb, who gave the first English account of his diwan, praised the strong and glowing verse of his lyric poems.

poets.name: Mary Lamb
poets.credit: Unknown artist, c. 1847 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Lamb was an English writer and the elder sister of Charles Lamb. Her prose and verse appeared mostly in collaboration with her brother, notably the children's books Tales from Shakespeare (1807) and Mrs. Leicester's School (1809).

After a family tragedy in 1796 she lived for long periods in the care of her brother, who looked after her for the rest of his life. Her own verse, mostly occasional pieces, was printed alongside his in the Works of Charles Lamb.

poets.name: Nikolay Karamzin
poets.credit: Portrait of Nikolay Karamzin by Vasily Tropinin (1818) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nikolay Mikhailovich Karamzin (1766–1826), born near Simbirsk, was the leading figure of Russian sentimentalism. His Letters of a Russian Traveller (1791–92) and the tale Poor Liza (1792) set a new, polished prose style, and his History of the Russian State (begun 1803, published from 1818) made him a national writer. Bowring called him “the most successful and the most popular” of Russia’s living writers.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Samuel Rogers
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Samuel Rogers was an English banker and poet whose The Pleasures of Memory (1792) made his name. He was a well-known host and patron in London literary society.
Palgrave includes two of his short poems.

poets.name: Grigory Khovansky
bio: Grigory Khovansky (1767–1796) was a minor Russian poet of the late eighteenth century who died young. Bowring prints one of his songs in the second part of the Specimens.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Nikolay Shatrov
bio: Nikolay Ivanovich Shatrov (1767–1841) was a Russian poet who wrote patriotic odes. Bowring prints his ode “To the Army of the Don”, written during the war with Napoleon. Bowring’s volumes give no separate notice of his life, so the dates are those supplied by the archive’s editor.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Ivan Krylov
poets.credit: Portrait of Ivan Krylov by Karl Bryullov (1839) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ivan Andreyevich Krylov (1769–1844) began as a satirical journalist and playwright. He turned to fables in 1809, many adapted from La Fontaine and Aesop, and became Russia’s best-loved fabulist; from 1812 he worked at the Imperial Public Library in St Petersburg. Bowring printed two of his fables in the first part.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Carolina Nairne
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Carolina Nairne, Lady Nairne, was a Scottish songwriter who adapted and wrote songs in the Scots tradition, often anonymously.
Palgrave includes her song "The Land o' the Leal".

poets.name: Richard Alfred Milliken
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Alfred Milliken was an Irish lawyer and humorous writer from County Cork. He is remembered for the burlesque song "The Groves of Blarney", written in the 1790s.
Yeats includes the song in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: William Wordsworth
poets.credit: ‘Wordsworth on Helvellyn’ by Benjamin Robert Haydon (1842) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) was an English Romantic poet who, with Coleridge, launched the movement in Lyrical Ballads (1798).
He made ordinary life and the natural world his subject, and served as Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death.

poets.name: William Charles Wentworth
bio: William Charles Wentworth (1790–1872) was an Australian explorer, barrister, newspaper proprietor and statesman, one of the three who first crossed the Blue Mountains in 1813.
While a student at Cambridge he wrote the poem Australasia (1823) for the Chancellor's medal, where it came second to Winthrop Mackworth Praed's entry; Stevens's anthology prints its opening lines.

poets.name: Sir Walter Scott
bio: Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832) was a Scottish poet and novelist whose verse romances — The Lay of the Last Minstrel, Marmion, The Lady of the Lake — made him the best-selling poet in Europe before Byron eclipsed him, and whose Waverley novels effectively invented the historical novel.

Trained as a lawyer in Edinburgh, Scott drew on a lifelong passion for Scottish Border ballads and Highland history; a private financial ruin late in life led him to write at a furious pace to pay off his debts, at the cost of his health.

poets.name: James Montgomery
poets.credit: Portrait of James Montgomery, early 19th century engraving · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Montgomery (1771–1854) was born in Irvine, Ayrshire, the son of a Moravian minister, and was educated at the Moravian school at Fulneck in Yorkshire. He settled in Sheffield, where he edited the Sheffield Iris newspaper, was twice imprisoned for political publications, and wrote on humanitarian causes including the abolition of the slave trade and the plight of child chimney sweeps.

He published long poems such as The Wanderer of Switzerland and The World before the Flood, but is remembered chiefly as one of the foremost English hymn writers; ‘Hail to the Lord’s Anointed’ and ‘Angels from the realms of glory’ remain widely sung. This selection is drawn from Sacred Poems and Hymns, for Public and Private Devotion (1854), with the author’s latest corrections.

poets.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
poets.credit: Portrait of Coleridge at age 42 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) was an English poet, critic, and philosopher, co-founder of the Romantic movement.
His visionary poems ‘The Rime of the Ancient Mariner’ and ‘Kubla Khan’ remain touchstones of the imagination he spent his life theorising.

poets.name: Robert Southey
poets.credit: Peter Vandyke, 1795 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Southey (1774–1843) was an English poet and man of letters, Poet Laureate from 1813 until his death, and one of the “Lake Poets” alongside his friends Wordsworth and Coleridge (whose sister-in-law he married).

He was, in his own day, best known for his grim and often macabre ballads of guilt, folklore and the supernatural, and for prose-poem “Eclogues” that gave a plain, compassionate voice to the rural poor — work that has aged rather better than the long epics on which he staked his reputation.

poets.name: John Leyden
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of John Leyden · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Leyden (1775–1811) was a Scottish poet, physician and orientalist, born at Denholm in Roxburghshire, the son of a shepherd. He studied at Edinburgh, became a friend and helper of Walter Scott, and supplied him with ballad material and original ballads for the Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border.

His own poems include Scenes of Infancy (1803). He went to India as an assistant surgeon in 1803, held posts in Mysore and Calcutta, studied Indian languages, and died of fever at Batavia in Java in 1811.

poets.name: Matthew Gregory Lewis
poets.credit: Portrait of Matthew Gregory Lewis by George Lethbridge Saunders, after an unknown artist · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Matthew Gregory Lewis (1775–1818), known as “Monk” Lewis, was an English novelist, playwright and poet, born in London. His Gothic novel The Monk (1796) made him famous, and he wrote plays and the ballad collections Tales of Wonder and Tales of Terror.
He was an early friend of Walter Scott, to whose Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border he contributed a ballad, and he died of yellow fever at sea in 1818 on a voyage home from his Jamaican estates.

poets.name: Matthew Arnold
poets.credit: Portrait of Matthew Arnold · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Matthew Arnold (1822–1888) was an English poet and cultural critic, Professor of Poetry at Oxford.
His poems — among them ‘Dover Beach’ and ‘The Scholar-Gipsy’ — register the anxious loss of religious certainty at the heart of the Victorian age.

poets.name: Walter Savage Landor
bio: Walter Savage Landor (1775–1864) was an English writer best known for Imaginary Conversations, a vast series of prose dialogues between historical figures, and for a small body of exquisitely polished short poems and epigrams that later poets — Swinburne, Pound, and others — prized above almost anything else of his era for their classical restraint.

Quarrelsome and litigious by temperament (he was expelled from Oxford and later drove himself into exile in Italy more than once), Landor lived to eighty-nine, still writing crisp, controlled verse almost to the end — including his own epitaph-poem, ‘I strove with none.’

poets.name: Charles Lamb
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charles Lamb was an English essayist and critic, famous for the Essays of Elia, and a close friend of Samuel Taylor Coleridge. He also wrote a small body of verse.
Palgrave includes several of his short poems, among them "The Old Familiar Faces".

poets.name: Thomas Campbell
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Campbell by Sir Thomas Lawrence · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Campbell (1777–1844) was a Scottish poet, born in Glasgow, the youngest of eleven children. He made his name at twenty-one with The Pleasures of Hope (1799), a didactic poem on hope, liberty and the wrongs of Poland and Africa, and followed it with the Pennsylvania tale Gertrude of Wyoming (1809).

He is best remembered for his patriotic and martial lyrics — ‘Ye Mariners of England’, ‘The Battle of the Baltic’, ‘Hohenlinden’ — and for the ballads ‘Lord Ullin’s Daughter’ and ‘Lochiel’s Warning’. He was also an early promoter of University College London and served as Lord Rector of Glasgow University; he died at Boulogne and is buried in Westminster Abbey.

poets.name: Alexey Merzlyakov
bio: Alexey Fyodorovich Merzlyakov (1778–1830) was a poet and critic and professor of rhetoric at Moscow University. His songs written in the folk manner were widely sung in Russia. Bowring prints his version of Isaiah’s oracle on the fall of Babylon and a pastoral “Duett”.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Thomas Moore
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Moore by Sir Thomas Lawrence (Trinity College, Cambridge; date not given on Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Moore (1779–1852) was Ireland's national poet in the Romantic era, celebrated above all for the Irish Melodies (issued in installments from 1808 to 1834), verses written to fit traditional Irish airs, which carried Irish nationalist feeling and folklore to drawing rooms across Britain and America.

A close friend of Byron (whose memoirs he controversially burned after the poet's death) and a fixture of literary London, Moore was also the author of the wildly popular Oriental verse-romance Lalla Rookh, though it is the Melodies — "The Minstrel Boy," "The Last Rose of Summer," "Believe Me, if All Those Endearing Young Charms" — that have lasted.

poets.name: Adam Oehlenschläger
poets.credit: Portrait of Adam Oehlenschläger by Christian Albrecht Jensen, 1825 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Adam Oehlenschläger (1779–1850) was a Danish poet and dramatist, born in Copenhagen. His poem "The Golden Horns" (1802) and the collection Poems of 1803 opened the Romantic movement in Danish literature, and he went on to write verse tragedies such as Hakon Jarl and Axel and Valborg, and the oriental drama Aladdin. In 1810 he became professor of aesthetics at the University of Copenhagen, and in 1829 the Swedish poet Esaias Tegnér crowned him in Lund cathedral as the laureate of the North.

Much of his work draws on Norse myth and saga. Nordens Guder (1819) is a cycle of poems on the Norse gods, here in William Edward Frye's English version, The Gods of the North (1845), which follows Thor and the trickster Lok through thirty cantos. He wrote also in German, and he is remembered in Denmark as the author of the national song 'There is a lovely land'.

poets.name: Alexander Voeikov
bio: Alexander Fyodorovich Voeikov (1779–1839) was a poet, critic and translator, and for a time a professor at the University of Dorpat. Bowring prints his poem “To My Future Bride” in the second part of the Specimens.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: John Marriott
bio: The Reverend John Marriott (1780–1825) was an English clergyman and poet, tutor to the family of the Duke of Buccleuch, the chief of Walter Scott’s clan, and later a curate and rector in Devon.
He wrote verses on Border subjects for the later editions of Scott’s Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, including The Feast of Spurs and Archie Armstrong’s Aith.

poets.name: Théophile Gautier
poets.credit: Portrait of Théophile Gautier by Nadar, c. 1856 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Théophile Gautier (1811–1872) was a French poet, novelist and critic, born in Tarbes and raised in Paris, where he first trained as a painter before turning to literature. A champion of Romanticism from the 1830s and the principal voice of "art for art's sake", he served as a journalist and theatre critic for most of his working life, and he is much admired by later poets, including the Parnassians and Baudelaire, who dedicated Les Fleurs du mal to him.

Émaux et Camées (Enamels and Cameos), first published in 1852 and enlarged until 1872, gathers his polished, sculptural short poems, in which he treats verse as a craft of enamel, marble and carved gem; the closing poem, "Art", is its manifesto. The original poems are in French. The English shown here is the translation by Agnes Lee, published in 1903 in the Complete Works of Théophile Gautier.

poets.name: Charles Kirkpatrick Sharpe
bio: Charles Kirkpatrick Sharpe (c. 1781–1851) was a Scottish antiquary, artist and wit, of the family of Hoddom in Dumfriesshire. He was educated at Oxford and became a noted collector of ballads, folklore and curious historical anecdote.
He contributed Border ballads to Walter Scott’s Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border and later edited Kirkton’s history of the Church of Scotland and other works.

poets.name: Esaias Tegnér
poets.credit: Johan Gustaf Sandberg, 1826 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
poets.bio:
Esaias Tegnér (1782–1846) was a Swedish poet, professor of Greek at Lund University and, from 1824, Bishop of Växjö. He was the leading voice of Swedish Romanticism and is regarded as the father of modern Swedish poetry.

His best-known work is Frithiofs saga (1825), a cycle of twenty-four cantos retelling an Icelandic saga, which was translated into English many times in the nineteenth century. This archive carries the 1876 version by Thomas A. E. Holcomb and Martha A. Lyon Holcomb.

poets.name: Robert Browning
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Browning · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Browning (1812–1889) was an English poet and playwright, master of the dramatic monologue — a poem spoken entirely in an invented character's voice.

This selection gathers his early collections Dramatic Lyrics (1842) and Dramatic Romances (1845); his stage plays and longer closet-dramas (Pauline, Paracelsus, Sordello, Pippa Passes) are not included here.

poets.name: Vasily Zhukovsky
poets.credit: Portrait of Vasily Zhukovsky by Karl Bryullov (1837) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Vasily Andreyevich Zhukovsky (1783–1852) was the founder of Russian Romanticism. His free translations and adaptations of English and German poetry, among them Gray’s “Elegy”, Bürger’s ballads and the ballad “Svetlana” (1813), brought a new emotional range to Russian verse. He later served as tutor to the future Alexander II and was an early mentor and friend of Pushkin.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Leigh Hunt
poets.credit: Portrait of Leigh Hunt by Benjamin Robert Haydon · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Leigh Hunt (1784–1859) was an English poet, essayist and editor, best remembered today as the friend and champion of Keats and Shelley. As editor of The Examiner he was imprisoned from 1813 to 1815 for libelling the Prince Regent, and he received visitors in his cell.
His own poems range from the narrative Story of Rimini (1816) to light verse, sonnets and short lyrics. “Abou Ben Adhem” and “Jenny Kiss’d Me” are the two that most readers know.

poets.name: Denis Davydov
bio: Denis Vasilyevich Davydov (1784–1839) was a cavalry officer, a leader of partisan raids against Napoleon’s army in 1812, and the poet of the “hussar” style of lively, convivial verse. Bowring prints a single short poem under the name “Davidov”; the archive’s editor identifies him with Denis Davydov, but Bowring himself gives no notice of the author.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Samuel Woodworth
poets.credit: Portrait of Samuel Woodworth, from The National Cyclopaedia of American Biography (1893) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Woodworth (1784–1842) was an American poet, journalist and editor, born at Scituate, Massachusetts. He worked as a printer and edited several periodicals in New York, including the New-York Mirror, which he founded with George Pope Morris.
He is remembered chiefly for “The Bucket”, better known as “The Old Oaken Bucket”, written in 1817 and one of the most popular American songs of the nineteenth century.

poets.name: Allan Cunningham
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Allan Cunningham was a Scottish poet and man of letters who began as a stonemason. He wrote songs in the Scots tradition and compiled collections of Scottish song.
Palgrave includes his sea song "A wet sheet and a flowing sea".

poets.name: Henry Kirke White
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Kirke White by Thomas Barber · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Kirke White (1785–1806) was born in Nottingham, the son of a butcher, and was put to work early in a stocking-loom and then a lawyer's office while he taught himself languages and wrote verse. His first volume, Clifton Grove (1803), won him the notice of Robert Southey, and with the help of patrons he went up to St John's College, Cambridge, to study for the church.

Overwork and the strain of competing for university honours broke his health, and he died of consumption at Cambridge at the age of twenty-one. Southey edited his Remains (1807), and Lord Byron's lines on his early death in English Bards and Scotch Reviewers made his name widely known. The poems here follow the Poetical Works with a memoir by Sir Harris Nicolas.

poets.name: Konstantin Batyushkov
poets.credit: Portrait of Konstantin Batyushkov by an unknown artist (1810s) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Konstantin Nikolayevich Batyushkov (1787–1855), born in Vologda, served as an officer in the Napoleonic wars and was wounded in 1807 and 1813–14. His smooth, sensuous elegies and epistles, drawing on Italian and French models, were a strong influence on the young Pushkin. From about 1821 he suffered from mental illness and wrote nothing more; he died in Vologda in 1855.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Lord Byron
poets.credit: Portrait by Thomas Phillips (1813) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lord Byron (George Gordon Byron, 1788–1824) was an English Romantic poet and satirist, one of the most celebrated — and scandalous — figures of his age.
He died at Missolonghi while supporting the Greek war of independence, and gave his name to the brooding ‘Byronic hero.’

poets.name: Richard Henry Wilde
poets.credit: Portrait of Richard Henry Wilde · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Henry Wilde (1789–1847) was an American lawyer, congressman and poet, born in Dublin, Ireland, and raised in Augusta, Georgia. He represented Georgia in Congress and later settled in New Orleans, where he died of yellow fever.
His short lyric “My Life is Like the Summer Rose”, sometimes called “The Lament of the Captive”, became one of the most widely reprinted American poems of its day.

poets.name: George Jehoshaphat Mountain
bio: George Jehoshaphat Mountain (1789–1863), born in England, was the Anglican Bishop of Quebec from 1836 until his death.
He published a small volume of verse, Songs of the Wilderness (1846). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Fitz-Greene Halleck
poets.credit: Photograph of Fitz-Greene Halleck, Brady-Handy Photograph Collection (Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Fitz-Greene Halleck (1790–1867) was an American poet, born at Guilford, Connecticut. He worked as a clerk and later as a business agent for John Jacob Astor in New York, and wrote satirical verse with Joseph Rodman Drake as the “Croakers”.
His elegy on Drake, “Green be the turf above thee”, and the ballad “Marco Bozzaris” were among the most admired American poems of the early nineteenth century.

poets.name: Lydia Huntley Sigourney
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Lydia Sigourney, 19th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lydia Huntley Sigourney (1791-1865) was born in Norwich, Connecticut, and lived most of her life in Hartford. She was among the best-known American poets of her day, nicknamed the "Sweet Singer of Hartford", and published some fifty books of verse and prose as well as many contributions to periodicals.

The poems here are the "In Memoriam" section of The Man of Uz, and Other Poems (Hartford, 1862), a sequence of elegies on neighbours, clergymen, children and public figures of Hartford and beyond who died between 1859 and 1862, a form of memorial verse for which she was especially known.

poets.name: Charles Wolfe
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charles Wolfe was an Irish clergyman and poet who died young. He is remembered for one poem.
Palgrave includes it: "The Burial of Sir John Moore at Corunna".

poets.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poets.credit: Portrait by Alfred Clint · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was an English Romantic poet, radical in politics and idealist in temper.
Author of ‘Ozymandias’ and ‘Ode to the West Wind,’ he drowned off the Italian coast before his thirtieth birthday.

poets.name: Pyotr Vyazemsky
bio: Prince Pyotr Andreyevich Vyazemsky (1792–1878) was a poet, critic and wit, a friend of Pushkin and a prominent member of the Arzamas circle. Bowring, who spells the name “Væsemsky”, prints three of his poems in the second part.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Mikhail Milonov
bio: Mikhail Vasilyevich Milonov (1792–1821) was a Russian poet who wrote satires and elegies and died young. Bowring prints his poem “The Fall of the Leaf” in the second part.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: John Keble
poets.credit: Portrait of John Keble by Miss Donkin (19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Keble (1792–1866) was an English Anglican priest and poet, born in Fairford, Gloucestershire. He took a double first at Oxford, became a fellow of Oriel College, and served as Oxford's Professor of Poetry from 1831 to 1841. He spent most of his working life as a country parish priest at Hursley in Hampshire.

His Assize Sermon on National Apostasy (1833) is traditionally taken as the starting point of the Oxford Movement. His best-known book of verse, The Christian Year (1827), gives a poem to each Sunday and holy day of the Book of Common Prayer and was among the most widely read volumes of the nineteenth century. Keble College, Oxford, was founded in his memory.

poets.name: John Clare
bio: John Clare (1793–1864) was an English labouring-class poet, the son of a Northamptonshire farm labourer, whose closely observed poems of birds, insects and the vanishing open fields of his native Helpston mark him as one of the great nature poets in the language.

His early success gave way to poverty and the destruction of the rural world he wrote from, as the enclosure acts fenced in the commons he had grown up roaming. He spent the last decades of his life in asylums, where he continued to write some of his most haunting poems, including "I Am."

poets.name: Felicia Hemans
poets.credit: Portrait of Felicia Hemans by William Edward West (before 1835) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Felicia Hemans (1793–1835), born Felicia Dorothea Browne in Liverpool and raised largely in Wales, published her first volume of poems at fourteen and became one of the most widely read poets of her day, in Britain and in America.

After her husband left for Italy in 1818 she brought up her five sons alone and supported them by her writing. Her best-known collections include Records of Woman (1828) and Songs of the Affections (1830), and poems such as “Casabianca” and “The Homes of England” were learned by heart by generations of schoolchildren. She died in Dublin at forty-one.

poets.name: John Keats
poets.credit: Portrait by William Hilton (c. 1822) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Keats (1795–1821) was an English Romantic poet whose odes are among the most celebrated in the language.
He trained as a surgeon before devoting himself to poetry, and died of tuberculosis in Rome at just twenty-five.

poets.name: Jeremiah Joseph Callanan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Jeremiah Joseph Callanan was born in Cork and studied at Maynooth and Trinity College Dublin. He worked as a tutor, made English versions of Irish songs, and died in Lisbon in 1829.
Yeats credited his translations from the Irish with first giving English-speaking Ireland an honest style. Yeats's anthology misprints his death year as 1839.

poets.name: George Darley
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Darley was born in Dublin and spent most of his working life in London, where he was a poet, mathematician and art and drama critic for The Athenaeum. His works include Sylvia; or, The May Queen (1827) and Nepenthe (1835).
He suffered from a severe stammer and wrote little for a wide audience in his lifetime.

poets.name: Heinrich Heine
poets.credit: Portrait of Heinrich Heine by Moritz Daniel Oppenheim (1831) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Heinrich Heine (1797–1856) was born in Düsseldorf to a Jewish family and studied law at Bonn, Berlin and Göttingen, taking his degree in 1825 after converting to Protestant Christianity. His Book of Songs (Buch der Lieder, 1827), with its plain, musical lyrics of love and disappointment, made him one of the most widely read German poets, and many of its poems were set to music by Schumann, Schubert and Mendelssohn.

In 1831 Heine moved to Paris, where he lived for the rest of his life, writing travel pieces, criticism and satirical verse, among them Germany: A Winter's Tale and Atta Troll. His work was banned in several German states. From the mid-1840s he suffered from a progressive paralysis and spent his last years confined to what he called his mattress-grave, producing the Romancero (1851) and the late poems. The translations here are by Edgar Alfred Bowring (1908 edition of the complete poems, in the original metres).

poets.name: Janet Hamilton
bio: Janet Hamilton (1795–1873) was a self-taught Scottish working-class poet who lived at Langloan, near Coatbridge, in the industrial west of Scotland. She learned to write late and lost her sight in her later years.

Her verse, in Scots and English, appeared in volumes from the 1860s such as Poems and Essays and Poems and Ballads; “A Ballad of Memorie”, in Scots, is the piece chosen for Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Hartley Coleridge
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Hartley Coleridge was an English poet and essayist, the eldest son of Samuel Taylor Coleridge. He spent much of his life in the Lake District, writing sonnets and short lyrics.
Palgrave includes one of his lyrics, "She is not fair to outward view".

poets.name: Giacomo Leopardi
poets.credit: Portrait of Giacomo Leopardi by A. Ferrazzi (c. 1820) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Giacomo Leopardi (1798–1837) was born in Recanati, in the Papal States, and educated in his father's great library, where he mastered the classical languages and ruined his health by study. He is regarded as the greatest Italian lyric poet of the nineteenth century, and a profound pessimist whose thought is also preserved in his prose Operette morali and the Zibaldone.

His Canti move from patriotic odes on Italy's fallen glory to the brief, intense idylls such as “The Infinite” and “To Silvia”, and finally to the late, stoic “The Genista”. He died in Naples in 1837, aged thirty-eight. The selection here is Francis Henry Cliffe's English verse translation of 1893.

poets.name: Alexander Pushkin
poets.credit: Portrait of Alexander Pushkin by Orest Kiprensky (1827) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin (1799–1837) was born in Moscow into an old noble family and educated at the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum. His early verse brought him fame, and his liberal poems led the authorities to send him into exile in southern Russia in 1820 and then to his family estate at Mikhailovskoye. He is widely regarded as the founder of modern Russian literature and its literary language.

Besides the verse novel Eugene Onegin, the drama Boris Godunov and the narrative poem The Bronze Horseman, he wrote many short lyrics, ballads and tales in verse. He died in St Petersburg in 1837 of a wound received in a duel. The versions here are by Ivan Panin (1888), who aimed at literal, line-for-line renderings, unrhymed, rather than at the music of the originals.

poets.name: John Banim
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Banim was born in Kilkenny and became a novelist, dramatist and poet. With his brother Michael he wrote the O'Hara Tales, a series of stories of Irish life.
His song "Soggarth Aroon" ("Priest, dear") is included in W. B. Yeats's A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Thomas Hood
poets.credit: Unknown artist, National Portrait Gallery, London · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Hood (1799–1845) was an English poet and humorist, famous in his own lifetime chiefly for comic verse and outrageous puns, but remembered today at least as much for a handful of serious social poems — above all ‘The Song of the Shirt’ and ‘The Bridge of Sighs’ — written from genuine anger at the suffering of the poor.

Chronically ill for most of his adult life, he supported a family through unrelenting magazine work, editing and writing comic annuals even as his health failed; he died at forty-five, not long after a government pension was finally arranged for him.

poets.name: Elias Lönnrot
poets.credit: Portrait of Elias Lönnrot, artist unknown, nineteenth century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elias Lönnrot (1802–1884) was a Finnish physician and philologist, born in Sammatti in southern Finland. From 1828 he made a series of collecting journeys through Finland and Russian Karelia, on foot, on horseback, by sledge and by canoe, writing down the rune-songs that country singers still chanted from memory. In 1835 he published the first Kalevala, and in 1849 an enlarged edition of fifty runes; the Finnish Literature Society, which he helped to found, issued both.

Lönnrot is the compiler-author of the Kalevala, not its sole poet. The verses are drawn from oral folk songs, which he selected, ordered and joined into a continuous narrative of the hero Wainamoinen, the smith Ilmarinen and the Sampo, in the unrhymed trochaic metre of the tradition. The poem became a foundation of Finnish national culture. He later served as professor of Finnish at Helsinki and compiled a Finnish dictionary. This archive holds John Martin Crawford's 1888 English translation.

poets.name: Edward Coote Pinkney
poets.credit: Frontispiece portrait of Edward Coote Pinkney, from The Life and Works of Edward Coote Pinkney (Macmillan, 1926) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Coote Pinkney (1802–1828) was an American poet, born in London and raised in Baltimore, who served as a midshipman in the United States Navy and later practised law. He died at the age of twenty-five.
His slender output, including Poems (1825), contains a few graceful songs that earned him a lasting place in anthologies, notably “A Health”.

poets.name: Harriet Martineau
poets.credit: Portrait of Harriet Martineau by Richard Evans (exhibited 1834) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Harriet Martineau (1802–1876) was an English writer and social theorist, born at Norwich, best known for her prose: the Illustrations of Political Economy (1832–34), Society in America (1837) and her abridged English version of Comte's philosophy. She was deaf from youth.

Her verse is slight beside her prose, but her brief hymn-like lyric “Onward” was chosen by Elizabeth A. Sharp to open Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890). She spent her later years at Ambleside in the Lake District.

poets.name: Sara Coleridge
poets.credit: Portrait of Sara Coleridge (1852) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sara Coleridge (1802–1852) was the daughter of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Sara Fricker, and the wife of her cousin Henry Nelson Coleridge. She was a translator and editor of her father's work, and published Pretty Lessons in Verse for Good Children (1834).
Her fairy romance Phantasmion (1837), a prose tale threaded with songs, is the source of several of the lyrics Elizabeth A. Sharp chose for Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Thomas Lovell Beddoes
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Lovell Beddoes by Nathan Cooper Branwhite (1824) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Lovell Beddoes (1803–1849) was an English poet, dramatist and physician, educated at Charterhouse and Oxford. He spent most of his adult life on the Continent, studying medicine in Germany and Switzerland.

His great work, the blank-verse tragedy Death’s Jest-Book, was begun in the 1820s and published only after his death in 1850. It is full of grave-haunted lyrics, such as “Dream-Pedlary” and “Old Adam, the Carrion Crow,” for which he is now chiefly read. He died in Basel in 1849.

poets.name: Samuel Lover
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Samuel Lover was a Dublin-born novelist, songwriter, painter and miniaturist. His novels include Rory O'More and Handy Andy, and he wrote and performed Irish songs and entertainments.
He died in Jersey in 1868.

poets.name: James Clarence Mangan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Clarence Mangan was born in Dublin and worked as a scrivener's clerk and library assistant. He contributed poems and translations, many of them English versions from the Irish, to The Nation and other periodicals.
He lived in poverty and ill health and died of cholera in 1849. His "Dark Rosaleen" is the most widely known of his poems.

poets.name: William Barnes
poets.credit: Photograph of William Barnes, 19th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Barnes (1801–1886) was an English poet, philologist and clergyman, born at Rushay in the Vale of Blackmore, Dorset. A largely self-taught scholar, he worked as a schoolmaster in Dorchester and later became rector of Winterborne Came, near Dorchester.

He is best known for his poems in the Dorset dialect, collected in three series of Poems of Rural Life in the Dorset Dialect (1844, 1859, 1862) and gathered in one volume in 1879. Thomas Hardy, who knew him in Dorchester, admired him and wrote of his death in a poem.

poets.name: Gerald Griffin
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Gerald Griffin was born in Limerick and became a novelist, dramatist and poet; his best-known novel is The Collegians (1829). In 1838 he joined the Christian Brothers.
He died in Cork in 1840.

poets.name: Jane Welsh Carlyle
poets.credit: Portrait of Jane Welsh Carlyle by Samuel Laurence · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jane Baillie Welsh Carlyle (1801–1866) was born at Haddington in Scotland and in 1826 married the historian Thomas Carlyle. She is remembered above all for her letters, which are among the most admired of the century.
She wrote little verse and published almost none in her lifetime; the poem “To a Swallow Building under our Eaves” is the piece by which she is usually represented in anthologies.

poets.name: Edward Walsh
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Edward Walsh was born in Londonderry and worked as a schoolmaster. He is known for his English versions of Irish songs, collected in Irish Popular Songs (1847).
He died in Cork in 1850.

poets.name: Lionel Johnson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Lionel Johnson (1867–1902) was an English poet and critic associated with the Rhymers' Club and the Decadent movement of the 1890s.
A convert to Catholicism, his spare, disciplined verse turned repeatedly to faith, monastic ideals, and the pull of dissipation he struggled against.

poets.name: Oscar Wilde
poets.credit: Portrait of Oscar Wilde · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oscar Wilde (1854–1900) was an Irish poet, playwright, and wit, one of the most celebrated figures of Victorian literary London before his 1895 trial and imprisonment.
His early verse is lush and Romantic in the Keatsian mode, while The Ballad of Reading Gaol, written after his release from prison, is a stark, plainspoken account of suffering and remorse.

poets.name: Douglas Brooke Wheelton Sladen
bio: Douglas Sladen (1856–1947) was an English-born poet and novelist who lectured at the University of Sydney from 1879 to 1884.
He edited the anthologies A Century of Australian Song and Australian Ballads and Rhymes (both 1888), and wrote many novels.

poets.name: Lewis Frank Tooker
bio: Lewis Frank Tooker (1855–1925) was an American editor and poet, for many years associated with the staff of The Century Magazine. He wrote verse and prose, including sea poems and memoirs of his years in magazine editing.
Knowles included his poem “The Return” in his anthology of American lyrics.

poets.name: Thomas Hardy
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Hardy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928) is best known as a novelist, but after finishing Jude the Obscure in 1895 he devoted the rest of his long career chiefly to poetry.
His verse is plain-spoken and often bleak, preoccupied with chance, loss, rural Wessex life, and the death of his first wife Emma, which produced some of his most admired elegies.

poets.name: Patrick Moloney
bio: Patrick Moloney (1843–1904) was a Melbourne doctor and writer of light and occasional verse.
His poem on Melbourne appeared in An Easter Omelette (1879).

poets.name: Thomas Bracken
bio: Thomas Bracken (1843–1898) was an Irish-born journalist, politician and poet who settled in New Zealand.
He published Musings in Maoriland (1890) and wrote the words of 'God Defend New Zealand', later the national hymn.

poets.name: Sarah Pratt McLean Greene
bio: Sarah Pratt McLean Greene (1856–1935) was an American writer, born at Simsbury, Connecticut, and educated at Mount Holyoke College. She is known for books of Cape Cod life such as Cape Cod Folks and Vesty of the Basins.
Rittenhouse included her dialect poem “De Massa ob de Sheepfol’”, which she judged destined to hold a lasting place.

poets.name: Namık Kemal
poets.credit: Photograph of Namık Kemal, 1878 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Namık Kemal (1840–1888) was an Ottoman poet, journalist, playwright and political thinker, born in Tekirdağ. A leading figure of the Young Ottomans, the reform-minded circle of the Tanzimat era, he argued for liberty, constitutional government and love of the fatherland in newspapers, plays and verse, and was later known as the "poet of the fatherland" (vatan şairi).

His writing brought him repeated trouble with the authorities: he spent years in exile in Europe in the 1860s, and after his patriotic play Vatan yahut Silistre (1873) he was banished to Magosa (Famagusta) in Cyprus. He later served as an Ottoman provincial governor and died on the island of Chios on 2 December 1888. The eight pieces here are taken from Turkish Wikisource, which lists his death year as 1889; the standard date is 1888.

poets.name: Alice Brown
poets.credit: Photograph of Alice Brown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alice Brown (1857–1948) was an American writer, born at Hampton Falls, New Hampshire, and educated at Robinson Seminary, Exeter. She is chiefly known as a novelist and short-story writer of New England life, with books such as Meadow Grass and Tiverton Tales.
In poetry she published one volume, The Road to Castaly (1896), reprinted with new poems in 1917. In 1915 her play Children of Earth won a ten-thousand-dollar prize and was produced in New York.

poets.name: Recaizade Mahmut Ekrem
poets.credit: Photograph of Recaizade Mahmut Ekrem, before 1900, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Recaizade Mahmut Ekrem (1847–1914) was a writer of the Tanzimat period, the Ottoman reform era, and one of the figures who helped turn Turkish literature toward new subjects and a plainer prose. He was born in Istanbul. He is remembered above all for his novel Araba Sevdası (1896) and for his critical writing, and he also wrote plays and a good deal of verse.

Nağme-i Seher ('Song of the Dawn') was a collection of his poems, dated 1288 AH (about 1871). It gathers classical forms (tevhîd and na't, praise poems, chronogram verses, gazels) alongside lighter songs (şarkı). The poems below are given in the Vikikaynak (tr.wikisource.org) Latin-alphabet transcription of the 1871 book, which keeps the book's circumflexed Ottoman spelling.

poets.name: William Ernest Henley
poets.credit: Portrait of William Ernest Henley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Ernest Henley (1849–1903) was an English poet and editor whose leg was amputated in youth after tubercular illness, an experience recorded directly in his sequence In Hospital.
He is best remembered for Invictus, and his robust, muscular verse and criticism made him an influential figure among younger writers of the 1890s.

poets.name: Harriet Eleanor Hamilton King
bio: Harriet Eleanor Hamilton King (1840–1920) was an English poet whose long narrative poems were inspired by the Italian struggle for unification, in which she took a warm interest. Her works include Aspromonte and Other Poems (1869) and The Disciples (1873).
Her heroic ballad “Baron Giovanni Nicotera”, on the Italian patriot imprisoned by the Bourbon government, is printed in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: William Douw Lighthall
poets.credit: Portrait of William Douw Lighthall, from Canadian Singers and Their Songs (c. 1919) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Douw Lighthall (1857–1954) was a Montreal lawyer, author and civic reformer, later mayor of Westmount, who edited a series of anthologies of Canadian poetry.
His own verse appeared in Thoughts, Moods and Ideals (1887); the poems here are those he included in his own anthology, Songs of the Great Dominion (1889).

poets.name: Charles Henry Luders
bio: Charles Henry Luders (1858–1891), also spelled Lüders, was an American poet, who died young at the age of thirty-three. Little is recorded of his life in the sources used for this archive.
Knowles included his lyric “The Four Winds” in his anthology of American songs and lyrics.

poets.name: Rosa Mulholland, Lady Gilbert
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Rosa Mulholland was born in Belfast and became a prolific novelist and poet. In 1891 she married the historian Sir John Gilbert and was afterwards known as Lady Gilbert.
Yeats's anthology prints her poem under the name Rosa Gilbert.

poets.name: A. E. Housman
poets.credit: Portrait of A. E. Housman · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: A. E. Housman (1859–1936) was an English classical scholar and poet whose reputation rests on two slim volumes, A Shropshire Lad (1896) and Last Poems (1922).
His terse, ballad-like lyrics of doomed youth, soldiering, and rural England were composed in a private grief masked by classical restraint.

poets.name: Edward Dowden
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Edward Dowden was born in Cork and became Professor of English Literature at Trinity College Dublin. He is best known for his Shakespeare criticism and his Life of Shelley.
He also published several volumes of verse.

poets.name: Violet Fane
bio: Violet Fane was the pen name of Mary Montgomerie Singleton (1843–1905), later Lady Currie, an English poet and novelist of the 1870s and 1880s. Her volumes include From Dawn to Noon (1872) and Denzil Place (1875).
Two of her lyrics, “Rest” and “Forbidden Love”, appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Andrew Lang
poets.credit: Portrait of Andrew Lang · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Andrew Lang (1844–1912) was a Scottish man of letters, folklorist, and translator, remembered today chiefly for his coloured Fairy Books but also a prolific poet.
His verse favours French forms revived by the 1870s ballade craze, along with translations and tributes to French and English poets he admired.

poets.name: Gerard Manley Hopkins
poets.credit: Photograph of Gerard Manley Hopkins, before 1889, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gerard Manley Hopkins (1844–1889) was an English poet, Roman Catholic convert and Jesuit priest. Born in Stratford, Essex, he studied at Balliol College, Oxford, became a Catholic in 1866 under the influence of John Henry Newman, and entered the Society of Jesus in 1868. He burned his early verses on joining the order and wrote little for several years, until the wreck of the Deutschland in December 1875 drew from him the long ode that opened his mature manner.

His poems, built on what he called sprung rhythm and a dense, coined vocabulary of sound and image, found almost no readers in his lifetime. He worked as a teacher and parish priest, and from 1884 as professor of Greek at University College, Dublin, where he wrote the so-called terrible sonnets and died of typhoid in 1889. His friend Robert Bridges published the first collected Poems in 1918, and Hopkins has since been counted among the major Victorian poets.

poets.name: Robert Bridges
poets.credit: Photograph of Robert Bridges, late 19th century, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Bridges (1844–1930) was an English poet and physician. Born at Walmer in Kent, he was educated at Eton and Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and trained in medicine at St Bartholomew's Hospital, practising until ill health led him to retire in 1882 and devote himself to poetry. He was a close friend of Gerard Manley Hopkins, whose poems he preserved and, in 1918, brought to the public.

His own verse, notable for its delicate lyrics and metrical experiment, including syllabic measures modelled on Milton's Samson Agonistes, appeared in small private editions such as the Daniel Press Poems of 1884. He became Poet Laureate in 1913, published the long philosophical poem The Testament of Beauty in 1929, and died at Boars Hill, near Oxford, in 1930.

poets.name: Paul Verlaine
poets.credit: Photograph of Paul Verlaine by Otto Wegener, 1893 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Paul Verlaine (1844–1896) was a French poet born in Metz and raised in Paris, where he worked briefly as a clerk at the Hôtel de Ville while publishing his first book, Poèmes saturniens (1866). His Fêtes galantes (1869) and La Bonne Chanson (1870), the latter written for his young fiancée Mathilde Mauté, established him as a master of fluid, musical verse among the Parnassian poets.

In 1871 he met Arthur Rimbaud, and in 1873 he was imprisoned in Belgium after shooting him; Romances sans paroles (1874) was written in these years and Sagesse (1881), a book of Catholic devotion, in the aftermath. He later published Jadis et naguère (1884) and Parallèlement (1889), and was named the leading living poet by the Symbolists, though he spent his last years in poverty and illness in Paris. These versions are from Gertrude Hall's English translation of 1895.

poets.name: Amy Levy
poets.credit: Portrait of Amy Levy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Amy Levy (1861–1889) was an English poet and novelist, among the first Jewish women to study at Cambridge, who took her own life at twenty-seven.
Her poems of London street life, unrequited love, and urban melancholy anticipate the modern lyric's compression and irony.

poets.name: George MacDonald
poets.credit: Portrait of George MacDonald · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George MacDonald (1824–1905) was a Scottish minister turned author, celebrated for fantasy novels such as Phantastes and The Princess and the Goblin, and a lifelong writer of devotional and reflective verse.
His poems return often to faith, fatherhood, nature, and the soul's struggle toward trust in a loving God.

poets.name: George Meredith
poets.credit: Portrait of George Meredith · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Meredith (1828–1909) was an English novelist and poet whose sonnet sequence Modern Love (1862) gave unusually candid, ironic voice to a marriage's collapse.
His nature poetry, especially The Lark Ascending, prizes close observation and intellectual vigour over conventional sentiment.

poets.name: Charles Baudelaire
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Baudelaire by Étienne Carjat (c. 1862) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Baudelaire (1821–1867) was a French poet, critic and translator of Edgar Allan Poe. Born in Paris, he spent his short life in the city's literary and artistic circles, and is widely regarded as a founder of modern poetry and a forerunner of the Symbolists.

His one major collection of verse, Les Fleurs du Mal (1857), drew a prosecution for offending public morality, and six of its poems were suppressed. Its themes of spleen, beauty, desire, the city and death shaped later poets across Europe. These versions are from Cyril Scott's English translation of 1909.

poets.name: Dora Greenwell
poets.credit: Photograph of Dora Greenwell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dora Greenwell (1821–1882) was an English poet and devotional writer born in County Durham. Her volumes include Poems (1848) and Carmina Crucis (1869), and she wrote essays on religious and social questions.
Her poem “Songs of Farewell: Death”, a meditation on the seasons that will return when the speaker is gone, was chosen for Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson
poets.credit: Portrait of Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson by Erwin Raupp, before 1909 (restored by Adam Cuerden; National Library of Norway) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson (1832–1910) was a Norwegian poet, novelist, dramatist and public campaigner, one of the “four great ones” of nineteenth-century Norwegian literature. He wrote the words of the national hymn “Yes, We Love This Land Forever,” and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1903.

The poems here are Arthur Hubbell Palmer’s English versions, made in the original meters and published as Poems and Songs (American-Scandinavian Foundation, 1915); Bjørnson’s originals are in Norwegian. Many began as songs inside his peasant tales and plays, such as Synnøve Solbakken and Arne, others as occasional verse for national causes.

poets.name: William Morris
poets.credit: Portrait of William Morris · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Morris (1834–1896) was an English designer, socialist, and poet, a central figure of the Pre-Raphaelite circle whose vast output includes the narrative cycle The Earthly Paradise and the Icelandic-inspired epic Sigurd the Volsung.
In later years his political convictions produced the direct, rallying verse of Chants for Socialists and The Pilgrims of Hope.

poets.name: James Brunton Stephens
bio: James Brunton Stephens (1835–1902) was a Scottish-born poet who emigrated to Queensland in 1866 and worked as a teacher and civil servant.
His books include Convict Once (1871) and Miscellaneous Poems; his poem The Dominion of Australia (1877) looked forward to federation.

poets.name: Giosuè Carducci
poets.credit: Photograph of Giosuè Carducci, late 19th or early 20th century (photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Giosuè Carducci (1835–1907) was the leading Italian poet of his age and the first Italian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1906. A professor of Italian literature at Bologna for over four decades, he set his classical learning and republican, anticlerical convictions against what he saw as the sentimental excesses of Italian Romanticism.

He is best known for the pagan, defiant “Hymn to Satan” and for the Odi barbare, which adapted Greek and Latin metres to Italian verse. The translations here are by the American writer Frank Sewall, from his 1893 English introduction to Carducci's work.

poets.name: Rabindranath Tagore
poets.credit: Rabindranath Tagore, 1909 photograph, published in Les Prix Nobel 1913 (1914) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) was a Bengali poet, songwriter, playwright, novelist and educator, born into a prominent family in Calcutta. He wrote chiefly in Bengali, founded a school at Santiniketan, and in 1913 became the first non-European to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.

The poems here are his own English prose renderings of his Bengali verse: Gitanjali (Song Offerings, 1912), the devotional poems that W. B. Yeats introduced to English readers, and The Gardener (1915), a gathering of love lyrics and poems of youth and life. Tagore translated them himself, and the English is often freer than the Bengali, abridging or paraphrasing as he saw fit.

poets.name: Katharine Tynan Hinkson
bio: Katharine Tynan Hinkson (dates as printed in Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920): 1861–1931) was an Irish poet and novelist, born in Dublin. A friend of the young W. B. Yeats and part of the Irish literary revival, she wrote devotional and pastoral verse as well as a great many novels.
She married the barrister Henry Hinkson. Her poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Owen Seaman
bio: Sir Owen Seaman (1861–1936) was an English parodist and light-verse writer who edited the humorous magazine Punch from 1906 to 1932. He was created a baronet in 1933.
His verse, as in To an Old Fogey and the war poem Thomas of the Light Heart, mixes satire with patriotic sentiment. The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Henry Newbolt
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Newbolt · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Newbolt (1862–1938) was an English poet best known for patriotic and naval verse such as Vitài Lampada and Drake's Drum, written to celebrate duty, empire, and the sea.
His confident public rhetoric made him one of the most widely recited poets of the pre-1914 era.

poets.name: Francis William Lauderdale Adams
bio: Francis William Lauderdale Adams (1862–1893) was a poet and journalist, born in Malta and educated in England, who went to Australia in 1884.
He published Songs of the Army of the Night (1888) and died young.

poets.name: Thomas William Heney
bio: Thomas William Heney (1862–1928) was an Australian journalist, poet and novelist, born in Sydney, who later edited the Sydney Morning Herald.
His verse was collected in In Middle Harbour, and Other Verse.

poets.name: John Bernard O'Hara
bio: John Bernard O'Hara (1862–1927) was an Australian poet.
His books include Songs of the South and Lyrics of Nature.

poets.name: Inez K. Hyland
bio: Inez K. Hyland (1863–1892) was an Australian poet who died young.
Her verse was collected in In Sunshine and in Shadow.

poets.name: John Sandes
bio: John Sandes (1863–1938) was an Australian journalist and poet.
His verse includes Ballads of Battle.

poets.name: George Essex Evans
bio: George Essex Evans (1863–1909) was an English-born poet who emigrated to Queensland as a young man and farmed on the Darling Downs.
His books include Loraine, and Other Verses (1898), and he wrote the Federation 'Ode for Commonwealth Day'.

poets.name: Mary Colborne-Veel
bio: Mary Colborne-Veel (1863–1923) was a New Zealand poet and writer.
Her verse was collected in The Fairest of the Angels, and Other Verse.

poets.name: Sydney Jephcott
bio: Sydney Jephcott (1864–1951) was an Australian poet and journalist who lived on the upper Murray in Victoria.
His books include The Secrets of the South (1892).

poets.name: Andrew Barton 'Banjo' Paterson
bio: Andrew Barton 'Banjo' Paterson (1864–1941) was an Australian bush poet, solicitor and journalist, born near Orange, New South Wales, who reported the Boer War as a correspondent.
He published The Man from Snowy River and Other Verses (1895) and Rio Grande's Last Race (1902), and wrote the words of 'Waltzing Matilda'.

poets.name: Jessie Mackay
bio: Jessie Mackay (1864–1938) was a New Zealand poet and journalist, born in Canterbury.
Her first volume was The Spirit of the Rangatira and Other Ballads (1889); she was a leading New Zealand verse writer of her time.

poets.name: Arthur O'Shaughnessy
poets.credit: Portrait of Arthur O'Shaughnessy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur O'Shaughnessy (1844–1881) was an English poet who worked as a herpetologist at the British Museum while publishing richly musical, melancholy verse.
His Ode, beginning "We are the music makers," is his most famous poem and a manifesto for the visionary power of artists.

poets.name: Marcus Clarke
bio: Marcus Clarke (1846–1881) was an English-born journalist and novelist who settled in Melbourne in 1863.
He is best known for the convict novel For the Term of His Natural Life (1874), and also wrote essays, plays and occasional verse.

poets.name: Ada Cambridge
bio: Ada Cambridge (1844–1926) was an English-born novelist and poet who emigrated to Australia in 1870 as the wife of a clergyman and lived in Victoria.
Her verse appeared in Unspoken Thoughts (1887) and later volumes, and she wrote the memoir Thirty Years in Australia (1903).

poets.name: Alexander Bathgate
bio: Alexander Bathgate (1845–1930) was a Scottish-born lawyer and writer who settled in Otago, New Zealand.
His verse was collected in Far South Fancies.

poets.name: Mary Hannay Foott
bio: Mary Hannay Foott (1846–1918) was a Scottish-born poet who emigrated to Australia as a girl and later lived on a Queensland station.
Her books include Where the Pelican Builds and Other Poems (1885) and Morna Lee and Other Poems.

poets.name: Richard Watson Gilder
poets.credit: Photograph of Richard Watson Gilder (before 1913) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Watson Gilder (1844–1909) was an American poet and editor, born at Bordentown, New Jersey. From 1881 until his death he edited The Century Magazine, one of the most influential American periodicals of the period.
His own poems, including the sonnet sequence The New Day (1875) and later lyrics, were admired for their delicacy and were frequently anthologised.

poets.name: Maurice Thompson
poets.credit: Portrait of Maurice Thompson (before 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Maurice Thompson (1844–1901) was an American novelist, poet, and essayist, born at Fairfield, Indiana, and raised in Georgia. He served in the Confederate army, then practised as an engineer and lawyer in Indiana, and became an expert on archery.
He is best known for the novel Alice of Old Vincennes (1900). His lyric poems on nature, such as “Fertility”, were collected in volumes including Songs of Fair Weather (1883).

poets.name: John Banister Tabb
bio: John Banister Tabb (1845–1909) was an American poet and Roman Catholic priest, born in Amelia County, Virginia. He served in the Confederate army, was captured and imprisoned at Point Lookout, where he met Sidney Lanier, and later taught at St Charles College in Maryland.
He wrote very short, finished lyrics, often of four lines, on nature, childhood, and faith.

poets.name: Louisa S. Bevington
bio: Louisa Sarah Bevington (1845–1895) was an English poet and essayist, a freethinker and later an anarchist. Her verse appeared in Key Notes (1876), Poems, Lyrics and Sonnets (1882) and Liberty Lyrics (1895).
Her long poem “The Valley of Remorse” is printed in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Emily H. Hickey
bio: Emily Henrietta Hickey (1845–1924) was an Irish poet and critic, born in County Wexford. She helped Frederick Furnivall to found the Browning Society in 1881.
Her poems include Verse Tales, Lyrics and Translations (1889); “Harebells”, “Madonna della Vita” and “A Sea Story” are in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Lloyd Mifflin
bio: Lloyd Mifflin (1846–1921) was an American poet and painter, born at Columbia, Pennsylvania, on the Susquehanna, where he lived most of his life. He is remembered chiefly for his sonnets, which draw on the classical world and the landscape of his own river valley.
Several of his short poems were included by Knowles in his anthology of American lyrics, and Jessie Rittenhouse later placed him among the older poets of the period.

poets.name: Robert Cameron Rogers
bio: Robert Cameron Rogers (1862–1912) was an American poet, born at Buffalo, New York, who died at Santa Barbara, California, in 1912.
He is remembered chiefly for his song-lyric “The Rosary”, which was set to music by Ethelbert Nevin and became one of the most popular parlour songs of its time.

poets.name: Algernon Charles Swinburne
poets.credit: Portrait of Algernon Charles Swinburne · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Algernon Charles Swinburne (1837–1909) was an English poet notorious in his own day for the sensuous, metrically dazzling, and often scandalous verse of Poems and Ballads.
An ardent republican, he also wrote fervent political verse cheering Italian unification and liberty, alongside a huge later output of odes, elegies, and sonnets.

poets.name: Henry Kendall
bio: Henry Kendall (1839–1882) was an Australian poet, born at Ulladulla, New South Wales, who worked as a clerk, a journalist and finally an inspector of forests.
His books include Poems and Songs (1862), Leaves from Australian Forests (1869) and Songs from the Mountains (1880).

poets.name: William Dean Howells
poets.credit: Photograph of William Dean Howells by Underwood & Underwood · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Dean Howells (1837–1920) was an American novelist, critic and editor, born at Martins Ferry, Ohio. He edited The Atlantic Monthly from 1871 to 1881, and championed literary realism in novels such as The Rise of Silas Lapham.
He began as a poet and, with John James Piatt, published Poems of Two Friends (1860); he continued to write occasional verse throughout his life.

poets.name: Byron Forceythe Willson
poets.credit: Portrait of Byron Forceythe Willson, from The Magazine of Poetry · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Byron Forceythe Willson (1837–1867) was an American poet born in Little Genesee, New York, and raised in Ohio. He wrote patriotic verse during the Civil War, including “The Old Sergeant”, which appeared in The Atlantic Monthly in 1863.
He died young, in 1867. Knowles included his lyric “No More” in his anthology of American lyrics.

poets.name: John Todhunter
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Todhunter was born in Dublin, practised as a physician and later turned to literature, writing poems and verse plays. He settled in Bedford Park, London.
Yeats printed his poems "The Banshee" and "Aghadoe" in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: James Ryder Randall
poets.credit: Photograph of James Ryder Randall by Blessing & Co., Baltimore (before 1908) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Ryder Randall (1839–1908) was an American poet and journalist, born at Baltimore, Maryland. He was teaching at Poydras College in Louisiana in April 1861 when news of the Baltimore riot moved him to write “Maryland, My Maryland”.
Set to the tune of “O Tannenbaum”, the poem became a rallying song of the Confederacy. Randall later worked as a newspaper editor in Georgia.

poets.name: Lady Charlotte Elliot
bio: Lady Charlotte Elliot (1839–1880) was an English poet, the author of Medusa and Other Poems (1878).
Her poem “The Wife of Loki”, on the Norse myth, is included in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: John Davidson
bio: John Davidson (1857–1909) was a Scottish poet, playwright and novelist, born in Barrhead, Renfrewshire. He came to London in the 1890s and made his name with Fleet Street Eclogues and the Ballads and Songs of 1894.

His verse ranges from vigorous ballads of city life to the Testaments of his later years. He took his own life in 1909. Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920) printed his long Ballad of Hell, given here.

poets.name: Duncan Campbell Scott
bio: Duncan Campbell Scott (1862–1947), born in Ottawa, was a civil servant in the Department of Indian Affairs and one of the Confederation poets.

His first collection, The Magic House and Other Poems, appeared in 1893; the poems here predate it. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Thomas William Rolleston
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas William Rolleston was born in County Offaly and was a poet, translator and essayist of the Irish literary revival. He co-edited a Treasury of Irish Poetry with Stopford Brooke.
He died in 1920.

poets.name: William Watson
bio: William Watson (1858–1935) was an English poet, born at Burley-in-Wharfedale, Yorkshire. He made his reputation in the 1890s with poems on public themes and with elegant, formal lyrics, and was often spoken of as a possible poet laureate.
He was knighted in 1917. His volumes include Wordsworth's Grave and Other Poems and The Hope of the World (1897). The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Victor James Daley
bio: Victor James Daley (1858–1905) was an Irish-born poet who came to Australia in 1878 and became a leading figure of Sydney's bohemian literary circle.
His books include At Dawn and Dusk (1898); Wine and Roses appeared after his death.

poets.name: Francis Thompson
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Thompson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Thompson (1859–1907) was an English poet who spent years destitute and addicted to opium on the streets of London before his talent was discovered and he found refuge among Catholic friends.
His best-known poem, The Hound of Heaven, describes a soul fleeing and finally yielding to divine pursuit.

poets.name: Alice Werner
bio: Alice Werner (1859–1935) was a British scholar of African languages and poet, later a professor at the School of Oriental Studies in London.
Her early verse, which includes the Australian ballad Bannerman of the Dandenong, was collected in A Time and Times.

poets.name: Helen Gray Cone
bio: Helen Gray Cone (1859–1934) was an American poet and teacher, born in New York City. She graduated from the Normal College in 1876 and from 1899 was professor of English literature at Hunter College.
Her volumes of verse include Oberon and Puck (1885), The Ride to the Lady (1893) and Soldiers of the Light (1911).

poets.name: Edward J. Wheeler
bio: Edward Jewitt Wheeler (1859–1922) was an American editor and poet, born at Cleveland, Ohio. He edited The Literary Digest from 1895 to 1905 and Current Opinion from 1905, and was literary editor of Funk and Wagnalls.
He was one of the founders of the Poetry Society of America in 1909 and served as its first president.

poets.name: Rose Kavanagh
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Rose Kavanagh was an Irish poet and journalist, born in County Tyrone, who wrote for Irish periodicals. She died young, in 1891.
Her poem "Lough Bray" was included by Yeats in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Charles G. D. Roberts
poets.credit: Photograph of Charles G. D. Roberts, 1904 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Charles George Douglas Roberts (1860–1943) was a Canadian poet and prose writer, born in Douglas, New Brunswick. He studied at the University of New Brunswick, taught and edited in Toronto and New York, and became famous for his animal stories as well as his poems.
His volumes of verse include Orion, and Other Poems (1880), Songs of the Common Day (1893) and New York Nocturnes (1898). Anthologists of his own time grouped him with the American poets.

poets.name: George Santayana
bio: George Santayana (1863–1952) was a philosopher, essayist and poet, born in Madrid and raised in Boston. He taught philosophy at Harvard and wrote The Sense of Beauty (1896) and Interpretations of Poetry and Religion (1900).
His poetry, mostly in sonnet form, includes Sonnets and Other Verses (1894) and Lucifer (1899). Rittenhouse printed three of his sonnets in 1913.

poets.name: Alfred Perceval Graves
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Alfred Perceval Graves was born in Dublin and worked as a school inspector, while writing songs and verse and collecting Irish and Welsh folk music. His song "Father O'Flynn" became widely popular.
He was the father of the poet Robert Graves and died in 1931.

poets.name: Lewis Carroll
poets.credit: Portrait of Lewis Carroll · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lewis Carroll, the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (1832–1898), was an Oxford mathematician best known for the Alice books, whose fondness for nonsense and wordplay also produced a distinctive body of comic and whimsical verse.
The Hunting of the Snark and the parodies collected in Phantasmagoria remain classics of English nonsense poetry.

poets.name: Adam Lindsay Gordon
bio: Adam Lindsay Gordon (1833–1870) was an Anglo-Australian poet, born in the Azores and educated in England, who emigrated to South Australia in 1853 and worked as a mounted trooper, horse-breaker and steeplechase rider.
He published Sea Spray and Smoke Drift (1867) and Bush Ballads and Galloping Rhymes (1870), and died by his own hand at Brighton, Victoria.

poets.name: Mary Woolsey Howland
bio: Mary Woolsey Howland (1832–1864) was an American poet from a New York family, one of the Woolsey sisters, who died in 1864. She is represented in this archive by a single poem, “In the Hospital”, which Knowles included in his anthology of American lyrics.
The poem was written during the years of the Civil War and is a quiet meditation on suffering and consolation.

poets.name: Edmund Clarence Stedman
poets.credit: Photograph of Edmund Clarence Stedman by Alman and Company, New York · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edmund Clarence Stedman (1833–1908) was an American poet and critic, born at Hartford, Connecticut. He earned his living as a stockbroker in New York while writing poetry and criticism, and edited, with Ellen Mackay Hutchinson, the Library of American Literature.
His critical books Victorian Poets (1875) and Poets of America (1885) were standard works; his own verse includes the satirical “Pan in Wall Street”.

poets.name: Sarah Anne Curzon
poets.credit: Portrait of Sarah Anne Curzon, Godey's Magazine (July 1897) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sarah Anne Curzon (1833–1898) was an English-born Canadian writer and advocate of women's suffrage, who lived in Toronto.
She wrote the poem and play Laura Secord, the Heroine of 1812 (1887). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Annie Adams Fields
