poets.credit: Portrait of Annie Adams Fields by John Singer Sargent, 1890 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Annie Adams Fields (1834–1915) was an American writer and literary hostess, born in Boston. As the wife of the publisher James T. Fields, she presided over a salon at 148 Charles Street, attended by Hawthorne, Longfellow, Dickens and other leading writers.
She wrote poems, memoirs and biographies, including Authors and Friends (1896) and Life and Letters of Harriet Beecher Stowe (1897).

poets.name: Rudyard Kipling
poets.credit: Portrait of Rudyard Kipling · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was an English author born in Bombay, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907, whose verse gave voice to soldiers, machines, and the British imperial experience in vigorous, ballad-like rhythms.
Poems such as If—, Gunga Din, and Recessional made him one of the most quoted poets in the English language.

poets.name: Arthur Symons
bio: Arthur Symons (1865–1945) was a Welsh-born poet and critic, a leading figure of the Decadent and Symbolist movements in Britain in the 1890s. His books of verse include Silhouettes (1892) and London Nights (1895).

His critical study The Symbolist Movement in Literature (1899) introduced French poets such as Verlaine and Mallarmé to English readers. The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: William Gay
bio: William Gay (1865–1897) was a Scottish-born poet who emigrated to Australia.
He published Christ on Olympus, and Other Poems (1893) and a volume of sonnets.

poets.name: Edward Dyson
bio: Edward Dyson (1865–1931) was an Australian journalist, poet and story writer, born in Victoria, who worked as a miner before turning to writing.
His books include Rhymes from the Mines, and Other Lines (1896).

poets.name: Dowell O'Reilly
bio: Dowell O'Reilly (1865–1923) was an Australian poet and short-story writer, born in Sydney, who also sat in the New South Wales parliament.
His verse was collected in Tears and Triumph (1913).

poets.name: Stephen Phillips
bio: Stephen Phillips (1868–1915) was an English poet and verse dramatist. He won sudden fame with his Poems of 1897 and with the plays Paolo and Francesca (1899), Herod (1900) and Ulysses (1902), which revived blank-verse drama on the London stage.
His popularity faded within a few years, and he died in 1915. The two short lyrics here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920); the extract from Herod printed there is not included.

poets.name: Jennings Carmichael
bio: Jennings Carmichael (1868–1904) was an Australian poet.
Her verse was published in a volume of Poems.

poets.name: Lord Alfred Douglas
bio: Lord Alfred Douglas (1870–1945) was an English poet, the younger son of the Marquess of Queensberry, and the close companion of Oscar Wilde, whose trials in 1895 made both their names notorious.
His own sonnets and lyrics, written in a clear late-Romantic manner, appeared in volumes such as The City of the Soul (1899). The poem here comes from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Nora Hopper Chesson
bio: Nora Hopper Chesson (1871–1906) was a poet and story-writer of Irish descent, born in Exeter, who drew on Irish folklore and song. She belonged to the Celtic revival of the 1890s and was praised by W. B. Yeats.
She married the writer W. H. Chesson in 1901 and died young, in 1906. Her poem here comes from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Alice Meynell
poets.credit: Portrait of Alice Meynell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alice Meynell (1847–1922) was an English poet, essayist, and suffragist, admired in her lifetime for the precision and restraint of her devout, closely observed lyrics.
A convert to Catholicism, she wrote often of motherhood, nature, and quiet spiritual attention.

poets.name: Anne Glenny Wilson
bio: Anne Glenny Wilson (1848–1930), who published as Mrs James Glenny Wilson, was an Australian poet and writer.
Her verse was collected in A Book of Verses.

poets.name: John Vance Cheney
poets.credit: Portrait of John Vance Cheney (1896) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Vance Cheney (1848–1922) was an American poet and librarian, born at Groveland, New York. He was librarian of the San Francisco Free Public Library from 1887 to 1894, and of the Newberry Library in Chicago until 1899, and then lived in California.
His volumes of verse include Thistle Drift (1887), Out of the Silence (1897), The Time of Roses (1908) and At the Silver Gate (1911).

poets.name: Arthur Hugh Clough
poets.credit: Portrait of Arthur Hugh Clough · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Hugh Clough (1819–1861) was an English poet and close friend of Matthew Arnold, whose verse candidly registers the Victorian crisis of religious faith and doubt.
His long poems Amours de Voyage and The Bothie of Tober-na-Vuolich experiment with conversational, unglamorous realism unusual for their time.

poets.name: Ernest Dowson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ernest Dowson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ernest Dowson (1867–1900) was an English poet of the 1890s Decadent movement, associated with the Rhymers' Club, who died of tuberculosis and drink at thirty-two.
His hallmark is a wistful, musical melancholy, most famous in the refrain "I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion," from his poem Non Sum Qualis Eram.

poets.name: Henry Lawson
bio: Henry Lawson (1867–1922) was an Australian poet and short-story writer, born near Grenfell, New South Wales.
His books include In the Days When the World Was Wide, and Other Verses (1896) and While the Billy Boils (1896); he is regarded as the voice of the bush and the working man.

poets.name: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
poets.credit: Portrait of Alfred, Lord Tennyson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892) was Poet Laureate of Great Britain for over four decades and the most popular and representative poet of the Victorian age.
His work ranges from the intimate grief of In Memoriam A.H.H., written for a dead friend, to the martial narrative verse of Enoch Arden and the ballad-like Maud.

poets.name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poets.credit: Portrait of Elizabeth Barrett Browning · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1806–1861) was one of the most celebrated English poets of her day, an invalid for much of her youth who eloped to Italy with fellow poet Robert Browning in 1846.
Her Sonnets from the Portuguese, written to Robert during their courtship, remain her best-loved work, alongside socially engaged narrative poems on slavery, child labour, and women's lives.

poets.name: Michael Doheny
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Michael Doheny was born in County Tipperary and became a lawyer and a Young Ireland nationalist. After the failed rising of 1848 he escaped to America, where he wrote The Felon's Track (1849).
He died in New York in 1863.

poets.name: Helen Selina Blackwood, Lady Dufferin
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Helen Selina Blackwood, Lady Dufferin, was a granddaughter of Richard Brinsley Sheridan and the mother of the diplomat Lord Dufferin. She wrote songs and verse and later became Countess of Gifford.
Her "Lament of the Irish Emigrant" is her best-known poem.

poets.name: George Frederick Cameron
poets.credit: Portrait of George Frederick Cameron, from Canadian Poets (1916) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Frederick Cameron (1854–1885) was a Nova Scotian lawyer, journalist and poet who died young.

His collected Lyrics on Freedom, Love and Death appeared in 1887 after his death. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Barry Straton
bio: Barry Straton (1854–1901) was a Canadian poet of the Confederation generation.

Little biographical detail is recorded here beyond his appearance in Lighthall's anthology. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Louise Chandler Moulton
poets.credit: Photograph of Louise Chandler Moulton by James E. Purdy, 1904 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Louise Chandler Moulton (1835–1908) was an American poet and journalist, born at Pomfret, Connecticut, and long resident in Boston. She contributed to the Boston Herald, and spent many seasons in London, where she knew leading writers of the day.
Her verse, collected in several volumes, is lyrical and often melancholy.

poets.name: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
poets.credit: Portrait of Dante Gabriel Rossetti · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dante Gabriel Rossetti (1828–1882) was an English poet and painter, a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, who worked in sister arts of image and verse throughout his career.
His sonnet sequence The House of Life traces the arc of love and loss with dense, jewelled imagery, while The Blessed Damozel imagines a dead woman watching for her lover from heaven.

poets.name: Daniel Henry Deniehy
bio: Daniel Henry Deniehy (1828–1865) was an Australian-born lawyer, journalist, orator and poet, remembered for his 1853 speech mocking a colonial 'bunyip aristocracy'.
He wrote verse for Sydney newspapers and edited the weekly The Southern Cross (1859–60).

poets.name: Richard Rowe
bio: Richard Rowe (1828–1879) was an English-born journalist and writer who lived for some years in Australia and wrote for Sydney newspapers.
He published Peter 'Possum's Portfolio, a collection of his Australian sketches and verse.

poets.name: William McLennan
bio: William McLennan (1856–1904) was a Montreal lawyer and writer who published Songs of Old Canada (1886), translations of French-Canadian folk-songs.
Only his original poem is included here. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Louis Stevenson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Louis Stevenson (1850–1894) was a Scottish novelist and poet, best known for Treasure Island and Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, who also wrote widely loved verse.
A Child's Garden of Verses captures the imaginative world of childhood, while Songs of Travel, mostly written in his final years in Samoa, turns to restlessness, distance, and mortality.

poets.name: Philip Joseph Holdsworth
bio: Philip Joseph Holdsworth (1851–1902) was an Australian poet, born in Sydney, who spent time in the Queensland outback.
His books include Station Hunting on the Warrego.

poets.name: John Liddell Kelly
bio: John Liddell Kelly (1850–1925) was an Australian poet.
His verse was collected in Heather and Fern.

poets.name: Robert Richardson
bio: Robert Richardson (1850–1901) was an Australian clergyman and poet.
His verse was collected in Willow and Wattle.

poets.name: James Lister Cuthbertson
bio: James Lister Cuthbertson (1851–1910) was a Scottish-born poet and schoolmaster who emigrated to Victoria and taught at Geelong Grammar School.
He published Barwon Ballads (1893) and other verse, including the poem Australia Federata.

poets.name: John Farrell
bio: John Farrell (1851–1904) was an Australian journalist and poet, born in Buenos Aires, who wrote for radical and labour newspapers.
His collected verse appeared as My Sundowner and Other Poems (1904).

poets.name: Arthur Patchett Martin
bio: Arthur Patchett Martin (1851–1902) was an English-born journalist and critic who worked in Australia and later settled in London.
He published The Withered Jester, and Other Verses.

poets.name: Charles Kingsley
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Kingsley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Kingsley (1819–1875) was an English clergyman, novelist, and poet, remembered as a children's author for The Water-Babies and as a muscular-Christian social reformer.
His poems range from the classical narrative Andromeda, written in unrhymed hexameters, to plain-spoken ballads and songs of the sea and English rural life.

poets.name: George Murray
bio: George Murray (1830–1910), born in Bermuda, was a Montreal schoolmaster and poet.
The poems here are those Lighthall selected for Songs of the Great Dominion (1889).

poets.name: Edward Lear
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward Lear · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Lear (1812–1888) was an English artist and writer who, alongside a career as a natural history and landscape painter, invented much of the English nonsense verse tradition.
His limericks, alphabets, and songs such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat and The Jumblies, collected across several Book of Nonsense volumes, delight in invented words and gentle absurdity.

poets.name: Charles Harpur
bio: Charles Harpur (1813–1868) was an Australian-born poet, born at Windsor, New South Wales, who spent much of his life in the bush as a farmer and later a gold-fields official.
He published Thoughts: A Series of Sonnets (1845) and The Bushrangers (1853), and wrote under the influence of Wordsworth and Shelley; his best work is in longer poems.

poets.name: Henry Parkes
bio: Sir Henry Parkes (1815–1896) was an English-born politician who emigrated to New South Wales in 1839, served several times as its Premier and is remembered as the 'Father of Federation'.
He was also a poet, publishing Stolen Moments (1842) and several further volumes of verse, among them Fragmentary Thoughts; he printed the early work of Henry Kendall in his paper The Empire.

poets.name: Charles Fenno Hoffman
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Fenno Hoffman by Cephas Giovanni Thompson, 1843 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Fenno Hoffman (1806–1884) was an American poet, novelist and editor, born in New York City. He edited several magazines, including the Knickerbocker, and wrote travel sketches of the American frontier as well as songs and ballads.
He suffered a mental breakdown in 1849 and spent his last decades in a hospital for the insane. His song “Sparkling and Bright” was widely sung.

poets.name: Jean Ingelow
poets.credit: Portrait of Jean Ingelow · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jean Ingelow (1820–1897) was an English poet and novelist, immensely popular in her lifetime, admired for narrative ballads and devotional lyrics of home, sea, and childhood.
Her poem The High Tide on the Coast of Lincolnshire (1571), a ballad of a great flood, remained a schoolroom favourite for generations.

poets.name: Menella Bute Smedley
bio: Menella Bute Smedley (1820–1877) was an English poet and novelist, a cousin of the novelist Frank Smedley, who published verse and prose fiction in the middle years of the century.
Elizabeth A. Sharp included two of her poems, “A Character” and “The Little Fair Soul”, in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Augusta Webster
bio: Augusta Webster (1837–1894), born Julia Augusta Davies, was an English poet, dramatist and essayist, and a supporter of women's suffrage who served on the London School Board. Her volumes include Dramatic Studies (1866), A Woman Sold and Other Poems (1867) and Portraits (1870).
She is admired for her dramatic monologues, among them “Circe”, which gives the enchantress her own voice; it and “English Stornelli” are in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: John Reade
bio: John Reade (1837–1919) was an Irish-born Canadian poet and journalist who settled in Montreal and long served as literary editor of the Montreal Gazette. He was a founding member of the Royal Society of Canada.
His best-known volume is The Prophecy of Merlin, and Other Poems (1870). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Charles Mair
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Mair, University of Alberta Libraries · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Mair (1838–1927) was a Canadian poet and public figure, born in Lanark, Upper Canada, who lived for many years on the western frontier.

He published Dreamland, and Other Poems (1868) and the verse drama Tecumseh (1886); only his lyric and narrative poems are included here. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: E. Pauline Johnson
poets.credit: Portrait of E. Pauline Johnson (Tekahionwake) by Cochran, c. 1895 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: E. Pauline Johnson (Tekahionwake, 1861–1913) was a Mohawk-English Canadian poet and performer, born on the Six Nations reserve near Brantford, Ontario.

Her best-known collection is The White Wampum (1895); the poems here predate it. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Archibald Lampman
poets.credit: Portrait of Archibald Lampman by William James Topley, 1889 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Archibald Lampman (1861–1899), born at Morpeth, Ontario, was a Post Office clerk in Ottawa and the leading poet of the Confederation generation.
His first book, Among the Millet and Other Poems, appeared in 1888. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Frederick George Scott
poets.credit: Portrait of Canon Frederick George Scott, from his book The Great War as I Saw It · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frederick George Scott (1861–1944) was a Canadian Anglican clergyman and poet, born in Montreal, who served as an army chaplain in the First World War.
His early volume The Soul's Quest (1888) supplies some of the poems here. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Henry Timrod
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Timrod (Review of Reviews Co.) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Timrod (1828–1867) was an American poet, born at Charleston, South Carolina, and often called the poet laureate of the Confederacy. He worked as a tutor and journalist, and wrote several of the best-known poems of the Southern cause during the Civil War.
He died of tuberculosis at Columbia, South Carolina, in 1867, in poverty. “Katie” and “Carolina” are among his best-known poems.

poets.name: Charles J. Kickham
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charles Joseph Kickham was born in County Tipperary and became a Fenian, a journalist, a poet and the author of the novel Knocknagow. An accident in youth left him with poor hearing and sight.
He died in 1882.

poets.name: Christopher Pearse Cranch
poets.credit: Portrait of Christopher Pearse Cranch (1892) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christopher Pearse Cranch (1813–1892) was an American poet, painter and Unitarian minister, born at Alexandria, Virginia. He belonged to the Transcendentalist circle, contributing to The Dial, and later lived for years in Europe as a landscape painter.
His volume Poems (1844) and his later books show a gentle idealism; he also translated Virgil’s Aeneid into blank verse.

poets.name: Edward FitzGerald
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward FitzGerald · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward FitzGerald (1809–1883) was an English writer whose free translation and adaptation of the medieval Persian quatrains of Omar Khayyam, The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, became one of the most quoted poems in the English language.
Reworked by FitzGerald through several editions, its meditations on wine, transience, and fate gave English verse a strikingly fatalistic, epicurean voice unlike anything else in the period.

poets.name: Alfred Domett
bio: Alfred Domett (1811–1887) was an English poet and friend of Robert Browning, who emigrated to New Zealand in 1842 and served as its Premier in 1862–63.
His long poem Ranolf and Amohia: A South-Sea Day-Dream (1872) is set in New Zealand.

poets.name: Sir Samuel Ferguson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Samuel Ferguson was born in Belfast and trained as a barrister. He was Deputy Keeper of the Public Records of Ireland and was knighted in 1878.
His verse drew on Irish legend and history, notably in Lays of the Western Gael (1865) and the long poem Congal (1872).

poets.name: Aubrey de Vere
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Aubrey de Vere was born at Curragh Chase, County Limerick, and published poetry, criticism and travel writing. He became a Roman Catholic in 1851.
His Irish poems include The Wedding of the Clans and The Bard Ethell. He is not to be confused with Edward de Vere, Earl of Oxford.

poets.name: Charles Heavysege
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Heavysege, Canadian Illustrated News (17 April 1875) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Heavysege (1816–1876), born in England, settled in Montreal in 1853 and worked as a carpenter and later as a journalist. He is best known for the dramatic poem Saul (1857).

The pieces here are short lyrics and sonnets from his verse drama Jephthah's Daughter (1865); his plays are not included. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Sir Daniel Wilson
bio: Sir Daniel Wilson (1816–1892) was a Scottish-born archaeologist and educator who became president of the University of Toronto.
He also wrote occasional verse, represented here by a single piece. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: William Wye Smith
bio: William Wye Smith (1827–1917) was a Scottish-born Canadian journalist and poet who wrote in English and in Scots, and later published a translation of the New Testament into Scots.
His Poems appeared in 1888. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: John James Piatt
poets.credit: Photograph of John James Piatt, c. 1900 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John James Piatt (1835–1917) was an American poet born in Indiana and raised in Ohio. With William Dean Howells he published Poems of Two Friends (1860), and he worked as a journalist and government clerk in Washington before serving as United States consul at Cork, Ireland.
He was married to the poet Sarah Morgan Bryan Piatt, and several of their volumes of verse appeared under both names.

poets.name: Coventry Patmore
poets.credit: Portrait of Coventry Patmore · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Coventry Patmore (1823–1896) was an English poet best known for The Angel in the House, a long narrative sequence idealizing married domestic love that became one of the era's most influential, and later most contested, poems.
A convert to Catholicism, his later odes turn toward mystical and religious themes.

poets.name: George Henry Boker
poets.credit: Photograph of George Henry Boker, 1855–65, Brady-Handy Photograph Collection (Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Henry Boker (1823–1890) was an American poet and dramatist, born in Philadelphia. His blank-verse tragedy Francesca da Rimini (1855) is the best known of his plays, and he later served as United States minister to Turkey and to Russia.
During the Civil War he wrote patriotic Union verse, collected in Poems of the War (1864), including “The Black Regiment” and “Dirge for a Soldier”.

poets.name: John Kells Ingram
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Kells Ingram was an Irish scholar, born in County Donegal, who became a fellow of Trinity College Dublin and later its librarian. He wrote on political economy as well as verse.
His ballad "The Memory of the Dead" was published in The Nation in 1843.

poets.name: Henry David Thoreau
poets.credit: Daguerreotype of Henry David Thoreau by Benjamin D. Maxham, 1856 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862) was an American essayist, naturalist and poet, born and long resident in Concord, Massachusetts. He is best known for Walden (1854) and for the essay “Civil Disobedience”.
He wrote verse throughout his life, much of it printed in The Dial and in his prose works; it is plain, observant poetry of the seasons and the countryside around Concord.

poets.name: William Allingham
poets.credit: Photograph of William Allingham · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Allingham (1824–1889) was an Irish poet born in Ballyshannon, County Donegal, where he spent his early working life as a customs officer. He published his first collection in 1850 and went on to Day and Night Songs (1854) and the long verse narrative Laurence Bloomfield in Ireland (1864), a portrait of the relations between landlords and tenants.

He later moved to England, edited Fraser's Magazine from 1874 to 1879, and married the illustrator Helen Paterson, who drew many of the pictures for his children's verse. He is remembered above all for the fairy poems, chiefly "The Fairies" ("Up the airy mountain"), and for the Donegal ballads and lyrics that W. B. Yeats chose for Sixteen Poems (1905) and the later Rhymes for the Young Folk.

poets.name: James Lionel Michael
bio: James Lionel Michael (1824–1868) was an English-born solicitor and poet who emigrated to Australia in the gold-rush years and practised in Sydney and later at Grafton on the Clarence River.
He gave early encouragement to the young Henry Kendall, who worked in his office; he wrote the poem John Cumberland and contributed verse to Sydney periodicals.

poets.name: Thomas Davis
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Davis was born in Mallow, County Cork, and in 1842 helped to found the newspaper The Nation, the voice of the Young Ireland movement. He wrote the ballads collected in The Spirit of the Nation.
He died of scarlet fever in 1845, aged thirty.

poets.name: Hester Sigerson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Hester Sigerson was an Irish poet, the wife of the physician and writer George Sigerson and the mother of the poet Dora Sigerson Shorter. She contributed verse to Irish periodicals.
Yeats printed her short "Mad Song" in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Adelaide Anne Procter
poets.credit: Portrait of Adelaide Anne Procter · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Adelaide Anne Procter (1825–1864) was an English poet and social activist, a devout Catholic and one of the best-selling poets of the Victorian era after Tennyson himself.
Her collection Legends and Lyrics gathers narrative ballads and devotional verse, often concerned with charity, suffering, and quiet endurance.

poets.name: Rolf Boldrewood (Thomas Alexander Browne)
bio: Thomas Alexander Browne (1826–1915), who wrote as 'Rolf Boldrewood', was an English-born pastoralist, police magistrate and gold commissioner in Australia.
He is best known for the bushranging novel Robbery Under Arms; he also wrote Old Melbourne Memories, and occasional verse.

poets.name: Richard Henry Stoddard
poets.credit: Photograph of Richard Henry Stoddard by Rockwood (before 1903) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Henry Stoddard (1825–1903) was an American poet and critic, born at Hingham, Massachusetts. He worked in an iron foundry as a young man, taught himself to write, and later became literary editor of the New York Mail and Express.
He was a central figure of the New York literary circle of his day, alongside Bayard Taylor and Edmund Clarence Stedman, and his polished lyrics were widely anthologised.

poets.name: Bayard Taylor
poets.credit: Portrait of Bayard Taylor · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bayard Taylor (1825–1878) was an American poet, travel writer and translator, born at Kennett Square, Pennsylvania. His accounts of journeys through Europe, Africa, and Asia made him a celebrated figure, and his verse translation of Goethe’s Faust (1870–71) was long standard.
He served as United States minister to Germany and died at Berlin in 1878. His lyrics, such as the “Bedouin Song”, were popular in his lifetime.

poets.name: Thomas D'Arcy McGee
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas D'Arcy McGee was born in Carlingford, County Louth, and was a Young Ireland writer and journalist. He emigrated, became a Canadian politician and one of the Fathers of Confederation.
He was assassinated in Ottawa in 1868.

poets.name: Pamelia Vining Yule
bio: Pamelia Vining Yule (1825–1897) was a Canadian poet.
Her Poems of the Heart and Home appeared in 1881. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Stephen Collins Foster
poets.credit: Portrait of Stephen Collins Foster, c. 1860 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Stephen Collins Foster (1826–1864) was an American songwriter, born at Lawrenceville, now part of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He wrote both the words and music of songs such as “Oh! Susanna” (1848), “Old Folks at Home” (1851) and “My Old Kentucky Home” (1853).
He died in New York City in 1864. His song lyrics, printed here as poems, were among the most widely sung in the United States.

poets.name: Dinah Maria Craik
poets.credit: Portrait of Dinah Maria Craik by Hubert von Herkomer · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dinah Maria Craik (1826–1887), born Dinah Maria Mulock in Stoke-on-Trent, was a novelist and poet, best known for the novel John Halifax, Gentleman (1856). In 1865 she married George Lillie Craik.
Her poems, which appeared in volumes from 1859, include the tender cradle-song “Philip, my King”; three of them are in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Emily Pfeiffer
poets.credit: Portrait of Emily Pfeiffer, 1890 (Charles Wells Moulton) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emily Jane Pfeiffer (1827–1890), born Emily Davis, was an English-language poet who published Poems (1876), Songs and Sonnets (1880) and Under the Aspens (1882), and wrote on the position of women. She married Jurgen Edward Pfeiffer in 1853.
She left money in her will for the higher education of women. Five of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Isa Blagden
poets.credit: Portrait of Isa Blagden (before 1873) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Isabella (Isa) Blagden (1817–1873) was an English writer who lived in Florence and was a close friend of Robert and Elizabeth Barrett Browning. She wrote novels, and her verse was collected in Poems (1873), published after her death.
Her short lyrics “Sorrow” and “Endurance” are included in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Rosanna Leprohon
poets.credit: Portrait of Rosanna Leprohon, from A Woman of the Century (1893) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rosanna Eleanor Leprohon (1829–1879), born in Montreal, was a Canadian novelist and poet.
Her poems were collected in 1881. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Emily Brontë
poets.credit: Portrait of Emily Brontë · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emily Brontë (1818–1848) is best known as the author of Wuthering Heights, but she also wrote intense, visionary lyric poetry, much of it set in the imagined world of Gondal she created with her sister Anne.

Published pseudonymously as "Ellis Bell" alongside her sisters' verse in 1846, her poems of longing, imprisonment, and the moors were far better received by contemporary critics than the sisters' novels first were.

poets.name: William Forster
bio: William Forster (1818–1882) was an Australian politician and writer who served as Premier of New South Wales in 1859–60.
He was also a poet and dramatist, the author of the verse drama Midas, from which Stevens takes his lyric.

poets.name: Eliza Cook
poets.credit: Portrait of Eliza Cook by William Etty, 1845 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Eliza Cook (1818–1889) was a London-born poet whose popular, plain-spoken verse made her one of the best-known women poets of the 1840s. Her first collection, Melaia and Other Poems, appeared in 1838, and “The Old Arm-Chair” became one of her best-loved songs.
From 1849 to 1854 she edited Eliza Cook's Journal, a weekly paper for working readers. Three of her lyrics appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: William Kirby
poets.credit: Portrait of William Kirby, c. 1865, from Le Chien d'or (1926 ed.) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Kirby (1817–1906) was an English-born Canadian writer who settled at Niagara-on-the-Lake. He is best known for the historical novel The Golden Dog (1877).
His verse includes the long poem The U. E.: A Tale of Upper Canada (1859). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Alexander McLachlan
bio: Alexander McLachlan (1818–1896), born in Scotland, emigrated to Canada in 1840 and farmed in Ontario while writing popular verse in the manner of Burns.
He was often called the Burns of Canada. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Nathaniel Parker Willis
poets.credit: Photograph of Nathaniel Parker Willis, Mathew Brady studio · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nathaniel Parker Willis (1806–1867) was an American poet, editor and journalist, born at Portland, Maine, and educated at Yale. He edited the New-York Mirror and later the Home Journal, and was among the best-paid magazine writers of his time.
His early scriptural and sentimental poems made him widely popular, and he was a prominent figure of the New York literary scene.

poets.name: Christina Rossetti
poets.credit: Portrait of Christina Rossetti · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christina Rossetti (1830–1894) was an English poet of devotional intensity and quiet formal mastery, sister of the painter-poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti.
Best known for ‘Goblin Market’ and the carol ‘In the Bleak Midwinter,’ she also wrote Sing-Song (1872), a book of nursery rhymes for children.

poets.name: Ellen O'Leary
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ellen O'Leary was an Irish poet, born in County Tipperary and the sister of the Fenian John O'Leary. Her collected verses, Lays of Country, Home and Friends, appeared in 1891, after her death.
She died in 1889.

poets.name: Isa Craig-Knox
bio: Isa Craig-Knox (1831–1903), born Isa Craig in Edinburgh, was a Scottish poet and journalist who worked with the women's movement of the 1850s and 1860s. In 1859 she won the prize for the ode written for the Burns centenary celebration at the Crystal Palace, and in 1866 she married John Knox.
Her “Ballad of the Brides of Quair” is the piece chosen for Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Walt Whitman
poets.credit: Portrait of Walt Whitman (George Collins Cox, 1887) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Walt Whitman (1819–1892) was an American poet, essayist, and journalist from Long Island, New York, widely regarded as the father of free verse and one of the most influential poets in American literature.

His single, ever-expanding book ‘Leaves of Grass’, first published in 1855 and revised throughout his life into the 1892 ‘deathbed’ edition used here, celebrated democracy, the body, and the American landscape in a sweeping, unrhymed line.

poets.name: Herman Melville
poets.credit: Joseph Oriel Eaton, 1870 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Herman Melville (1819–1891) was an American novelist, short-story writer and poet, born in New York City. He is best known for the sea novel Moby-Dick (1851), which was little appreciated in his lifetime.

Battle-Pieces and Aspects of the War (1866) was his first book of verse, a sequence of poems on the American Civil War, from John Brown to the surrender at Appomattox and its aftermath. Melville turned chiefly to poetry in his later years and worked for many years as a customs inspector in New York.

poets.name: Emily Dickinson
poets.credit: Portrait of Emily Dickinson (daguerreotype, c. 1847) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) was an American poet who lived a famously reclusive life in Amherst, Massachusetts, writing nearly 1,800 poems of which barely a dozen were published in her lifetime.

Her tightly compressed, slant-rhymed verse on death, nature, faith, and the inner mind — much of it untitled and left in small hand-sewn booklets — was published posthumously and is now considered among the most original in American literature.

poets.name: Helen Hunt Jackson
poets.credit: Photograph of Helen Hunt Jackson by Charles F. Conly, c. 1884 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Helen Hunt Jackson (1830–1885) was an American writer, born at Amherst, Massachusetts, and a childhood friend of Emily Dickinson. She wrote poems, essays, and stories, signing some of them “H.H.”, and settled in Colorado Springs after her second marriage.
She is best known for A Century of Dishonor (1881), a protest against the treatment of Native Americans, and for the novel Ramona (1884).

poets.name: John Hunter-Duvar
bio: John Hunter-Duvar (1821–1899) was a Scottish-born poet and dramatist who settled on Prince Edward Island.

His verse dramas include The Enamorado (1879) and De Roberval (1888); only his lyric pieces are included here. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: George Martin
bio: George Martin (1822–1900) was a Canadian poet.

His poem Marguerite; or, The Isle of Demons (1887), a verse retelling of a sixteenth-century Quebec legend, supplies two of the pieces here. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Charles Sangster
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Sangster, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Sangster (1822–1893) was born in Kingston, Upper Canada, and worked as a journalist and civil servant. He is often called the first important native-born Canadian poet.

His principal books are The St. Lawrence and the Saguenay, and Other Poems (1856) and Hesperus, and Other Poems and Lyrics (1860). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Harriet Prescott Spofford
poets.credit: Photograph of Harriet Prescott Spofford by Brown Brothers, New York · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Harriet Prescott Spofford (1835–1921) was an American writer born at Calais, Maine, who lived for many years at Newburyport, Massachusetts. She became known in 1859 for her story “In a Cellar” in The Atlantic Monthly and wrote novels, stories, and poems.
Her verse is lyrical and compressed, and several short poems were taken up by anthologists of her time.

poets.name: Edgar Allan Poe
poets.credit: Portrait of Edgar Allan Poe (daguerreotype, 1849) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edgar Allan Poe (1809–1849) was an American writer, editor, and literary critic best known for tales of mystery and the macabre, but he considered himself first a poet and a founder of the detective and horror genres.

His musical, tightly-wrought verse — including ‘The Raven’, ‘Annabel Lee’, and ‘The Bells’ — explores loss, beauty, and death, and made him one of the most widely imitated poets in the English language.

poets.name: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (Julia Margaret Cameron, 1868) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1807–1882) was an American poet and Harvard professor, and by far the most popular and widely read American poet of the 19th century, both at home and in Europe.

A leading figure among the ‘Fireside Poets’, he wrote narrative epics such as ‘The Song of Hiawatha’ and ‘Paul Revere’s Ride’ alongside shorter lyrics on nature, faith, and everyday life, in verse prized for its clarity and musicality.

poets.name: Charles Dawson Shanly
bio: Charles Dawson Shanly (1811–1875) was an Irish-born writer who spent part of his life in Canada and the United States.
He is remembered chiefly for the ballad The Walker of the Snow. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ralph Waldo Emerson (Josiah Johnson Hawes, 1857) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) was an American essayist, lecturer, and poet from Concord, Massachusetts, and the leading voice of the Transcendentalist movement, which prized intuition, nature, and individual conscience over inherited tradition.

Best known for essays such as ‘Self-Reliance’ and ‘Nature’, he also wrote compact, philosophical verse — including ‘Concord Hymn’, ‘The Rhodora’, and ‘Brahma’ — that distilled his ideas into poetic form.

poets.name: William Cullen Bryant
poets.credit: Portrait of William Cullen Bryant — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Cullen Bryant (1794–1878) was an American poet and long-time editor of the New York Evening Post, whose meditative nature poetry helped establish a distinctly American Romantic voice.
Written when he was only seventeen, ‘Thanatopsis’ remains his best-known work, and poems such as ‘To a Waterfowl’ and ‘The Prairies’ celebrate the American landscape with a solemn, elevated calm.

poets.name: Joseph Rodman Drake
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Joseph Rodman Drake, 19th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joseph Rodman Drake (1795–1820) was an American poet born in New York City. Orphaned young, he studied medicine at Columbia College and married Sarah Eckford in 1816. He became a close friend of the poet Fitz-Greene Halleck, and the two wrote the satirical Croaker verses for the New York Evening Post in 1819.

His fairy poem The Culprit Fay, written in 1819, drew on the scenery of the Hudson Highlands. He died of consumption in 1820, aged twenty-five. His collected poems were published posthumously in 1835 by his daughter, and the 1836 edition is the source of this selection; Halleck's elegy for him, "Green be the turf above thee", is among the best remembered American elegies.

poets.name: John Richardson
bio: Major John Richardson (1796–1852), born at Queenston, Upper Canada, served in the War of 1812 and later wrote novels, notably Wacousta (1832).
His narrative poem Tecumseh; or, The Warrior of the West appeared in 1828. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: James Russell Lowell
poets.credit: Portrait of James Russell Lowell (1855) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Russell Lowell (1819–1891) was an American poet, critic, and diplomat from Cambridge, Massachusetts, who edited the Atlantic Monthly and later served as U.S. minister to Spain and Britain.

A member of the ‘Fireside Poets’, he wrote lyric and narrative verse — most famously ‘The Vision of Sir Launfal’ — alongside satirical and abolitionist poetry that engaged directly with the politics of his day.

poets.name: Julia Ward Howe
poets.credit: Photograph of Julia Ward Howe, 1895 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Julia Ward Howe (1819–1910) was an American poet, abolitionist and campaigner for women’s suffrage, born in New York City. She was married to the reformer Samuel Gridley Howe, with whom she edited the antislavery paper The Commonwealth.
Her “Battle Hymn of the Republic”, written in 1861 and printed in The Atlantic Monthly in February 1862, became the most famous song of the Union cause.

poets.name: Thomas William Parsons
bio: Thomas William Parsons (1819–1892) was an American poet and translator, born in Boston, who practised as a dentist. He spent decades translating Dante’s Inferno into English verse, a work that earned him a lasting if modest reputation.
His original poems, such as “On a Bust of Dante”, are classical in manner and were admired by his Boston contemporaries.

poets.name: George Eliot
poets.credit: Portrait of George Eliot by François d'Albert Durade (replica of a work of 1849) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880), the Warwickshire-born novelist of Adam Bede, The Mill on the Floss, Middlemarch and Daniel Deronda. She also translated Strauss and Feuerbach.

She wrote verse throughout her career, including the dramatic poem The Spanish Gypsy (1868) and the collection The Legend of Jubal and Other Poems (1874); her lines beginning “O, may I join the choir invisible” are among her most famous.

poets.name: John Greenleaf Whittier
poets.credit: Portrait of John Greenleaf Whittier — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Greenleaf Whittier (1807–1892) was an American Quaker poet and dedicated abolitionist from Massachusetts, who used verse throughout his life to campaign against slavery and to record New England legend and rural memory.
His long autobiographical poem ‘Snow-Bound’ (1866), recalling his family snowed in at their farmhouse, became one of the most beloved American poems of the 19th century.

poets.name: Caroline Norton
poets.credit: Portrait of Caroline Norton by George Hayter · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Caroline Norton (1808–1877) was a granddaughter of Richard Brinsley Sheridan, a poet and novelist of the 1830s and 1840s whose collections include The Sorrows of Rosalie (1829), The Undying One (1830) and The Dream and Other Poems (1840).

After a failed and bitter marriage she campaigned against the legal position of married women; her pamphlets helped bring about the Custody of Infants Act (1839) and the Matrimonial Causes Act (1857).

poets.name: Oliver Wendell Holmes
poets.credit: Photograph of Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., c. 1879 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. (1809–1894) was a Boston physician, Harvard professor of anatomy and physiology, essayist and poet, one of the Fireside Poets who made New England verse a household possession. His 1830 poem “Old Ironsides” is credited with helping to save the frigate Constitution from being broken up.

His genial comic and occasional verse — “The Deacon’s Masterpiece,” “The Last Leaf,” the dinner poems read for his Harvard classmates — sits beside the more serious “The Chambered Nautilus,” first printed in his Atlantic Monthly series “The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table” (1857–58). The poems here follow his collected Poetical Works as issued in 1893.

poets.name: Mary Cowden Clarke
poets.credit: Photograph of Mary Cowden Clarke by G. B. Sciutto & Co., c. 1870 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Victoria Cowden Clarke (1809–1898), born Novello, was the daughter of the music publisher Vincent Novello and in 1828 married Charles Cowden Clarke. She compiled The Complete Concordance to Shakespeare (1845), the first of its kind in English, and wrote The Girlhood of Shakespeare's Heroines.
Her poem “At Midnight of ‘All Souls’” was included by Elizabeth A. Sharp in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Frances Anne Kemble
poets.credit: Portrait of Fanny Kemble by Thomas Sully, 1834 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frances Anne (Fanny) Kemble (1809–1893) came from the great theatrical family of Kemble and Siddons, and was herself a celebrated actress before her marriage to Pierce Butler of Georgia. Her Journal of a Residence on a Georgian Plantation records her experience of slavery.
She also wrote verse throughout her life, and published Poems in 1844; the nature sonnet “Winter” and two other sonnets appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: James Aldrich
bio: James Aldrich (1810–1856) was an American poet, and has no connection with the better-known Thomas Bailey Aldrich. He is remembered almost entirely for one short poem, “A Death-bed”, widely reprinted in nineteenth-century anthologies.
Little is recorded about his life, and this archive makes no claim beyond his dates and the single poem Knowles printed.

poets.name: Bret Harte
poets.credit: Napoleon Sarony, c. 1870s · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Brett Harte (1836-1902) was an American short-story writer and poet, born in Albany, New York. He went to California in the 1850s, worked as a typesetter and journalist in San Francisco, and edited the Overland Monthly, in which his stories of the Gold Rush country, including The Luck of Roaring Camp (1868), first appeared.

His verse, notably the comic ballad known as Plain Language from Truthful James (1870), made him famous across the United States and Britain. From 1878 he lived abroad as a U.S. consul in Krefeld and Glasgow and then in London, where he died. East and West: Poems (1871), from which these poems are taken, gathers his Californian and Civil War verse with a second part of parodies and humorous pieces.

poets.name: Thomas Bailey Aldrich
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Bailey Aldrich (photograph, c. 1885–1907, photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Bailey Aldrich (1836–1907) was an American poet, novelist and editor, born in Portsmouth, New Hampshire. He edited The Atlantic Monthly from 1881 to 1890 and wrote the boyhood memoir The Story of a Bad Boy (1869).
In verse he was admired for small, polished lyrics and epigrams, which he refined steadily over his career.

poets.name: John Hay
poets.credit: Portrait of John Hay (photograph, 1902, Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Hay (1838–1905) was an American diplomat and writer, born in Salem, Indiana, who served as private secretary to Abraham Lincoln and later as Secretary of State.
His dialect ballads, gathered in Pike County Ballads (1871) and including “Jim Bludso”, made him widely known as a poet.

poets.name: Abram Joseph Ryan (Father Ryan)
poets.credit: Photograph of Father Abram J. Ryan, c. 1875 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Abram Joseph Ryan (1838–1886) was an American Catholic priest and poet, born in Maryland or Virginia and raised in Missouri. Ordained in the 1860s, he served as a chaplain to Confederate troops during the Civil War, and afterwards ministered in parishes in the South, notably in Mobile, Alabama.

Known as the 'Poet-Priest of the South', he wrote devotional verse as well as elegies for the Confederate cause, among them 'The Conquered Banner' and 'The Sword of Robert Lee'. His collected Poems: Patriotic, Religious, Miscellaneous appeared in 1880 and was reprinted in the 1890s.

poets.name: William Winter
bio: William Winter (1836–1917) was an American poet and drama critic, born at Gloucester, Massachusetts. He wrote for the New York Tribune for more than forty years and became the leading theatre critic of his day, publishing many books on actors and the stage.
His own verse, gathered in several volumes, is quiet and elegiac; Knowles took “After All” from his collection Wanderers (1892).

poets.name: Ellice Hopkins
bio: Ellice Hopkins (1836–1904) was an English writer and social-purity campaigner who worked for the protection of girls and for the moral reform of public life. She wrote prose and also devotional and reforming verse.
Two of her poems, “Life in Death” and “A Vision of Womanhood”, are included in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Joaquin Miller
poets.credit: Portrait of Joaquin Miller (photograph by Mathew Brady, c. 1870s) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joaquin Miller (the pen name of Cincinnatus Heine Miller, 1841–1913) was an American poet of the Pacific coast who styled himself the “Poet of the Sierras”.
His Songs of the Sierras (1871) won him a reputation in England as well as in the United States, and he later lived in the hills above Oakland, California.

poets.name: Edward Rowland Sill
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward Rowland Sill (photograph, before 1887) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Rowland Sill (1841–1887) was an American poet and teacher, born in Windsor, Connecticut, who taught English at the University of California.
His thoughtful short poems, among them “The Fool’s Prayer”, were widely admired and several were collected after his death.

poets.name: Mathilde Blind
poets.credit: Portrait of Mathilde Blind by Lucy Madox Brown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mathilde Blind (1841–1896) was born Mathilde Cohen at Mannheim and came to England as a girl, taking the surname of her stepfather. She wrote poems, a biography of George Eliot and translations, and was a friend of the Rossettis and of Ford Madox Brown.
Her books include The Prophecy of Saint Oran (1881) and The Ascent of Man (1889). Five of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: James David Edgar
poets.credit: Portrait of James David Edgar by the Topley Studio, 1896 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James David Edgar (1841–1899), born in Quebec, was a lawyer and politician who became Speaker of the House of Commons of Canada, and wrote verse and songs.
The poems here are those Lighthall chose for his 1889 anthology, Songs of the Great Dominion.

poets.name: Sidney Lanier
poets.credit: Portrait of Sidney Lanier — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sidney Lanier (1842–1881) was an American poet and musician from Georgia who served in the Confederate army, was imprisoned as a prisoner of war, and spent much of his short life battling the tuberculosis that eventually killed him.
A trained flautist, he brought a musician’s sense of rhythm and sound to poems such as ‘The Marshes of Glynn’ and ‘The Song of the Chattahoochee’, which celebrate the landscape of the American South.

poets.name: Charles Edward Carryl
bio: Charles Edward Carryl (1842–1920) was an American businessman and writer, born in New York City, and the father of the poet Guy Wetmore Carryl.
He is remembered for the children’s fantasy Davy and the Goblin (1885), whose nonsense verses include “The Plaint of the Camel”.

poets.name: James Whitcomb Riley
poets.credit: Photograph of James Whitcomb Riley, 1913 (Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Whitcomb Riley (1849–1916) was born in Greenfield, Indiana, and became the best-loved poet of the American Midwest, known as the “Hoosier Poet.” He worked as a sign painter and travelling performer before newspaper verse in Indiana dialect brought him a wide following, and he spent most of his later life in Indianapolis.

His most popular poems, such as “Little Orphant Annie” and “The Raggedy Man,” are written in rural Indiana speech and draw on childhood, farm life and storytelling. Riley toured widely as a reader of his own work, and Riley Child-Rhymes (1905), illustrated by Will Vawter, gathered many of his best-known verses for children.

poets.name: Eugene Field
poets.credit: Photograph of Eugene Field, c. 1890s (Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Eugene Field (1850–1895) was an American journalist and poet, born in St. Louis. He wrote a widely read newspaper column, first in Denver and then for the Chicago Daily News, and became known above all for his verses about children.

His best-loved poems, among them “Wynken, Blynken and Nod,” “Little Boy Blue” and “The Sugar-Plum Tree,” were gathered in With Trumpet and Drum (1892) and Love-Songs of Childhood (1894). The poems here follow the combined Poems of Childhood issued by Charles Scribner’s Sons in 1904.

poets.name: Emma Lazarus
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Emma Lazarus (19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emma Lazarus (1849–1887) was an American poet and essayist, born in New York City to a prosperous Sephardic Jewish family. She published her first book of verse at seventeen, won the admiration and friendship of Ralph Waldo Emerson, and wrote narrative poems such as Admetus and Tannhauser before turning to lyric and sonnet forms.

From 1881, after the pogroms in Russia, she took up Jewish themes in poems such as The Banner of the Jew and The Crowing of the Red Cock, and worked on behalf of refugees. Her sonnet The New Colossus (1883), written for a fund-raising auction for the Statue of Liberty pedestal, is now inscribed there. She died in New York at the age of 38.

poets.name: Ella Wheeler Wilcox
poets.credit: Photograph of Ella Wheeler Wilcox (Library of Congress, LCCN 2014709802) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ella Wheeler Wilcox (1850–1919) was an American poet and journalist, born in Johnstown Center, Wisconsin. She began publishing verse as a girl and became one of the most widely read popular poets of her day, writing for newspapers and magazines as well as in book form.

Poems of Passion (1883), a collection of her love poems, drew a storm of public criticism for its frankness and, with it, a great many readers; Maurine and Other Poems appeared in 1888. Her best-known lines, such as “Laugh, and the world laughs with you” (from “Solitude”), became proverbial in English.

poets.name: Arthur Wentworth Hamilton Eaton
poets.credit: Portrait of Arthur Wentworth Hamilton Eaton, from Canadian Poets (1916) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Wentworth Hamilton Eaton (1849–1937), born in Kentville, Nova Scotia, was an Episcopal clergyman, historian and poet who spent much of his career in the United States.
He wrote on the history and legends of Acadia. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: E. W. Thomson
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward William Thomson, 1913 (Toronto Public Library) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward William Thomson (1849–1924) was a Canadian-born journalist and author who worked for many years in Boston.

He is best known for his short stories, such as Old Man Savarin and Other Stories (1895). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Edwin Markham
poets.credit: Portrait of Edwin Markham (portrait, 1919) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edwin Markham (1852–1940) was an American poet, born in Oregon City, Oregon, and raised in California, who later taught and lived in New York.
“The Man with the Hoe” (1899), written after seeing Millet’s painting, made him famous as a poet of social protest.

poets.name: C. E. S. Wood
poets.credit: Portrait of C. E. S. Wood (photograph, 1910) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: C. E. S. Wood (Charles Erskine Scott Wood, 1852–1944) was an American soldier, lawyer and writer, a West Point graduate who practised law in Portland, Oregon.
His long poem The Poet in the Desert (1915) is the best known of his verse.

poets.name: Irwin Russell
bio: Irwin Russell (1853–1879) was an American poet from Port Gibson, Mississippi, who died at the age of twenty-six.
His “Christmas-Night in the Quarters” (1878) is often described as one of the earliest literary poems to use Black Southern dialect.

poets.name: Edith M. Thomas
poets.credit: Portrait of Edith M. Thomas (photograph, 1890) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edith M. Thomas (1854–1925) was an American poet, born in Chatham, Ohio, who lived chiefly in New York City.
Her books of verse include A New Year’s Masque (1885) and The Inverted Torch (1890).

poets.name: Isabella Valancy Crawford
poets.credit: Portrait of Isabella Valancy Crawford, reproduced in E. S. Caswell, Canadian Singers and Their Songs (c. 1919) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Isabella Valancy Crawford (1850–1887) was born in Dublin and raised in Ontario, and supported herself and her family by writing poems and stories for periodicals.

Her only book in her lifetime was Old Spookses' Pass, Malcolm's Katie, and Other Poems (1884), which brought her little notice until after her death. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Arthur John Lockhart
bio: Arthur John Lockhart (1850–1926) was a Canadian clergyman and poet.
His poems here come partly from his Masque of Minstrels (1887). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: George Edward Woodberry
poets.credit: Portrait of George Edward Woodberry (photograph by Hollinger, by 1903) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Edward Woodberry (1855–1930) was an American poet, critic and scholar, born in Beverly, Massachusetts, and a professor of comparative literature at Columbia University.
His verse includes The North Shore Watch (1890) and Wild Eden (1899).

poets.name: H. C. Bunner
poets.credit: Portrait of H. C. Bunner (portrait, 1899) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: H. C. Bunner (Henry Cuyler Bunner, 1855–1896) was an American writer, born in Oswego, New York, who edited the humorous weekly Puck from 1877 until his death.
He was a master of light and occasional verse, collected in volumes such as Airs from Arcady and Elsewhere (1884).

poets.name: Florence Earle Coates
poets.credit: Photograph of Florence Earle Coates (before 1912) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Florence Earle Coates (1850–1927) was an American poet, born in Philadelphia and educated at private schools there and in Europe. She was a prominent member of the Philadelphia literary world and was known for her devotional and patriotic poems.
Her volumes include Poems (1898), Mine and Thine (1904), Lyrics of Life (1909) and The Unconquered Air (1912); a two-volume collected Poems appeared in 1916.

poets.name: Lizette Woodworth Reese
poets.credit: Portrait of Lizette Woodworth Reese (portrait from A Woman of the Century (1893)) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lizette Woodworth Reese (1856–1935) was an American poet, born near Baltimore, Maryland, who taught English in Baltimore schools for many years.
Her first book, A Branch of May (1887), began a long career of spare, finely made lyrics, among them the sonnet “Tears”.

poets.name: May Probyn
bio: May Probyn (1856–1909) was an English poet whose verse appeared in the magazines and anthologies of the 1880s and 1890s.
Two of her poems, “Sudden Death” and a villanelle, are included in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Horace Traubel
bio: Horace Traubel (1858–1919) was an American poet and editor, born in Camden, New Jersey, and a close friend and disciple of Walt Whitman.
He recorded Whitman’s last years in With Walt Whitman in Camden and edited the monthly The Conservator.

poets.name: Constance Naden
bio: Constance Caroline Woodhill Naden (1858–1889) was born in Birmingham, studied science at Mason College, and wrote philosophical essays as well as verse. Her collections are Songs and Sonnets of Springtime (1881) and A Modern Apostle (1887).
Her poems often take evolution and the new science as subjects, sometimes with wit. She died at thirty. Two of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: E. Nesbit
poets.credit: Photograph of E. Nesbit · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edith Nesbit (1858–1924), who published verse as E. Nesbit, is best remembered today as the author of children's classics such as Five Children and It (1902) and The Railway Children (1906). She was a founder member of the Fabian Society.
Her early poems were collected in Lays and Legends (1886; second series 1892). Two of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Frank Dempster Sherman
poets.credit: Portrait of Frank Dempster Sherman (photograph by Bain News Service, 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frank Dempster Sherman (1860–1917) was an American poet and professor of graphics at Columbia University, born in Peekskill, New York.
His delicate, finely finished short lyrics were collected in volumes such as Madrigals and Catches (1887).

poets.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
poets.credit: Portrait of Charlotte Perkins Gilman (photograph by Charles Fletcher Lummis, c. 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charlotte Perkins Gilman (1860–1935) was an American writer and lecturer on women’s rights and social reform, born in Hartford, Connecticut.
She is best known for Women and Economics (1898) and the story “The Yellow Wall-Paper”, and she also published satirical verse in In This Our World (1893).

poets.name: William Wilfred Campbell
poets.credit: Portrait of William Wilfred Campbell, from Canadian Poets (1916) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Wilfred Campbell (1860–1918), born at Newmarket, Ontario, was an Anglican clergyman who later became a civil servant and one of the Confederation poets.
His Lake Lyrics and Other Poems appeared in 1889. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Louise Imogen Guiney
poets.credit: Portrait of Louise Imogen Guiney (photograph, before 1894) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Louise Imogen Guiney (1861–1920) was an American poet and essayist, born in Boston, who spent her later years in England.
Her poems appeared in volumes such as Songs at the Start (1884) and A Roadside Harp (1893).

poets.name: Bliss Carman
poets.credit: Portrait of Bliss Carman (photograph by Pirie MacDonald, 1903) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bliss Carman (1861–1929) was a Canadian-born poet, born in Fredericton, New Brunswick, who spent much of his career in the United States.
With Richard Hovey he wrote the vagabond lyrics of Songs from Vagabondia (1894).

poets.name: Richard Burton
bio: Richard Burton (1861–1940) was an American poet, critic and teacher, born in Hartford, Connecticut, who taught English at the University of Minnesota.
His volumes of verse include Dumb in June (1895) and Lyrics of Brotherhood (1899).

poets.name: May Kendall
bio: May Kendall (1861–1943), born Emma Goldworth Kendall, was an English poet and novelist who wrote witty verse on science and modern life. Her books include That Very Mab (1885, with Andrew Lang) and Dreams to Sell (1887).
Her humorous poems on evolution, geology and the education of women made her popular in the 1880s. Two of them appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Mary C. Gillington
bio: Mary Clarissa Gillington (1861–1936) was an English poet, sister of the poet Alice E. Gillington.
Two of her poems, “A Dead March” and “The Home Coming”, appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Henry van Dyke
poets.credit: Photograph of Henry van Dyke by Harris & Ewing (before 1918) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry van Dyke (1852–1933) was an American clergyman, professor and poet, born at Germantown, Pennsylvania. He was a Presbyterian minister in New York, a professor of English literature at Princeton, and United States minister to the Netherlands and Luxembourg from 1913 to 1916.
He wrote many volumes of verse and essays, and the story The Other Wise Man (1895). His nature lyrics on American birds were among his most anthologised poems.

poets.name: Oliver Herford
poets.credit: Portrait of Oliver Herford (photograph, c. 1916) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oliver Herford (1863–1935) was an English-born American humorist, illustrator and writer of light verse.
He wrote and drew many small books of whimsy, such as The Bashful Earthquake (1898).

poets.name: Alice E. Gillington
bio: Alice E. Gillington (1863–1934) was an English poet and writer on Romani (Gypsy) life, sister of the poet Mary C. Gillington.
Two of her pieces, “A West-Country Love-Song” and “Nocturnes”, close Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Richard Hovey
poets.credit: Portrait of Richard Hovey (photograph, before 1908) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Hovey (1864–1900) was an American poet, born in Normal, Illinois, who lectured at Columbia University.
With Bliss Carman he wrote Songs from Vagabondia (1894), and he left unfinished a cycle of dramas on the Arthurian legend.

poets.name: Elizabeth Gostwycke Roberts
bio: Elizabeth Gostwycke Roberts (1864–1922) was a Canadian poet, the sister of Charles G. D. Roberts.
The poem here is the one Lighthall chose for Songs of the Great Dominion (1889).

poets.name: Arthur Weir
bio: Arthur Weir (1864–1902) was a Montreal poet and journalist.
His volume Fleurs-de-Lys and Other Poems appeared in 1889. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Madison Cawein
poets.credit: Portrait of Madison Cawein (photograph, 1905) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Madison Cawein (1865–1914) was an American poet, born in Louisville, Kentucky, who wrote chiefly of the woods and fields of his native state.
He published many volumes of verse, beginning with Blooms of the Berry (1887).

poets.name: Bert Leston Taylor
poets.credit: Portrait of Bert Leston Taylor (photograph, 1921) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bert Leston Taylor (1866–1921) was an American newspaper columnist and humorist, who conducted the column “A Line o’ Type or Two” in the Chicago Tribune.
His light verse and parodies appeared first in that column and were then gathered in book form.

poets.name: Ronald Ross
poets.credit: Photograph of Ronald Ross (U.S. National Library of Medicine) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Ronald Ross (1857–1932) was a British physician born in Almora, India. A surgeon in the Indian Medical Service, he showed that malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes, and received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1902. He later held a chair in tropical medicine at Liverpool and worked at the Ross Institute in London.

Alongside his scientific career he wrote poems, novels and plays. Edward Marsh included his lyric 'Hesperus', from Lyra Modulata, in the first Georgian Poetry volume (1911-1912), and it is the piece reproduced here.

poets.name: A. Mary F. Robinson
bio: Agnes Mary Frances Robinson (1857–1944) was an English poet and scholar who later wrote under the names Madame Darmesteter and Madame Duclaux after her two marriages, to James Darmesteter (1888) and Emile Duclaux (1901). She lived much in France.
Her early volumes include A Handful of Honeysuckle (1878), The Crowned Hippolytus (1881) and An Italian Garden (1886). Four of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Edgar Lee Masters
poets.credit: Photograph of Edgar Lee Masters as a young man · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edgar Lee Masters (1868–1950) was an American lawyer and writer, born in Garnett, Kansas, and raised in Petersburg and Lewistown, Illinois. He practised law in Chicago for three decades, partly as law partner of Clarence Darrow, and wrote poetry, plays, novels and biography alongside his legal career.

Spoon River Anthology, first published in 1915 and expanded in 1916 with The Spooniad and the Epilogue, is a sequence of free-verse epitaphs spoken by the dead of an imagined Midwestern town, drawing on the Illinois towns of his youth. It was an immediate sensation and remains his most famous work; the later volumes never matched its success.

poets.name: William Vaughn Moody
poets.credit: Portrait of William Vaughn Moody (photograph by W. C. Ward, before 1906) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Vaughn Moody (1869–1910) was an American poet and dramatist, born in Spencer, Indiana, who taught at the University of Chicago.
His work includes the “Ode in Time of Hesitation”, the verse drama The Fire-Bringer (1904) and the play The Great Divide (1906).

poets.name: George Sterling
poets.credit: Portrait of George Sterling (photograph by Johan Hagemeyer, 1926) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Sterling (1869–1926) was an American poet, born in Sag Harbor, New York, and a central figure of the bohemian literary circle of San Francisco and Carmel.
His books include The Testimony of the Suns (1903) and A Wine of Wizardry (1909).

poets.name: Stephen Crane
poets.credit: Photograph of Stephen Crane, c. 1899 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Stephen Crane (1871–1900) was an American novelist, short-story writer and poet, born in Newark, New Jersey. He is best remembered for the Civil War novel The Red Badge of Courage (1895) and for stories such as "The Open Boat", and worked as a journalist and war correspondent.

The Black Riders and Other Lines, his first book of verse, appeared in 1895. Its short, untitled, numbered pieces in unrhymed free verse, often parables addressing God, institutions and the self, were unusual for their time and are often compared with Emily Dickinson's. Crane died of tuberculosis in 1900, aged twenty-eight.

poets.name: Edwin Ford Piper
poets.credit: Portrait of Edwin Ford Piper (portrait, 1924) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edwin Ford Piper (1871–1939) was an American poet and professor of English at the University of Iowa, born in Nebraska.
He wrote poems of the Middle Western plains, such as those in Barbed Wire and Other Poems (1917).

poets.name: T. A. Daly
bio: T. A. Daly (Thomas Augustine Daly, 1871–1948) was an American newspaper columnist and poet, born in Philadelphia.
He was best known for comic verse in Italian-American dialect, collected in books such as Canzoni (1906) and Carmina (1909).

poets.name: James Weldon Johnson
poets.credit: Portrait of James Weldon Johnson, Library of Congress · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938) was born in Jacksonville, Florida, and became a poet, lyricist, novelist, diplomat and civil-rights leader. He graduated from Atlanta University, studied at Columbia, was admitted to the Florida bar, and served as U.S. consul in Venezuela and Nicaragua. With his brother J. Rosamond Johnson he wrote songs for the stage, including “Lift Every Voice and Sing.”

Fifty Years & Other Poems (1917), his first book of verse, marked the fiftieth anniversary of emancipation and gathered formal lyrics, sonnets and a closing group of dialect poems. He later became a leading secretary of the NAACP and a figure of the Harlem Renaissance, publishing God’s Trombones (1927) and editing The Book of American Negro Poetry.

poets.name: Paul Laurence Dunbar
poets.credit: Photograph of Paul Laurence Dunbar, c. 1890 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906) was an African American poet, novelist and short-story writer born in Dayton, Ohio, to parents who had been enslaved. He published his first poems while still in school and issued ‘Oak and Ivy’ (1893) at his own expense; ‘Majors and Minors’ (1895) and ‘Lyrics of Lowly Life’ (1896), the latter introduced by William Dean Howells, brought him national fame.

He wrote both in standard English and in the plantation dialect that audiences of his day expected, and was long best known for the latter, though he regretted that it overshadowed his other work. Poems such as ‘We Wear the Mask’, ‘Sympathy’ and ‘Ode to Ethiopia’ speak directly of race and hidden suffering. He died of tuberculosis at the age of thirty-three.

poets.name: Lola Ridge
bio: Lola Ridge (1873–1941) was an Irish-born poet, raised in New Zealand and Australia, who settled in New York in 1907.
Her poems of immigrant life include those in The Ghetto and Other Poems (1918).

poets.name: Guy Wetmore Carryl
poets.credit: Portrait of Guy Wetmore Carryl (photograph, before 1902) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Guy Wetmore Carryl (1873–1904) was an American humorist and poet, born in New York City, the son of Charles Edward Carryl, who died young.
He is remembered for Fables for the Frivolous (1898), which retold Aesop and the fairy tales in comic verse.

poets.name: H. H. Knibbs
bio: H. H. Knibbs (Henry Herbert Knibbs, 1874–1945) was a Canadian-born American writer of verse and Western novels.
His poems of the desert and the trail include those in Riders of the Stars (1916).

poets.name: Douglas Hyde
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Douglas Hyde was born in Castlerea, County Roscommon, and was a scholar of Irish. He founded the Gaelic League in 1893 and later served as the first President of Ireland (1938–45).
His English versions of Irish folk songs, such as those in Love Songs of Connacht (1893), were widely admired.

poets.name: Graham R. Tomson
poets.credit: Photograph of Rosamund Marriott Watson, c. 1880 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Graham R. Tomson was the name under which Rosamund Marriott Watson (1860–1911) published her poems in the late 1880s and early 1890s, after her marriage to the painter Arthur Graham Tomson; she later lived with the writer H. B. Marriott Watson. Her books include Tares (1884) and The Bird-Bride (1889).
She was admired for her ballades and other fixed forms. Three of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Arthur Colton
bio: Arthur Colton (1868–1943) was an American writer, born in Washington, D.C. He studied at Yale, took his doctorate there in 1893, taught English at Yale, and from 1906 was librarian of the University Club of New York.
He published essays and fiction, and one volume of poetry, Harps Hung Up in Babylon (1907).

poets.name: W. B. Yeats
poets.credit: Portrait of W. B. Yeats by George Charles Beresford (1911) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Butler Yeats (1865–1939) was an Irish poet and dramatist, born in Dublin, who led the Irish literary revival and co-founded the Abbey Theatre. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923 and served as a senator of the Irish Free State.

His poetry moved from the Celtic Twilight lyrics of The Rose and The Wind Among the Reeds, through the harder manner of Responsibilities and The Wild Swans at Coole, to the visionary poems of Michael Robartes and the Dancer and The Tower. The poems here are drawn from his books published up to 1928.

poets.name: Richard Le Gallienne
poets.credit: Photograph of Richard Le Gallienne by Alfred Ellis (19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Le Gallienne (1866–1947) was an English poet, critic and novelist, born at Liverpool. A member of the 1890s circle of the Rhymers’ Club and the Yellow Book, he moved to the United States in 1903 and spent much of his later life there.
His books of verse include English Poems (1892), New Poems (1909) and The Lonely Dancer (1913), and a free paraphrase of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam.

poets.name: Bernard O'Dowd
bio: Bernard O'Dowd (1866–1953) was an Australian poet, born at Ballarat, Victoria, who worked as a barrister and librarian.
His books include Dawnward? (1903) and The Bush (1912); his work is notable for its radical and visionary themes.

poets.name: Dora Sigerson Shorter
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Dora Sigerson Shorter was born in Dublin, the daughter of George and Hester Sigerson. She published Ballads and Poems in 1899 and married the editor Clement Shorter in 1896. She also worked as a sculptor.
She died in London in 1918.

poets.name: George William Russell (A.E.)
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
