bio: George William Russell, who wrote under the initials A.E., was born in Lurgan and became a poet, painter, mystic and editor. He worked for the Irish Agricultural Organisation Society and edited The Irish Homestead.
He is not to be confused with the American poet of the same surname already in this archive. He died in 1935.

poets.name: Roderic Quinn
bio: Roderic Quinn (1867–1949) was a Sydney-born Australian poet and journalist.
His books include The Hidden Tide (1899) and The Circling Hearths (1901).

poets.name: Charles Weekes
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charles Weekes was an Irish poet associated with the literary revival of the 1890s.
Yeats printed two of his short poems, "That" and "Think", in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Laurence Binyon
poets.credit: Portrait of Laurence Binyon by William Strang (1901) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Laurence Binyon (1869–1943) was an English poet, playwright and art historian, born in Lancaster and educated at St Paul’s School and Oxford. He worked at the British Museum, where he became Keeper of Prints and Drawings and a leading authority on Asian art.

He is best known for “For the Fallen,” published in The Times in September 1914, whose fourth stanza is read at Remembrance services. He also wrote odes, narrative poems and a verse translation of Dante’s Divine Comedy.

poets.name: Edwin James Brady
bio: Edwin James Brady (1869–1952) was an Australian poet and journalist, born in New South Wales.
His books include The Ways of Many Waters (1899), poems of the sea.

poets.name: David McKee Wright
bio: David McKee Wright (1869–1928) was an Irish-born poet and clergyman who spent many years in New Zealand and later in Sydney.
His books include Station Ballads and Other Verses (1897) and Aphrodite and Other Poems (1898).

poets.name: Edwin Arlington Robinson
poets.credit: Photograph, c. 1910s · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edwin Arlington Robinson was born on 22 December 1869 at Head Tide, Maine, and grew up in the nearby town of Gardiner, which he later transformed into the 'Tilbury Town' of his verse. He attended Harvard as a special student from 1891 to 1893, then returned to Maine and later settled in New York, where he lived for years in poverty and worked briefly in the Custom House.

His early books, The Torrent and the Night Before (1896) and The Children of the Night (1897), are filled with compact character studies and sonnets, ballades and villanelles in a plain, ironic idiom. The Man Against the Sky (1916) established his reputation, and he went on to win three Pulitzer Prizes for poetry. He died in New York on 6 April 1935. The texts below come from the Project Gutenberg editions of The Children of the Night and The Man Against the Sky.

poets.name: Mehmet Emin Yurdakul
bio: Mehmet Emin Yurdakul was born in Beşiktaş, Istanbul, in 1869, the son of a fisherman. He made his name with 'Cenge Giderken' ('Going to War'), published in 1897 during the Greco-Turkish War. He wrote in plain spoken Turkish and the syllabic metre of folk poetry instead of the Persian-derived metres of Ottoman court verse, and became known as 'the Turkish poet'.

He served as an Ottoman provincial governor and an Ottoman deputy, and from 1923 until his death in 1944 sat in the Turkish Grand National Assembly. The poems below come from Türk Sazı ('The Turkish Saz', 1914). The text follows the third edition in modern Turkish letters (Atlas Kitabevi, 1979) as transcribed on tr.wikisource.org.

poets.name: Charlotte Mew
poets.credit: Photograph of Charlotte Mew (c. 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charlotte Mew (1869–1928) was an English poet, born in Bloomsbury, London. She lived for most of her life with her sister and her mother, in straitened circumstances, and published only two books of poems in her lifetime.

The Farmer’s Bride (1916; enlarged in 1921) won the admiration of Thomas Hardy and other poets and made her reputation. Her poems are dramatic and irregular, with voices ranging from a Devon farmer to a nun and a grieving lover. She died in 1928.

poets.name: Elsa Barker
poets.credit: Photograph of Elsa Barker, 1914 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elsa Barker (1869–1954) was an American writer, born at Leicester, Vermont. She worked as a teacher and newspaper writer and edited material for Hampton’s Magazine in 1909 and 1910.
Her books of poetry include The Frozen Grail, and Other Poems (1910), The Book of Love (1912) and Songs of a Vagrom Angel (1916). She also wrote Letters of a Living Dead Man (1914).

poets.name: Frederic Lawrence Knowles
bio: Frederic Lawrence Knowles (1869–1905) was an American poet and anthologist, born at Lawrence, Massachusetts. He graduated from Wesleyan University in 1894 and Harvard in 1896, and worked as an editor for Houghton Mifflin, L. C. Page and Dana Estes, dying in 1905.
He edited The Golden Treasury of American Songs and Lyrics, a major source for this archive, and published two books of his own verse, On Life’s Stairway (1900) and Love Triumphant (1904).

poets.name: Cenap Şahabettin
poets.credit: Photograph of Cenap Şahabettin, c. 1900 (unknown photographer) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Cenap Şahabettin (Cenab Şahabeddin) was born in Manastır in 1870 and died in Istanbul in 1934. He trained as a physician and became one of the leading poets of the Servet-i Fünun ("Wealth of Sciences") circle of the 1890s, the group around Tevfik Fikret that brought French Parnassian and Symbolist manners into late Ottoman poetry. His verse is dense with Persian and Arabic vocabulary. The only book of poems he published, Tâmât (1886), is juvenile work in the old divan manner; the poems that made him the movement's most refined and most mocked stylist, Elhan-ı Şita among them, appeared in the periodicals of the 1890s and were never collected in his lifetime. He also wrote travel prose, essays and aphorisms.

A note on the texts: the poems below are the ones printed in periodicals between 1885 and 1925 (Saadet, Sebat, Mekteb, Servet-i Fünûn, Malûmat, Hazine-i Fünûn, Donanma and others), transcribed on tr.wikisource.org from scans of the original issues. They are in the original Turkish, in the Latin-letter transliteration of the Ottoman text that Wikisource uses, and the old spellings (ñ, â, î, û, the apostrophe for ayn) are kept as transcribed. Titles and printing dates follow the table on the author's Wikisource page; the poem's periodical and date stand in place of a book title. The Tâmât volume itself is not included, and a few short pieces (such as Elhan-ı Şita) are given in a modern transliteration.

poets.name: T. Sturge Moore
bio: Thomas Sturge Moore (1870–1944) was an English poet, wood-engraver and critic, the brother of the philosopher G. E. Moore. He was a close friend of W. B. Yeats and designed book covers for him.
His verse favours classical and mythological subjects. The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Christopher John Brennan
bio: Christopher John Brennan (1870–1932) was an Australian poet, born in Sydney, who became professor of German and comparative literature at the University of Sydney.
His books include XXI Poems: Towards the Source (1897) and Poems (1913), and he is regarded as a leading Symbolist poet of Australia.

poets.name: Anthony C. Deane
bio: Anthony C. Deane (1870–1946) was an English clergyman and writer of light verse, best known for his parodies, gathered in New Rhymes for Old (1901).
His two pieces here, a sea-ballad burlesque and a rustic song, come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: J. M. Synge
bio: John Millington Synge (1871–1909) was an Irish playwright and poet, best known for Riders to the Sea and The Playboy of the Western World (1907), plays written for the Abbey Theatre in the speech of the west of Ireland.

He wrote only a small body of verse, collected in Poems and Translations (1909), the year of his death. The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920); his version from Petrarch is not included.

poets.name: John Le Gay Brereton
bio: John Le Gay Brereton (1871–1933) was an Australian poet and scholar who became professor of English literature at the University of Sydney.
His verse includes Sea and Sky (1904) and Oithona.

poets.name: W. H. Davies
poets.credit: Photograph of W. H. Davies by Alvin Langdon Coburn (1913) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Henry Davies (1871–1940) was a Welsh poet and writer, born in Newport, Monmouthshire. He spent years as a tramp in America and Britain, losing a foot while trying to jump a freight train, and wrote of that life in The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp (1908).

His short, simple lyrics about birds, flowers, tramps and the poor made him one of the Georgian poets. “Leisure,” first published in Songs of Joy (1911), is his best-known poem; the other poems here are from Foliage (1913).

poets.name: Hilaire Belloc
poets.credit: Portrait of Hilaire Belloc (c. 1917) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hilaire Belloc (1870–1953) was a French-born English writer and Liberal MP, educated at Balliol College, Oxford, who wrote history, travel books, essays, novels and verse. He was a close friend of G. K. Chesterton, and a Catholic apologist.

His verse, from Verses and Sonnets (1896) and Verses (1910), ranges from serious lyrics of Sussex and of faith to comic and satirical ballads such as the “Dedicatory Ode” and “Lines to a Don.” The Cautionary Tales and Bad Child’s Book of Beasts are his best-known children’s verse.

poets.name: John McCrae
poets.credit: Photograph of John McCrae in uniform (c. 1914) by William Notman and Son · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John McCrae (1872–1918) was a Canadian physician, soldier and poet, born in Guelph, Ontario. He served as a gunner in the South African War and as a medical officer in the First World War, and taught medicine at McGill University.

He wrote “In Flanders Fields” at Ypres in May 1915 after the death of a friend. It was first published in Punch that December and became one of the best-known poems of the war. He died of pneumonia in France in January 1918, and In Flanders Fields and Other Poems appeared in 1919.

poets.name: Eva Gore-Booth
bio: Eva Gore-Booth (1872–1926) was an Irish poet, born at Lissadell House in County Sligo, and the sister of the revolutionary Constance Markievicz. She worked for women's suffrage and for working women's trade unions in Manchester.
Her poetry, mystical and often set in the Sligo landscape, was admired by Yeats. The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Cale Young Rice
poets.credit: Photograph of Cale Young Rice (before 1904) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Cale Young Rice (1872–1943) was an American poet and dramatist, born at Dixon, Kentucky. He studied at Cumberland University and Harvard, and published many volumes of lyrics as well as poetic dramas such as Yolanda of Cyprus (1906).
He was married to the novelist Alice Hegan Rice. His lyric collections include From Dusk to Dusk (1898), Many Gods (1910) and Far Quests (1912).

poets.name: Arthur H. Adams
bio: Arthur H. Adams (1872–1936) was a New Zealand-born novelist, playwright, journalist and poet who worked in Australia and England.
His books include the verse collection Maoriland, and Other Verses (1899).

poets.name: Willa Cather
bio: Willa Sibert Cather (1873–1947) was an American writer, best known as a novelist of the American plains: O Pioneers! (1913), My Ántonia (1918) and Death Comes for the Archbishop (1927). She grew up in Nebraska and was a magazine editor in New York before turning to fiction.
Her only book of poems, April Twilight (1903), preceded her novels; Rittenhouse printed one poem from it.

poets.name: Robert Calverley Trevelyan
bio: Robert Calverley Trevelyan (1872–1951) was an English poet and translator, a member of the Trevelyan family and a brother of the historians G. M. Trevelyan and Sir Charles Trevelyan. He published volumes of verse and verse plays, and translated Theocritus and Lucretius, among others.
Edward Marsh printed his short lyric 'Dirge' in the first Georgian Poetry volume (1911-1912); that is the poem reproduced here.

poets.name: Ford Madox Hueffer
bio: Ford Madox Hueffer (1873–1939), the name printed in this anthology, was an English novelist, editor and poet who later styled himself Ford Madox Ford. He edited the English Review and is best known for the novels The Good Soldier (1915) and Parade's End.
He served in the First World War, and his war poems, such as Clair de Lune here, use free verse to catch the experience of the trenches. The poems come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Dora Wilcox
bio: Dora Wilcox (1873–1953) was a New Zealand-born poet who lived for many years in Australia and England.
Her first book was Verses from Maoriland (1905).

poets.name: George Cabot Lodge
poets.credit: Portrait of George Cabot Lodge, from the Harvard College Class of 1895 Twenty-Fifth Anniversary Report (1920) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Cabot Lodge (1873–1909) was an American poet, born in Boston. He studied at Harvard and at the University of Paris, and belonged at Harvard to a circle that included Trumbull Stickney and William Vaughn Moody.
His lyric and dramatic poems, in a classical manner, were collected in Poems and Dramas (1911), after his death in 1909.

poets.name: G. K. Chesterton
poets.credit: Portrait of G. K. Chesterton by Ernest Herbert Mills (1909) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gilbert Keith Chesterton (1874–1936) was an English writer, born in London, known for his journalism, his Father Brown stories and his Christian apologetics, and also a prolific poet. He wrote on politics, history, and literature with a style full of paradox.

His poems range from the rousing ballad “Lepanto” and the long “Ballad of the White Horse” (1911) to comic verses on wine and inns, such as “The Rolling English Road.” The poems here are drawn from The Wild Knight (1900), Poems (1915), Wine, Water and Song (1915), and The Ballad of St. Barbara (1922).

poets.name: Amy Lowell
poets.credit: Photograph of Amy Lowell by Moffett Studio, 1916 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Amy Lowell (1874–1925) was born into a prominent Brookline, Massachusetts family; she was the sister of A. Lawrence Lowell, later president of Harvard. Educated privately, she came to poetry in her late twenties, and her first book, A Dome of Many-Coloured Glass, appeared in 1912, when she was thirty-eight.

After Sword Blades and Poppy Seed (1914), which mixed rhymed verse, unrhymed cadence and narrative poems, she became the energetic leader of the Imagist movement in America, editing the anthologies Some Imagist Poets (1915–17) and lecturing widely. She also wrote the critical works Six French Poets (1915) and Tendencies in Modern American Poetry (1917), and a biography of John Keats; she died in 1925.

poets.name: Anna Hempstead Branch
poets.credit: Portrait of Anna Hempstead Branch (portrait from the Smith College Class Book, 1897) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anna Hempstead Branch (1875–1937) was an American poet, born in New London, Connecticut, and a graduate of Smith College.
Her volumes include The Heart of the Road (1901) and Rose of the Wind (1910), and her long poem “The Monk in the Kitchen” is among her best known.

poets.name: Ridgely Torrence
poets.credit: Portrait of Ridgely Torrence (photograph, before 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ridgely Torrence (1875–1950, the dates this anthology prints) was an American poet and dramatist, born in Xenia, Ohio, who later served as poetry editor of The New Republic.
His Plays for a Negro Theater (1917) were an early attempt at serious drama for Black actors on the American stage.

poets.name: William Ellery Leonard
bio: William Ellery Leonard (1876–1944) was an American poet and professor of English at the University of Wisconsin, born in Plainfield, New Jersey.
He was also a translator, turning Beowulf and Lucretius’s De rerum natura into English.

poets.name: Theodosia Garrison
poets.credit: Portrait of Theodosia Garrison, from Life (21 December 1901) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Theodosia Garrison (1874–1944), later Mrs Frederick J. Faulks, was an American poet, born at Newark, New Jersey. She was educated at private schools in New York and contributed regularly to magazines.
Her two collections of verse are Joy o’ Life (1908) and The Earth Cry (1910).

poets.name: Josephine Preston Peabody
poets.credit: Photograph of Josephine Preston Peabody, Bain News Service (Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Josephine Preston Peabody (1874–1922) was an American poet and dramatist, born in New York City and educated in Boston and at Radcliffe College. She taught English at Wellesley College from 1901 to 1903, and later married Lionel Marks.
Her verse includes The Singing Leaves (1903) and The Singing Man (1911); her verse play The Piper won the Stratford-on-Avon prize in 1910.

poets.name: Gordon Bottomley
poets.credit: Photograph of Gordon Bottomley, from To-day (published no later than 1921) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gordon Bottomley (1874–1948) was an English poet and verse dramatist, born in Keighley, Yorkshire. Ill health kept him from regular work, and he spent most of his life at Silverdale on the Lancashire coast, near the Cartmel peninsula of his poem 'New Year's Eve, 1913'. His early volumes included The Gate of Smaragdus (1904) and Chambers of Imagery (1907 and 1912).

He was among the poets Edward Marsh gathered in the Georgian Poetry anthologies, appearing in the volumes of 1911-1912, 1916-1917 and 1918-1919. He is remembered chiefly for his poetic plays, which are not included here; the pieces in this archive are the shorter poems he contributed to those anthologies.

poets.name: Trumbull Stickney
poets.credit: Portrait of Trumbull Stickney, from the Harvard College Class of 1895 Twenty-Fifth Anniversary Report (1920) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joseph Trumbull Stickney (1874–1904) was an American poet, born at Geneva, Switzerland, and educated in Europe and at Harvard. He took a doctorate at the University of Paris in 1903, the first American to do so, and became an instructor in Greek at Harvard.
He died in Boston on 11 October 1904. His Dramatic Verses appeared in 1902, and his Poems were collected in 1905 by his friends George Cabot Lodge and William Vaughn Moody.

poets.name: Charles Hanson Towne
bio: Charles Hanson Towne (1877–1949) was an American poet and editor, born at Louisville, Kentucky. He edited The Smart Set, The Delineator, The Designer and McClure’s Magazine, and became a figure of literary New York.
His books of verse include The Quiet Singer, and Other Poems (1908), Manhattan (1909), and Beyond the Stars (1912).

poets.name: Arthur Upson
bio: Arthur Upson (1877–1908) was an American poet, born at Camden, New York, and educated at Camden Academy and the University of Minnesota. He died in August 1908, at the age of about thirty-one.
His books include Westwind Songs (1902), Octaves in an Oxford Garden (1902), The City: A Poem Drama (1905) and The Tides of Spring (1907).

poets.name: Edward Thomas
poets.credit: Photograph of Edward Thomas (c. 1905) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) was an English-Welsh writer who made his living as a critic, biographer and country writer before turning to poetry in 1914 at the urging of his friend Robert Frost. He wrote nearly all of his poems in the last two and a half years of his life.

He enlisted in 1915 and was killed at Arras on 9 April 1917. His first collection, Poems, appeared in October 1917 under the pseudonym Edward Eastaway, followed by Last Poems in 1918. Quiet and exact, his poems are among the most admired English poems of the war years, although few of them mention the war directly.

poets.name: Adelaide Crapsey
poets.credit: Portrait of Adelaide Crapsey (photograph, c. 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Adelaide Crapsey (1878–1914) was an American poet who taught at Smith College and died of tuberculosis at thirty-six.
She devised the cinquain, a five-line form of two, four, six, eight and two syllables, and her only book, Verse, appeared in 1915 after her death.

poets.name: Don Marquis
poets.credit: Portrait of Don Marquis (photograph by Bain News Service, c. 1910–15) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Don Marquis (1878–1937) was an American humorist, born in Walnut, Illinois, who wrote newspaper columns in New York.
He is best remembered for archy and mehitabel, comic verses supposedly typed by a cockroach, but he also wrote serious poems.

poets.name: John Erskine
bio: John Erskine (1879–1951) was an American writer and teacher, born in New York City, and a professor of English at Columbia University.
He wrote poems, essays and novels, including The Private Life of Helen of Troy (1925), and later served as president of the Juilliard School.

poets.name: Wallace Stevens
bio: Wallace Stevens (1879–1955) was an American poet, born in Reading, Pennsylvania, who spent his working life as an insurance executive in Hartford, Connecticut.
“Peter Quince at the Clavier”, which this archive takes from Untermeyer’s 1921 anthology, first appeared in 1915 and was later collected in Harmonium (1923).

poets.name: Harold Monro
bio: Harold Monro (1879–1932) was a British poet and publisher, born in Brussels, who founded the Poetry Bookshop in London in 1913 and published the Georgian Poetry anthologies and many young poets there.
His own books include Strange Meetings (1917), from which the title piece here is drawn. The poems come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: T. M. Kettle
bio: Thomas Michael Kettle (1880–1916) was an Irish economist, journalist and Nationalist member of Parliament, who joined the army in the First World War and was killed at Ginchy on the Somme in September 1916.
His sonnet to his infant daughter, written shortly before his death, is the best known of his few poems. It comes from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: James Stephens
bio: James Stephens (1882–1950) was an Irish poet and storyteller, born in Dublin, best known for the fantasy The Crock of Gold (1912). His poetry collections include Insurrections (1909) and The Hill of Vision (1912).
His verse mixes Irish humour, pity for the poor and a mystical sense of wonder. The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: James Joyce
bio: James Joyce (1882–1941) was an Irish novelist, author of Ulysses and Finnegans Wake, who also wrote lyric verse. His first book of poems, Chamber Music, appeared in 1907.
The one poem here, I Hear an Army, is taken from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Vachel Lindsay
poets.credit: Photograph of Vachel Lindsay, 1913 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nicholas Vachel Lindsay (1879–1931) was an American poet born in Springfield, Illinois. He studied at Hiram College and trained as an artist in Chicago and New York before turning to poetry, and for years he travelled on foot through the American Midwest and South, trading rhymes for food and lodging and preaching what he called a "Gospel of Beauty".

Lindsay became known as a founder of modern "singing poetry", verse written to be chanted or performed aloud with a strong ragtime beat. "General William Booth Enters into Heaven" appeared in Harriet Monroe's magazine Poetry in January 1913 and gave its name to his first widely read book that year. The Congo and Other Poems followed in 1914. He died in Springfield in 1931.

poets.name: Louis V. Ledoux
bio: Louis Vernon Ledoux (1880–1948) was an American poet, born in New York City, who graduated from Columbia University in 1902. He later became a noted collector and authority on Japanese prints.
His books of verse include Songs from the Silent Land (1905), The Soul’s Progress (1907), The Shadow of Etna (1914), and the lyrical drama The Story of Eleusis (1916).

poets.name: Alice Corbin (Henderson)
bio: Alice Corbin Henderson (1881–1949) was an American poet and editor, born in St. Louis, who helped edit Poetry magazine in Chicago before moving to New Mexico.
She published as Alice Corbin; her books include The Spinning Woman of the Sky (1912) and Red Earth (1920).

poets.name: Nora May French
poets.credit: Photograph of Nora May French by Arnold Genthe (before 1907) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nora May French (1881–1907) was an American poet, born at East Aurora, New York. She lived in California and died at Carmel on 14 November 1907, at the age of twenty-six.
A small volume of her poems was edited after her death by her friend George Sterling.

poets.name: John Drinkwater
poets.credit: Photograph of John Drinkwater by Bain News Service (1919) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Drinkwater (1882–1937) was an English poet and dramatist, born in Leytonstone, Essex, and brought up in Oxford and Birmingham. He worked for many years as an insurance clerk while writing, was one of the Dymock poets, and appeared in all five volumes of Georgian Poetry. He also became closely associated with the Birmingham Repertory Theatre.

The poems here come from Poems 1908-1919 (1919), which gathers his verse of the decade and includes the long poems Reverie and The Fires of God, and from Tides (1917), a small book printed by the Beaumont Press, of which only the poems not already in the larger collection are given. His verse plays, among them Abraham Lincoln (1918), are not included.

poets.name: James Oppenheim
bio: James Oppenheim (1882–1932) was an American poet and editor, born in St. Paul, Minnesota, who founded the magazine The Seven Arts in 1916.
His verse includes Songs for the New Age (1914), and his poem “Bread and Roses” became a slogan of the labour movement.

poets.name: Arthur Davison Ficke
bio: Arthur Davison Ficke (1883–1945) was an American poet and lawyer, born in Davenport, Iowa.
His books include Sonnets of a Portrait Painter (1914), and with Witter Bynner he took part in the Spectra hoax of 1916.

poets.name: Thomas S. Jones, Jr.
bio: Thomas Samuel Jones, Jr. (1882–1932) was an American poet, born at Boonville, New York, who graduated from Cornell in 1904 and worked on the staff of the New York Times and The Pathfinder.
His volumes of verse include The Rose-Jar (1906), Interludes (1908), the elegy Ave Atque Vale for Arthur Upson (1909) and The Voice in the Silence (1911).

poets.name: Marguerite Wilkinson
bio: Marguerite Wilkinson (1883–1928) was an American poet and critic.
Her books include the verse collection Bluestone (1920) and New Voices (1919), a study of modern poetry.

poets.name: Eunice Tietjens
poets.credit: Portrait of Eunice Tietjens (photograph, before 1920) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Eunice Tietjens (1884–1944) was an American poet, born in Chicago, and an associate editor of Poetry magazine.
Her travels in Asia shaped her first book, Profiles from China (1917).

poets.name: Sara Teasdale
poets.credit: Photograph of Sara Teasdale by the Gerhard Sisters (c. 1910), Missouri History Museum · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sara Teasdale (1884–1933) was an American lyric poet, born in St. Louis, Missouri, and later resident in New York City. Her early books, Sonnets to Duse (1907) and Helen of Troy and Other Poems (1911), were followed by Rivers to the Sea (1915) and Love Songs (1917), the latter of which won the first Columbia University Poetry Society Prize, a forerunner of the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.
Her work is known for its compressed, song-like short lyrics of love, solitude, nature and the passing of time, in plain diction and tight rhyme. She died in New York in 1933.

poets.name: Gladys Cromwell
bio: Gladys Cromwell (1885–1919) was an American poet, born in New York City, who with her twin sister served with the Red Cross in France during the First World War.
Her poems were collected in The Gates of Utterance (1915) and in a volume published after her death in 1919.

poets.name: Francis Brett Young
poets.credit: Photograph of Francis Brett Young, from Everybody's Magazine (October 1924) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Brett Young (1884–1954) was an English novelist, poet and physician, born in Halesowen, Worcestershire. He qualified in medicine at Birmingham and served as a ship's doctor and as an army medical officer in East Africa during the First World War. He is best known for novels set in the Midlands, such as My Brother Jonathan (1928).
He also wrote verse throughout his career. Edward Marsh included his poems in Georgian Poetry 1918-1919 and 1920-1922, from which the pieces here are taken.

poets.name: James Elroy Flecker
poets.credit: Photograph of James Elroy Flecker at Cambridge (c. 1910) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Elroy Flecker (1884–1915) was an English poet, born in London and educated at Uppingham and at Oxford, who afterwards read Oriental languages at Cambridge. He entered the Levant Consular Service and was posted to Constantinople, Smyrna and Beirut. His verse is Parnassian in manner, with a taste for the East, for classical and legendary subjects, and for polished craft.

Forty-Two Poems (London, J. M. Dent, 1911) gathers poems from his earlier books together with new ones, including the Ballad of Iskander and the War Song of the Saracens. His later volume The Golden Journey to Samarkand appeared in 1913, and his verse play Hassan was published after his death. Suffering from tuberculosis, he died at Davos, Switzerland, in January 1915.

poets.name: D. H. Lawrence
poets.credit: Passport photograph of D. H. Lawrence (1929) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: David Herbert Lawrence (1885–1930) was an English novelist, essayist and poet, born in Eastwood, Nottinghamshire, the son of a coal miner. He wrote Sons and Lovers, The Rainbow and Women in Love, and also much poetry from his early lyrics of Nottinghamshire to the free-verse poems of his years abroad.

The poems here come from Love Poems and Others (1913), Look! We Have Come Through! (1917), New Poems (1918) and Birds, Beasts and Flowers (1923), the last of which contains his best-known animal poems. He died in Vence, France, in 1930.

poets.name: Elinor Wylie
poets.credit: Photograph of Elinor Wylie by an unidentified photographer (c. 1921) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elinor Wylie (1885–1928) was an American poet and novelist, born Elinor Hoyt in Somerville, New Jersey, and raised in Pennsylvania and Washington, D.C. Her first book of verse, Nets to Catch the Wind (1921), made her reputation, and was followed by Black Armour (1923), Trivial Breath (1928) and Angels and Earthly Creatures (1929).

Her poems are known for their polished, exact diction, crystalline imagery and tightly wrought forms, often turning on silver, glass, snow and metal. She also wrote novels, among them Jennifer Lorn (1923) and The Venetian Glass Nephew (1925). She died in New York in 1928.

poets.name: Ahmet Haşim
bio: Ahmet Haşim was born in Baghdad in the mid-1880s (sources differ on the year) and came to Istanbul at about twelve, after his mother's death. At the Galatasaray school he discovered French poetry and the Symbolists. In 1909 he joined the Fecr-i Âtî ('Dawn of the Future') group and published his poems in its magazine, Servet-i Fünûn.

He published two books of verse, Göl Saatleri ('Lake Hours', 1921) and Piyale ('The Wine Cup', 1926), made of short, musical poems about evening, water and light. He died in Istanbul on 4 June 1933. The texts below are the original Turkish, taken from tr.wikisource.org.

poets.name: John Freeman
bio: John Freeman (dates as printed in Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920): 1885–1929) was an English poet who worked as an insurance executive while writing verse and criticism. He was associated with the Georgian poets; his book Stone Trees appeared in 1916.
The poem here comes from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Joyce Kilmer
poets.credit: Joyce Kilmer, Columbia University yearbook photograph, 1908 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joyce Kilmer (1886–1918) was an American poet, journalist and critic, born in New Brunswick, New Jersey, and educated at Rutgers College and Columbia University, where he graduated in 1908. He worked as a teacher, a lexicographer's assistant at Funk and Wagnalls, literary editor of The Churchman, and a member of the staff of the New York Times. He converted to Roman Catholicism in 1913, and his faith colours much of his later verse.

Trees and Other Poems (1914), his best-known volume, contains the brief lyric "Trees", first published in Poetry magazine in 1913 and among the most widely recited American poems of the century. Kilmer enlisted in the New York National Guard in 1917, served in France with the 165th Infantry (the "Fighting 69th"), and was killed by a sniper's bullet at the second battle of the Marne on 30 July 1918, aged 31. A second collection, Main Street and Other Poems, appeared in 1917.

poets.name: John Gould Fletcher
bio: John Gould Fletcher (1886–1950) was an American poet, born in Little Rock, Arkansas, who lived in London from 1909 to 1933.
A leading Imagist, he later won the Pulitzer Prize for his Selected Poems (1939).

poets.name: William Rose Benét
bio: William Rose Benét (1886–1950) was an American poet, editor and critic, the brother of Stephen Vincent Benét.
He helped found The Saturday Review of Literature and won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry in 1942.

poets.name: Shaemas O Sheel
poets.credit: Portrait of Shaemas O Sheel (photograph by Bachrach Studios, 1927) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Shaemas O Sheel (1886–1954) was an American poet and writer of Irish descent.
His best-known poem, “They Went Forth to Battle, But They Always Fell”, is a much-anthologised tribute to those who die in war.

poets.name: Rupert Brooke
poets.credit: Photograph of Rupert Brooke by Sherril Schell (1913), from Collected Poems (1918) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rupert Brooke (1887–1915) was an English poet, born at Rugby and educated at King’s College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow. He was a leading figure among the Georgian poets, and travelled in America and the South Seas in 1913–1914.

He joined the Royal Naval Division in 1914 and wrote the sonnet sequence 1914, which includes “The Soldier.” He died of blood poisoning aboard a French hospital ship off the Greek island of Skyros on 23 April 1915, on his way to Gallipoli, and was buried there.

poets.name: Orrick Johns
bio: Orrick Johns (1887–1946) was an American poet, born in St. Louis, Missouri.
His book Asphalt and Other Poems (1917) established his reputation.

poets.name: Francis Ledwidge
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Ledwidge, frontispiece to The Complete Poems (1919) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Ledwidge (1887–1917) was an Irish poet, the son of a farm labourer from Slane, County Meath, who worked as a farmhand, miner and road worker. Lord Dunsany read his early verse, encouraged him and arranged the publication of Songs of the Fields (1915).

He enlisted in the Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers, served at Gallipoli, in Serbia and in France, and wrote poems of the Irish countryside and of the war, including an elegy for Thomas MacDonagh. He was killed at Boezinge, near Ypres, on 31 July 1917.

poets.name: Alan Seeger
poets.credit: Photograph of Alan Seeger · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alan Seeger (1888–1916) was an American poet born in New York City and educated at Harvard. After graduating in 1910 he lived for some years in the Latin Quarter of Paris, and his early verse, much of it in the manner of the late Romantics and the Pre-Raphaelites, celebrates beauty, travel and love.

When war broke out in 1914 he enlisted in the French Foreign Legion, serving on the Aisne and in Champagne. He was killed at Belloy-en-Santerre on 4 July 1916. His Poems, with an introduction by William Archer, appeared in 1916 and made him widely known, above all for “I Have a Rendezvous with Death.”

poets.name: T. P. Cameron Wilson
bio: T. P. Cameron Wilson (1889–1918) was an English schoolmaster and poet who served as an officer in the First World War and was killed in action in March 1918.
His best-known poem, Sportsmen in Paradise, is taken here from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Claude McKay
poets.credit: Portrait of Claude McKay by James L. Allen · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Claude McKay (1889–1948) was born in Sunny Ville, Clarendon Parish, Jamaica, and published two volumes of dialect verse there before emigrating to the United States in 1912. He studied briefly at Tuskegee Institute and Kansas State, then settled in New York, where he became a leading figure in the literature of the Harlem Renaissance.

Harlem Shadows (1922), his first book of poems in standard English, gathered sonnets and lyrics of racial protest, urban life and homesickness for Jamaica, among them "If We Must Die" and "America". It carries an introduction by Max Eastman. McKay also wrote novels, including Home to Harlem (1928), and died in Chicago in 1948.

poets.name: W. J. Turner
bio: Walter James Turner (1889–1946) was a poet and critic, born in Melbourne, Australia, who settled in England and became known as a music and drama critic as well as a Georgian poet.
His poem Romance, here taken from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920), is his most famous.

poets.name: Isaac Rosenberg
poets.credit: Self-portrait of Isaac Rosenberg (before 1918) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Isaac Rosenberg (1890–1918) was an English poet and painter, born in Bristol to Jewish immigrant parents from Lithuania and raised in the East End of London. He studied art at the Slade School, and his first pamphlets of verse were printed at his own expense.

He enlisted in 1915 and wrote his war poems, among them “Break of Day in the Trenches” and “Dead Man’s Dump,” in the trenches, scribbling them on scraps of paper. He was killed on 1 April 1918. His Poems, edited by Gordon Bottomley with a memoir by Laurence Binyon, appeared in 1922.

poets.name: Ivor Gurney
bio: Ivor Gurney (1890–1937) was an English poet and composer, born in Gloucester and a chorister at Gloucester Cathedral, who studied music at the Royal College of Music under Stanford. His work is bound up with the Severn valley and the Gloucestershire countryside.

He served as a private with the 2/5th Gloucesters on the Western Front, was wounded and gassed, and published two books of poems in his lifetime, Severn and Somme (1917) and War’s Embers (1919). He suffered a long mental illness and spent his last fifteen years in an asylum, where he went on writing.

poets.name: Edward Shanks
bio: Edward Shanks (1892–1953) was an English poet, novelist and critic, associated with the Georgian poets and with the London Mercury, which J. C. Squire edited.
His poem here comes from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Edna St. Vincent Millay
poets.credit: Photograph of Edna St. Vincent Millay by Arnold Genthe (c. 1914) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edna St. Vincent Millay (1892–1950) was an American poet and playwright, born in Rockland, Maine. She became famous at nineteen with "Renascence", published in 1912 and collected in Renascence and Other Poems (1917). She studied at Vassar College and afterwards lived in Greenwich Village, New York, where her lyrics and sonnets of love, loss and independence made her a leading voice of the 1920s.

Her collection The Harp-Weaver and Other Poems (1923) won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1923, the first awarded to a woman for poetry. This edition takes her poems from the London volume Poems (Martin Secker, 1923) and adds two poems from Renascence and Other Poems that Secker omitted. She died at her home at Steepletop, near Austerlitz, New York, in 1950.

poets.name: Maxwell Bodenheim
bio: Maxwell Bodenheim (1892–1954) was an American poet and novelist of the Greenwich Village bohemia, born in Hermanville, Mississippi.
His early books include Minna and Myself (1918) and Advice (1920).

poets.name: Winifred Welles
bio: Winifred Welles (1893–1939) was an American poet whose first book, Shadows of Sails, appeared in 1915.
Her short lyrics were published in magazines and in the anthologies of her day.

poets.name: Herbert S. Gorman
bio: Herbert S. Gorman (1893–1954) was an American poet, critic and biographer.
His James Joyce: His First Forty Years (1924) was among the first books written about Joyce.

poets.name: Wilfred Owen
poets.credit: Portrait of Wilfred Owen (frontispiece to Poems, 1920) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Wilfred Owen (1893–1918) was an English poet and soldier whose unsparing poems of the Western Front made him the best-known poet of the First World War. Only a handful of his poems were published in his lifetime.

He served with the Manchester Regiment, was treated for shell-shock at Craiglockhart, where he met Siegfried Sassoon, and returned to the front in 1918. He won the Military Cross and was killed on 4 November 1918, a week before the Armistice. His Poems, edited by Sassoon, appeared in 1920.

poets.name: Stephen Vincent Benét
poets.credit: Stephen Vincent Benét, Yale College yearbook photograph (class of 1919), photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Stephen Vincent Benét (1898–1943) was an American poet, short-story writer and novelist, born in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, the younger brother of the poet William Rose Benét. He studied at Yale, where he published Five Men and Pompey (1915) while still an undergraduate, and Young Adventure (1918), the first of the two books in this archive, was published by Yale University Press.

He went on to win two Pulitzer Prizes for poetry, for the Civil War narrative John Brown's Body (1929) and, posthumously, for Western Star (1944), and wrote some of the best-known American short stories of his generation. Heavens and Earth (1920), his second collection of verse, followed soon after his Yale years. Only these two early books are included here.

poets.name: Robert Nichols
bio: Robert Nichols (1893–1944) was an English poet who served as an artillery officer in the First World War and was invalided home. His war poems appeared in Invocation (1915) and Ardours and Endurances (1917).
He later taught English literature in Japan. His poem here comes from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Countee Cullen
poets.credit: Portrait of Countee Cullen by R. W. Bullock, 1927 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) was an American poet, born in 1903 and raised in New York City, where he attended New York University and Harvard and became one of the best-known poets of the Harlem Renaissance. He wrote in traditional forms, the sonnet, the quatrain and the ballad, often turning them to questions of race, faith and mortality.

Color (1925) was his first book, and includes "Yet Do I Marvel", "Heritage" and "Incident" along with a run of short epitaphs. The Black Christ & Other Poems (1929) followed, written in part with the aid of a Guggenheim Fellowship; its title poem is a long narrative of a lynching and a resurrection. He later wrote further verse, a novel and children's books, and died in New York in 1946.

poets.name: Charles Hamilton Sorley
bio: Charles Hamilton Sorley (1895–1915) was a Scottish-born English poet, educated at Marlborough College. He was commissioned in the Suffolk Regiment in 1914 and was killed near Hulluch, in France, on 13 October 1915, aged twenty.
His only book, Marlborough and Other Poems, appeared posthumously in 1916. The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Sabahattin Ali
poets.credit: Sabahattin Ali, c. 1940 (photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sabahattin Ali (1907–1948) was born in Eğridere (now Ardino), in what is today Bulgaria, and trained as a teacher; he studied German in Potsdam and Berlin in the late 1920s and later taught in Anatolian schools. He is better known today as a novelist and short-story writer, the author of Kuyucaklı Yusuf and Kürk Mantolu Madonna (Madonna in a Fur Coat), but he also wrote verse throughout his life, much of it in the plain, song-like rhythms of Turkish folk poetry.

He was imprisoned in 1932 for a satirical quatrain, and again in the 1940s for his political views; the bitterness and longing of that experience colour poems such as Gurbet Hapishanesi ("The Prison of Exile"). He was killed near the Bulgarian border in April 1948 while trying to leave Turkey. Only seven poems, those transcribed on Turkish Wikisource, are given here; many of his best-loved poems are not included.

poets.name: Orhan Veli Kanık
poets.credit: Portrait photograph of Orhan Veli Kanık (photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Orhan Veli Kanık (1914–1950) was born in Istanbul and grew up partly in Ankara, where he studied at the Gazi High School before reading philosophy at Istanbul University. With his school friends Oktay Rifat and Melih Cevdet he published the volume Garip ("Strange") in 1941, prefaced by a manifesto that attacked rhyme, metre, conventional poetic imagery and the idea that poetry needed an elevated vocabulary. The three poets became known as the Garip movement, and the book is regarded as a turning point in modern Turkish poetry.

His own poems are built from the speech of the street, the ferry, the café and the neighbourhood: short lines, everyday objects, humour and an unforced tenderness, with Istanbul, the sea and ordinary people as constant subjects. He followed Garip with further collections, among them Vazgeçemediğim (1945), Destan Gibi (1946), Yenisi (1947) and Karşı (1949), and also worked as a translator and essayist. He died in Istanbul in November 1950, aged thirty-six, after an accident; his plain-speech revolution outlived him and shaped almost every Turkish poet who came after.

poets.name: Rüştü Onur
bio: Rüştü Onur was born in 1920 in Devrek, in the Zonguldak region of Turkey's Black Sea coast. He died of tuberculosis in 1942, aged 22. His friend Muzaffer Tayyip Uslu, another young poet from Zonguldak who also died young of the disease, is remembered beside him: anthologies have long presented the two together as the 'poets of Zonguldak'.

His poems were gathered after his death; a posthumous collection was published by Yeditepe Yayınları in 1956. This is a first instalment of four poems, not his complete poems. The texts are the original Turkish, taken from tr.wikisource.org.

works.title: The Aeneid
works.author: Virgil
works.note: Project Gutenberg #228 carries no title page; Dryden's Virgil was published by Jacob Tonson in 1697, and Dryden died in 1700.
works.blurb: Virgil's Latin epic of Aeneas, the Trojan refugee who carries his gods to Italy and founds the line of Rome, in twelve books, rendered into English heroic couplets by John Dryden.

works.title: Andreas
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation. Once widely attributed to Cynewulf on stylistic grounds; modern scholarship no longer accepts the attribution.
works.blurb: The apostle Andrew's perilous sea voyage to rescue Matthew from the cannibalistic Mermedonians, told in a style deliberately recalling Beowulf's heroic diction.

works.title: Atta Troll
works.subtitle: A Summer Night's Dream
works.author: Heinrich Heine
works.note: From Bowring's The Poems of Heine, Complete (Bohn's Standard Library, George Bell and Sons, 1908 reprint), Project Gutenberg #52882. Footnote marks are removed and the translator's notes are left out. Heine's verse dedication to Varnhagen von Ense stands within Caput XXVII.
works.blurb: Heine's mock-heroic satire in twenty-seven cantos, written in 1841 and published in 1847: a dancing bear escapes from his master at Cauterets in the Pyrenees, and the pursuit becomes a burlesque of the political poets and doctrinaire radicals of the day.

works.title: The Barons' Wars
works.subtitle: In the Reign of Edward the Second (Books II–VI)
works.author: Michael Drayton
works.blurb: Drayton's verse chronicle of the civil wars under Edward II, in ottava rima — this edition preserves Books II through VI.

works.title: Beowulf
works.author: Beowulf Poet
works.note: Anonymous Old English original; this is Francis Barton Gummere's 1910 alliterative verse translation, prepared for the Harvard Classics and in the public domain.
works.blurb: The Geatish hero Beowulf crosses the sea to rid the Danish hall of Heorot of the monster Grendel, then Grendel's vengeful mother, and in old age faces a dragon guarding a cursed hoard — the oldest surviving epic in English.

sections.title: Prelude of the Founder of the Danish House

works.title: The Canterbury Tales
works.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
works.note: Original Middle English text (modernized spelling, D. Laing Purves edition, 1870s). Unfinished at Chaucer's death; the Cook's Tale breaks off and the Parson's Tale closes the collection in prose.
works.blurb: A fellowship of pilgrims riding from Southwark to Canterbury pass the road in stories — chivalric romance, low comedy, sermon, and fable — in the original Middle English, the foundation of English narrative poetry.

works.title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage
works.author: Lord Byron
works.note: Text of Project Gutenberg #5131, which prints no edition date; the four cantos appeared between 1812 and 1818. Byron's prose preface, the prose dedication of Canto IV and the end-notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Byron's Spenserian travelogue in four cantos follows a world-weary young pilgrim through Portugal, Spain, Greece, Belgium, the Rhine and Italy, turning from personal gloom to meditations on liberty, ruin and the sublime.

works.title: Christ I
works.subtitle: The Advent Lyrics
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation. Unsigned; grouped with Christ II and Christ III in the Exeter Book as a single sequence on the life of Christ, though the three are almost certainly by different, mostly anonymous poets.
works.blurb: A sequence of lyric meditations, based on the liturgical O Antiphons of Advent, anticipating the coming of Christ.

works.title: Christ II
works.subtitle: The Ascension
works.author: Cynewulf
works.note: Prose translation. One of Cynewulf's four signed poems.
works.blurb: Cynewulf's account of Christ's Ascension into heaven, drawing on a homily of Gregory the Great, and of the gifts of grace bestowed on humankind.

works.title: Christ III
works.subtitle: Judgment Day
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation. Unsigned.
works.blurb: A vision of the Last Judgment: Christ's sudden return, the terror of sinners and the joy of the blessed, closing the Exeter Book's Christ sequence.

works.title: Christ and Satan
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation.
works.blurb: The last poem of the Junius Manuscript: the lament of the fallen angels in hell, Christ's Harrowing of Hell and Ascension, and finally Satan's temptation of Christ in the wilderness.

works.title: Chronicle of the Cid
works.author: Anonymous (Poem of the Cid)
works.note: Prose translation and compilation from medieval Spanish chronicle and ballad sources; not a verse rendering of the Cantar de Mio Cid itself.
works.blurb: Robert Southey’s English compilation of the medieval Spanish chronicles and ballads recounting the life and legend of Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, El Cid.

works.title: Comus
works.subtitle: A Mask Presented at Ludlow Castle
works.author: John Milton
works.blurb: A masque of chastity and temptation, performed at Ludlow Castle in 1634 — a Lady lost in the wood and the enchanter Comus.

works.title: Confessio Amantis
works.subtitle: Tales of the Seven Deadly Sins
works.author: John Gower
works.note: Original Middle English text, edited by G. C. Macaulay (The Works of John Gower, Oxford, 1899–1902).
works.blurb: A lover confesses to Venus's priest Genius, who works through the Seven Deadly Sins with a great gathering of exemplary tales — classical, biblical, and romance — in eight books of octosyllabic couplets.

works.title: Daniel
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation.
works.blurb: A verse paraphrase of the Book of Daniel: Nebuchadnezzar's pride and madness, the three youths in the fiery furnace, and Belshazzar's feast and the writing on the wall.

works.title: The Divine Comedy
works.subtitle: La Divina Commedia
works.author: Dante Alighieri
works.blurb: Dante's vision of the afterlife in a hundred cantos, from the dark wood through Inferno and Purgatorio to the Paradiso, in Longfellow's blank-verse tercets.

works.title: Don Juan
works.author: Lord Byron
works.note: Text of Project Gutenberg #21700, which follows an 1857 edition; the cantos appeared between 1819 and 1824, and Canto XVII was left a fragment at Byron's death.
works.blurb: Byron's unfinished comic epic in ottava rima follows a young Spaniard through seductions, shipwreck, war and the courts of Europe, mocking cant, politics and poetry itself along the way.

works.title: Elene
works.author: Cynewulf
works.note: One of Cynewulf's four signed poems; his runic signature appears near the close.
works.blurb: Cynewulf's retelling of the legend of St. Helena, mother of the Emperor Constantine, and her journey to Jerusalem in search of the True Cross, opening with Constantine's vision of the Cross before his battle at the Milvian Bridge.

works.title: Endymion
works.subtitle: A Poetic Romance
works.author: John Keats
works.note: Text of the 1818 first edition, from Project Gutenberg #24280. Printer's errata are left as printed; the Preface and dedication are omitted.
works.blurb: Keats's four-book retelling of the myth of the shepherd prince Endymion, loved by the moon goddess and wandering the earth, sea and underworld in search of her.

works.title: An Essay on Man
works.subtitle: In Four Epistles to Henry St John, Lord Bolingbroke
works.author: Alexander Pope
works.blurb: Pope’s attempt, in polished couplets, to ‘vindicate the ways of God to Man’ — four epistles on man’s place in the universe, himself, society, and happiness.

works.title: Exodus
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation.
works.blurb: A dense, martial retelling of the Israelites' flight from Egypt and crossing of the Red Sea, cast largely in the diction of Old English heroic poetry.

works.title: The Faerie Queene
works.subtitle: Books I–VI, with the Mutabilitie Cantos
works.author: Edmund Spenser
works.blurb: Spenser's vast allegorical epic of knights, virtues, and the Faerie court — six completed Books (Holinesse, Temperaunce, Chastitie, Friendship, Iustice, Courtesie) plus the fragmentary Mutabilitie Cantos, in the original 1590s spelling.

works.title: The Fates of the Apostles
works.author: Cynewulf
works.note: Prose translation. One of Cynewulf's four signed poems; his runic signature closes it.
works.blurb: A brief martyrology recounting, in turn, the missionary travels and deaths of Christ's twelve apostles, closing the Vercelli Book poem with Cynewulf's runic signature.

works.title: Fridthjof's Saga
works.subtitle: A Norse Romance
works.author: Esaias Tegnér
works.translator: trans. Thomas A. E. Holcomb and Martha A. Lyon Holcomb (1876)
works.note: Project Gutenberg #3759. English version by Thomas A. E. Holcomb and Martha A. Lyon Holcomb, with a translators' note dated October 1876. The translators' note, contents, list of characters and glossary are omitted.
works.blurb: Tegnér's Swedish romantic epic in twenty-four cantos, drawn from an Icelandic saga: the farmer's son Fridthjof loves Ingeborg, daughter of King Bele, and is parted from her by her brothers, outlawed, and finally reconciled, here in English verse by the Holcombs.

Canto XVIII: The Ride on the Ice
Canto XXIII: Fridthjof at his Father's Grave

works.title: The Dispensary
works.subtitle: A Poem in Six Cantos
works.author: Sir Samuel Garth
works.blurb: A mock-heroic satire on the apothecaries who opposed the College of Physicians' free dispensary for the poor, told as an epic battle of drugs, doctors and allegorical spirits. Text of the first edition (London, 1699), with its original spelling.

works.title: Genesis
works.subtitle: Genesis A and Genesis B
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation. Once attributed to Caedmon; the manuscript's Genesis is now known to be composite, a longer Genesis A into which a distinct poem, Genesis B (itself apparently translated from an Old Saxon original), was inserted.
works.blurb: A verse paraphrase of Genesis running from the Creation and the fall of the rebel angels through Abraham and the near-sacrifice of Isaac, opening the Junius Manuscript.

works.title: Germany: A Winter Tale
works.subtitle: Deutschland. Ein Wintermärchen
works.author: Heinrich Heine
works.blurb: Heine's satirical verse journey home from exile in Paris to Hamburg in twenty-seven cantos, mocking Prussian authority and German nationalism.

works.title: The Gods of the North
works.subtitle: An Epic Poem
works.author: Adam Oehlenschläger
works.note: From Frye's English verse translation (1845) of Oehlenschläger's Nordens Guder, Project Gutenberg #49696. Frye's preface on Norse mythology and his Notes and Elucidations are left out, as are footnote marks and the translator's prose notes. The source prints the heading Canto XI twice. The second block is not a new canto but Frye's experimental rendering of the same eleventh canto in alliterative verse, so it is kept as its own section, 'Canto XI (second)', and the numbering from Canto XII onward follows the source.
works.blurb: Oehlenschläger's cycle of thirty cantos retelling the Norse myths, chiefly the adventures of Thor and the mischief of Lok, among the Aesir and the giants, in Frye's English rhymed and blank verse.

works.title: Gondibert
works.subtitle: An Heroick Poem
works.author: Sir William Davenant
works.blurb: Davenant’s unfinished heroic poem in decasyllabic quatrains — three books and twenty cantos of love, war and statecraft among the Lombards.

works.title: Guthlac
works.subtitle: Guthlac A and Guthlac B
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation of both Guthlac A and Guthlac B, presented here as Kennedy translated them, as one continuous work. Guthlac B breaks off mid-sentence at the end of a damaged manuscript page.
works.blurb: The life of St. Guthlac of Crowland, a former warrior turned hermit who does battle with demons in the Lincolnshire fens (Guthlac A), and an account, closely based on Felix's Latin Life, of his final illness and death (Guthlac B).

works.title: The Hind and the Panther
works.subtitle: A Poem, in Three Parts
works.author: John Dryden
works.blurb: A long allegorical fable in which the milk-white Hind (the Catholic Church) and the Panther (the Church of England) debate faith and politics after James II’s accession.

works.title: The Homeric Hymns
works.author: Homer
works.note: Prose translation, Loeb Classical Library.
works.blurb: Thirty-three anonymous hymns of invocation to the Greek gods, transmitted alongside Homer’s epics since antiquity and traditionally (though almost certainly wrongly) attributed to him.

works.title: Idylls of the King
works.subtitle: In Twelve Books
works.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
works.note: Text of Project Gutenberg #610, which carries no edition year; the idylls were published between 1859 and 1885.
works.blurb: Tennyson's cycle of twelve idylls retelling the rise and fall of King Arthur's court, from The Coming of Arthur to The Passing of Arthur, framed by a dedication to Prince Albert and an epilogue to Queen Victoria.

works.title: The Iliad
works.author: Homer
works.note: Prose translation.
works.blurb: Samuel Butler’s brisk, plain-spoken prose translation of Homer’s epic of the wrath of Achilles and the last year of the siege of Troy.

works.title: The Iliad
works.author: Homer
works.note: Verse translation in heroic couplets.
works.blurb: Alexander Pope’s celebrated heroic-couplet translation of the Iliad, one of the great achievements of Augustan English verse.

works.title: Jerusalem Delivered
works.subtitle: Gerusalemme Liberata
works.author: Torquato Tasso
works.blurb: Tasso's epic of the First Crusade and the siege of Jerusalem under Godfrey of Bouillon, in twenty books of ottava rima, in Edward Fairfax's English version.

works.title: Judith
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.translator: trans. Cosette Faust Newton & Stith Thompson (1918)
works.note: Prose-verse translation; the surviving text is a fragment (roughly the poem's last third).
works.blurb: A retelling, in the Nowell Codex alongside Beowulf, of the apocryphal Book of Judith: the widow Judith beheads the drunken Assyrian general Holofernes and delivers her people, recast in the heroic idiom of Old English verse.

works.title: Juliana
works.author: Cynewulf
works.note: Prose translation.
works.blurb: One of Cynewulf's four signed poems: the passion of the virgin martyr Juliana of Nicomedia, who resists both an unwanted marriage to a pagan prefect and torture by a demon sent to break her faith.

works.title: The Kalevala
works.subtitle: The Epic Poem of Finland
works.author: Elias Lönnrot
works.note: Finnish epic compiled by Elias Lönnrot from oral rune-songs (1835; enlarged 1849). This is John Martin Crawford's 1888 English translation in unrhymed trochaic verse, from Project Gutenberg #5186. The translator's preface and glossary are omitted.
works.blurb: Fifty runes of Finnish folk song gathered into one epic: the birth of the sage Wainamoinen, the rivalry of Finns and the people of Pohjola for the Sampo, the doomed Kullervo, and the hero's departure as a new age arrives.

works.title: The Lady of the Lake
works.author: Sir Walter Scott
works.blurb: A romance of the Scottish Highlands, unfolding over six days on the shores of Loch Katrine, that made Sir Walter Scott the most popular poet in Europe.

works.title: Lalla Rookh
works.subtitle: An Oriental Romance
works.author: Thomas Moore
works.note: Project Gutenberg #8187 (Moore's poetical works) carries no edition year; Lalla Rookh was first published in 1817 and Moore died in 1852. Only the four verse tales are given here: Moore's prose frame (the journey of Lalla Rookh, Feramorz and the critic Fadladeen), the songs sung inside that frame, and his notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Thomas Moore's best-selling Oriental romance: four verse tales told to a princess on her journey from Delhi to Kashmir, by the young poet Feramorz.

works.title: The Lusiads
works.subtitle: Os Lusíadas
works.author: Luís de Camões
works.note: Burton's rendering of 1880, in the original ottava rima; his archaic diction is deliberate. The unnumbered stanza in Canto X that follows stanza 40 (‘Then waxt the woeful wail a sorer strain’) is Burton's own interpolation, a lament for the Prince Imperial killed in Zululand in 1879; it is not in Camoes.
works.blurb: Camões's national epic of Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and the story of Portugal, in ten cantos of ottava rima, rendered into English by Sir Richard Francis Burton.

works.title: Marmion
works.subtitle: A Tale of Flodden Field
works.author: Sir Walter Scott
works.blurb: A verse romance of treachery and doomed love set against the Scottish army's march to its catastrophic defeat at Flodden in 1513.

works.title: Metamorphoses
works.author: Ovid
works.note: Prose translation.
works.blurb: Ovid’s vast narrative poem in fifteen books, retelling the myths of transformation from the creation of the world to the deification of Julius Caesar.

works.title: M'Fingal
works.subtitle: A Modern Epic Poem, in Four Cantos
works.author: John Trumbull
works.note: Text of the 1795 Hartford edition, with the plate captions, editor's preface and Trumbull's own footnotes omitted. One unrecognised punctuation mark per occurrence in the digital transcription is omitted.
works.blurb: Hudibrastic satire on a Tory squire in revolutionary Massachusetts.

works.title: Miss Kilmansegg and Her Precious Leg
works.subtitle: A Golden Legend
works.author: Thomas Hood
works.note: From 'The Comic Poems of Thomas Hood', 'A New and Complete Edition', with a preface by Thomas Hood the Younger (London: E. Moxon, Son, and Company; year not printed; Hood d. 1845). Source: Project Gutenberg #56712.
works.blurb: Hood's comic narrative of an heiress whose golden leg, bought after a riding accident, makes her fortune and her ruin: a satire on money, marriage and the worship of gold, told in eighteen sections.

works.title: The Moallakát
works.subtitle: The Seven Arabian Poems which were suspended on the Temple at Mecca
works.author: The Mu'allaqat Poets
works.note: Sir William Jones's 1782 English prose translation, numbered verse by verse, from the proofread Wikisource transcription of the reprint in W. A. Clouston, Arabian Poetry for English Readers (1881). Jones's prose arguments and Clouston's notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Seven great odes of pre-Islamic Arabia, said to have been hung on the Kaaba at Mecca, by Imru' al-Qais, Tarafa, Zuhayr, Labid, Antara, Amr ibn Kulthum and al-Harith ibn Hilliza.

works.title: Of the Nature of Things
works.author: Lucretius
works.note: Gutenberg #785 carries no date; the first edition is Dent/Dutton, 1916 (Internet Archive ofnatureofthings00lucrrich). Leonard died in 1944.
works.blurb: Lucretius's Latin didactic poem De rerum natura, an exposition of Epicurean atomism in six books, rendered into English blank verse by William Ellery Leonard.

works.title: The Nibelungenlied
works.author: Anonymous (Middle High German)
works.note: Needler's English verse translation (1904, University College, Toronto), from Project Gutenberg #7321. Stanza numerals, the translator's footnotes and his preface and introduction are omitted. The ' / ' marks the mid-line pause of the original long line, as in the transcription.
works.blurb: The Middle High German epic of Siegfried, Kriemhild and the fall of the Burgundians, composed in Austria around 1200, in thirty-nine adventures and 2,379 four-line stanzas, rendered into English verse by George Henry Needler.

works.author: Ludovico Ariosto
works.blurb: Ariosto's romance epic of Charlemagne's paladins, Orlando's love-madness, and the love of Ruggiero and Bradamante, in William Stewart Rose's eight-line stanzas.

works.title: Paradise Lost
works.subtitle: A Poem in Twelve Books
works.author: John Milton
works.blurb: Milton’s epic of the war in Heaven and the fall of man — twelve books of blank verse, from Satan’s rebellion to the expulsion from Eden.

works.title: Paradise Regain'd
works.subtitle: A Poem in Four Books
works.author: John Milton
works.blurb: The brief epic sequel: Christ in the wilderness, tempted by Satan and refusing every worldly power.

works.title: The Parliament of Fowls
works.subtitle: The Assembly of Fowls
works.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
works.note: Original Middle English text (modernized spelling, D. Laing Purves edition, 1870s).
works.blurb: A Valentine's Day dream vision in which birds of every rank gather before Nature to choose their mates — often read as an allegory of courtship and royal marriage.

works.title: Pearl
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.note: Anonymous Middle English original (Cotton Nero A.x). This is Sophie Jewett's 1908 verse translation, made in the metre and stanza-form of the original and long in the public domain.
works.blurb: A grieving father falls asleep on the grave of his infant daughter and dreams her transfigured into a maiden of Heaven, radiant among the elect — an elegy of loss answered by consolation, in interlocking rhymed stanzas.

works.title: Pharsalia
works.subtitle: De Bello Civili (The Civil War)
works.author: Lucan
works.note: Verse translation; the poem was left unfinished at Lucan’s death.
works.blurb: Lucan’s unfinished epic of the Roman civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey, notable for banishing the gods from its narrative entirely.

works.title: The Phoenix
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.translator: trans. Cosette Faust Newton & Stith Thompson (1918)
works.blurb: A richly decorative description of the mythical phoenix and its cyclical death and rebirth in a paradisal eastern land, allegorized in the poem's second half as a figure of Christian resurrection.

works.title: Piers Plowman
works.subtitle: The Vision of Piers Ploughman
works.author: William Langland
works.note: Original Middle English text, B-text, edited by Thomas Wright (1842 edition, Library of Old Authors; text as reprinted on Project Gutenberg).
works.blurb: Falling asleep on the Malvern Hills, the dreamer Will sees a field full of folk and sets out through a sequence of visions to find Do-well, Do-bet, and Do-best — a vast alliterative satire of church, court, and commons.

works.title: The Poetic Edda
works.subtitle: Lays of the Gods and Lays of the Heroes, translated from the Icelandic with the stanza numbering of the standard editions
works.author: Anonymous (Old Norse)
works.blurb: The great Old Norse collection of mythological and heroic lays preserved in the Codex Regius, in Bellows's 1923 verse translation, with the Eddas' own prose links kept in place.

works.title: The Rámáyan of Válmíki
works.author: Valmiki
works.note: Project Gutenberg #24869. London: Trübner & Co.; Benares: E. J. Lazarus and Co., 1870–1874. Includes Griffith's Invocation and Books I–VI. Griffith's footnote numbers, his bracketed notes on omitted cantos, the contents list, the Appendix, the prose summary of the Uttarakánda, the Additional Notes, index and footnotes are left out. Griffith omitted some cantos, so numbering in places is not continuous.
works.blurb: The Sanskrit epic of Rama, prince of Ayodhya: his exile, the abduction of Sita by the demon Ravana, the alliance with the monkey host and the war in Lanka, rendered into English verse by Ralph T. H. Griffith.

works.title: The Rape of the Lock
works.subtitle: An Heroi-Comical Poem, in Five Cantos
works.author: Alexander Pope
works.blurb: A mock-epic on a society scandal — a lock of hair snipped in jest — blown up with the full machinery of Homeric epic, sylphs and all.

works.title: Samson Agonistes
works.subtitle: A Dramatic Poem
works.author: John Milton
works.blurb: A tragedy on the Greek model — the blinded, captive Samson among the Philistines, moving toward his final act.

works.title: The Shepheard’s Calender
works.subtitle: Twelve Æglogues Proportionable to the Twelve Monethes
works.author: Edmund Spenser
works.blurb: Spenser’s first major work: twelve eclogues, one for each month, mixing pastoral love-complaint, satire of the clergy, and elegy in a deliberately archaic English.

works.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
works.subtitle: A Middle-English Arthurian Romance
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.note: Anonymous Middle English original (Cotton Nero A.x). This is Jessie L. Weston's 1898 prose translation (David Nutt, London), long in the public domain — chosen over any 20th-century verse translation (Tolkien, Borroff, Armitage), which remain under copyright.
works.blurb: A green-skinned knight rides into Arthur's Christmas feast with an impossible challenge; Sir Gawain's answer sends him on a year-long quest that tests his courage, his courtesy, and his honesty alike.

works.title: The Song of Hiawatha
works.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
works.blurb: A trochaic epic drawing on Ojibwe legend, following the life of the hero Hiawatha — his childhood, wooing, feats, and eventual departure — in a rhythm modeled on the Finnish Kalevala.

poems.title: The Seafarer
poems.excerpt:
I can utter a true song about myself, tell of my travels, how in toilsome days I often suffered a time of hardship, how I have borne bitter sorrow in my breast, made trial of many sorrowful abodes on ships; dread was the rolling of the waves. There the hard night-watch at the boat's prow was often my task, when it tosses by the cliffs. Afflicted with cold, my feet were fettered by frost, by chill bonds. There my sorrows, hot round my heart, were sighed forth; hunger within rent the mind of the sea-weary man. The man who fares most prosperously on land knows not how I, careworn, have spent a winter as an exile on the ice-cold sea, cut off from kinsmen, hung round with icicles. The hail flew in showers. I heard naught there save the sea booming, the ice-cold billow, at times the song of the swan. I took my gladness in the cry of the gannet and the sound of the curlew instead of the laughter of men, in the screaming gull instead of the drink of mead. There storms beat upon the rocky cliffs; there the tern with icy feathers answered them; full often the dewy-winged eagle screamed around. No protector could comfort the heart in its need. And yet he who has the bliss of life, who, proud and flushed with wine, suffers few hardships in the city, little believes how I often in weariness had to dwell on the ocean path. The shadow of night grew dark, snow came from the north, frost bound the earth; hail fell on the ground, coldest of grain. And yet the thoughts of my heart are now stirred that I myself should make trial of the high streams, of the tossing of the salt waves; the desire of the heart always exhorts to venture forth that I may visit the land of strange people far hence. And yet there is no man on earth so proud, nor so generous of his gifts, nor so bold in youth, nor so daring in his deeds, nor with a lord so gracious unto him, that he has not always anxiety about his seafaring, as to what the Lord will bestow on him. His thoughts are not of the harp, nor of receiving rings, nor of delight in a woman, nor of joy in the world, nor of aught else save the rolling of the waves; but he who sets out on the waters ever feels longing. The groves put forth blossoms; cities grow beautiful; the fields are fair; the world revives; all these urge the heart of the eager-minded man to a journey, him who thus purposes to fare far on the ways of the flood. Likewise the cuckoo exhorts with sad voice; the harbinger of summer sings, bodes bitter sorrow to the heart. The man knows not, the prosperous being, what some of those endure who most widely pace the paths of exile. And yet my heart is now restless in my breast, my mind is with the sea-flood over the whale's domain; it fares widely over the face of the earth, comes again to me eager and unsatisfied; the lone-flier screams, resistlessly urges the heart to the whale-way over the stretch of seas.

Wherefore the joys of the Lord are more inspiring for me than this dead fleeting life on earth. I have no faith that earthly riches will abide for ever. Each one of three things is ever uncertain ere its time comes; illness or age or hostility will take life away from a man doomed and dying. Wherefore the praise of living men who shall speak after he is gone, the best of fame after death for every man, is that he should strive ere he must depart, work on earth with bold deeds against the malice of fiends, against the devil, so that the children of men may later exalt him and his praise live afterwards among the angels for ever and ever, the joy of life eternal, delight amid angels. …

poems.title: Riddle IX. A Cuckoo
poems.excerpt: Father and mother gave me up dead in these days, nor was life or stir yet within me. Then one, a kinswoman very gracious, began to cover me with garments, held and guarded me, covered me as honourably with a protecting robe as her own child, till beneath her bosom, as my destiny was, I became mighty in spirit among those who were no kin of mine. The beautiful kinswoman afterwards fed me, till I grew up, could set out more widely on journeys; she had the fewer of her own dear sons and daughters by what she did thus.
poems.translator: trans. R. K. Gordon, Anglo-Saxon Poetry (Everyman’s Library, 1926)

poems.title: Riddle XI. Night
poems.excerpt: Grey is my garment; adornments bright, red, and shining are in my raiment. I lead astray the stupid, and urge the foolish on to rash journeys; others I hinder from a useful journey. I know not at all why they, thus maddened, deprived of mind, led astray in deed, praise my crooked ways to everyone. Woe to them for their custom, when the High One brings the dearest of treasures, if they cease not from folly ere that.
poems.translator: trans. R. K. Gordon, Anglo-Saxon Poetry (Everyman’s Library, 1926)

poems.title: Riddle XVII. A Ballista
poems.excerpt: I am the guardian of my family, an enclosure firm with wires, filled within with noble treasures. Often by day I spit out terror of spears; the greater my fullness, the greater the success. The master beholds how the war-darts fly from my womb. Sometimes I swallow dark brown weapons, bitter points, deadly poisoned spears. My stomach is serviceable, the foison of my womb is fair, precious to proud men. Men forget not what passes through my mouth.
poems.translator: trans. R. K. Gordon, Anglo-Saxon Poetry (Everyman’s Library, 1926)

poems.title: Riddle XXIV. A Jay
poems.excerpt: I am a wondrous creature, I vary my voice; sometimes I bark like a dog; sometimes I bleat like a goat; sometimes I cry like a goose; sometimes I scream like a hawk; sometimes I mimic the grey eagle, the laugh of the war-bird; sometimes with a kite's voice I speak with my mouth; sometimes the song of the gull where I sit in my gladness. They call me G, also A and R; O gives aid and H and I. Now I am named as these six letters clearly signify.

poems.title: Riddle XXIX. Moon and Sun
poems.excerpt: I saw a wondrous creature, a radiant air-vessel artfully adorned, bringing booty between her horns, spoil homewards from the foray. She wished to build herself a bower in the stronghold, set it up with skill, if so it might be. Then came a wondrous creature over the mountain-top — he is known to all dwellers on earth — snatched the spoil and drove the wanderer to her home against her will. Thence she departed westward on a journey of vengeance; she hastened forth. Dust rose to the heavens; dew fell on the earth; night went hence. No man afterwards knew where the creature journeyed.
poems.translator: trans. R. K. Gordon, Anglo-Saxon Poetry (Everyman’s Library, 1926)

poems.title: Riddle XXXIII. An Iceberg
poems.excerpt: The monster came sailing, wondrous along the wave; it called out in its comeliness to the land from the ship; loud was its din; its laughter was terrible, dreadful on earth; its edges were sharp. It was malignantly cruel, not easily brought to battle but fierce in the fighting; it stove in the ship's sides, relentless and ravaging. It bound it with a baleful charm; it spoke with cunning of its own nature: "My mother is of the dearest race of maidens, she is my daughter grown to greatness, as it is known to men, to people among the folk, that she shall stand with joy on the earth in all lands."
poems.translator: trans. R. K. Gordon, Anglo-Saxon Poetry (Everyman’s Library, 1926)

poems.title: Riddle XXXIV. A Rake
poems.excerpt: I saw a creature in the cities of men who feeds the cattle; it has many teeth; its beak is useful; it goes pointing downward; it plunders gently and returns home; it searches through the slopes, seeks herbs; always it finds those which are not firm; it leaves the fair ones fixed by their roots, quietly standing in their station, gleaming brightly, blowing and growing.
