poems.title: Riddle XXXV. A Coat of Mail
poems.excerpt: The dewy earth, wondrous cold, first brought me forth from its womb. I know in my thoughts I am not made of the fleeces of wool, of hairs, through excellent skill. Woofs are not wound round me, nor have I warp, nor does a thread of mine resound through the thrust of many strokes, nor does the whirring shuttle move in me, nor shall a weaver's rod smite me from anywhere. Silkworms, who deck the yellow precious web with adornments, did not weave me with the strength of the fates. Yet far and wide over the earth before men they will call me delightful. O thou skilled in cunning thoughts, learned in words, tell in true speech what is this garment.
poems.translator: trans. R. K. Gordon, Anglo-Saxon Poetry (Everyman’s Library, 1926)

poems.title: Riddle XXXVIII. A Bullock

A man spoke; he said to me: "The creature, if he lives breaks the downs; if he dies, he binds the living."

poems.title: Riddle LIII. A Battering Ram
poems.excerpt: I saw the tree tower up in the wood glorious with branches; that tree was in joy, a growing timber. Water and earth fed it well, until, grown old in other days, it was sorely stricken in its downfall, silent in bonds, its wounds fettered over, adorned in front with dark trappings. Now by the might of its head it clears the way for another malicious foe. Often together, mid storm, they have plundered the hoard. The second was swift and restive if the former fell into danger. No one could venture to grapple with it.

Verily it behoves every man that he himself should ponder his soul's state, how sound that is, when death comes, sunders the union which existed before, body and soul. Long is it after that till the soul receives from God Himself either bale or bliss, even as the body won for it erstwhile on earth. The spirit, the soul, shall come, loud in its sorrows, always on the seventh night, for three hundred years, to find the body which long since it wore, unless ere that the great King, Almighty God, the Lord of lords, will bring the end of the world. But come hither, if ever before thou didst hear my voice afar, and listen, and leaving thy father's golden house camest with chariot yoked, and fair fleet sparrows drew thee, flapping fast their wings around the dark earth, from heaven through mid sky. Quickly arrived they; and thou, blessed one, smiling with immortal countenance, didst ask What now is befallen me, and Why now I call, and What I in my mad heart most desire to see. 'What Beauty now wouldst thou draw to love thee? Who wrongs thee, Sappho? For even if she flies she shall soon follow, and if she rejects gifts shall yet give, and if she loves not shall soon love, however loth.' When the wave rises, it is the water; and when it falls, it is the same water again.  Tell me, Sir, where is the distinction? …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XV: Where Spring, the lord of the seasons, reigneth
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XVI: Between the poles of the conscious and the unconscious
poems.excerpt:
Between the poles of the conscious and the unconscious, there has the mind made a swing:
Thereon hang all beings and all worlds, and that swing never ceases its sway.
Millions of beings are there: the sun and the moon in their courses are there: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XVII: The light of the sun, the moon, and the stars shines bright:
poems.excerpt:
The light of the sun, the moon, and the stars shines bright:
The melody of love swells forth, and the rhythm of love's detachment beats the time.
Day and night, the chorus of music fills the heavens; and Kabîr says …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XVIII: The middle region of the sky, wherein the spirit dwelleth
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XIX: O my heart!  the Supreme Spirit, the great Master, is near you: wake
poems.excerpt:
O my heart!  the Supreme Spirit, the great Master, is near you: wake, oh wake!
Run to the feet of your Beloved: for your Lord stands near to your head.
You have slept for unnumbered ages; this morning will you not wake?
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XX: To what shore would you cross, O my heart
poems.excerpt:
To what shore would you cross, O my heart?  there is no traveller before you, there is no road:
Where is the movement, where is the rest, on that shore?
There is no water; no boat, no boatman, is there; …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXI: Lamps burn in every house, O blind one! and you cannot see them.
poems.excerpt:
Lamps burn in every house, O blind one! and you cannot see them.
One day your eyes shall suddenly be opened, and you shall see: and the fetters of death will fall from you.
There is nothing to say or to hear, there is nothing to do: it is he who is living, yet dead, who shall never die again. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXII: O brother, my heart yearns for that true Guru
poems.excerpt:
O brother, my heart yearns for that true Guru, who fills the cup of true love, and drinks of it himself, and offers it then to me.
He removes the veil from the eyes, and gives the true Vision of Brahma:
He reveals the worlds in Him, and makes me to hear the Unstruck Music: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXIII: The shadows of evening fall thick and deep
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXIV: More than all else do I cherish at heart that love which makes me to…
poems.excerpt:
More than all else do I cherish at heart that love which makes me to live a limitless life in this world.
It is like the lotus, which lives in the water and blooms in the water: yet the water cannot touch its petals, they open beyond its reach.
It is like a wife, who enters the fire at the bidding of love. She burns and lets others grieve, yet never dishonours love. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXV: My Lord hides Himself, and my Lord wonderfully reveals Himself:
poems.excerpt:
My Lord hides Himself, and my Lord wonderfully reveals Himself:
My Lord has encompassed me with hardness, and my Lord has cast down my limitations.
My Lord brings to me words of sorrow and words of joy, and He Himself heals their strife. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXVI: All things are created by the Om;
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXVII: It is the mercy of my true Guru that has made me to know the unknown;
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXVIII: Before the Unconditioned, the Conditioned dances: "Thou and I are one
poems.excerpt:
Before the Unconditioned, the Conditioned dances: "Thou and I are one!" this trumpet proclaims.
The Guru comes, and bows down before the disciple:
This is the greatest of wonders.
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXIX: Gorakhnath asks Kabîr:
poems.excerpt:
Gorakhnath asks Kabîr:
"Tell me, O Kabîr, when did your vocation begin?  Where did your love have its rise?"
Kabîr answers: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXX: On this tree is a bird: it dances in the joy of life
poems.excerpt:
On this tree is a bird: it dances in the joy of life. None knows where it is: and who knows what the burden of its music may be?
Where the branches throw a deep shade, there does it have its nest: and it comes in the evening and flies away in the morning, and says not a word of that which it means.
None tell me of this bird that sings within me. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXXI: A sore pain troubles me day and night, and I cannot sleep;
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXXII: Dance, my heart!  dance to-day with joy.
poems.excerpt:
Dance, my heart!  dance to-day with joy.
The strains of love fill the days and the nights with music, and the world is listening to its melodies:
Mad with joy, life and death dance to the rhythm of this music. The hills and the sea and the earth dance.  The world of man dances in laughter and tears. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXXIII: Where is the need of words, when love has made drunken the heart?
poems.excerpt:
Where is the need of words, when love has made drunken the heart?
I have wrapped the diamond in my cloak; why open it again and again?
When its load was light, the pan of the balance went up: now it is full, where is the need for weighing? …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXXIV: How could the love between Thee and me sever?
poems.excerpt:
How could the love between Thee and me sever?
As the leaf of the lotus abides on the water: so thou art my Lord, and I am Thy servant.
As the night-bird Chakor gazes all night at the moon: so Thou art my Lord and I am Thy servant. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXXV: My body and my mind are grieved for the want of Thee;
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXXVI: O friend, awake, and sleep no more!
poems.excerpt:
O friend, awake, and sleep no more!
The night is over and gone, would you lose your day also?
Others, who have wakened, have received jewels; …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXXVII: Where is the night, when the sun is shining?  If it is night
poems.excerpt:
Where is the night, when the sun is shining?  If it is night, then the sun withdraws its light.  Where knowledge is, can ignorance endure?
If there be ignorance, then knowledge must die.
If there be lust, how can love be there?  Where there is love, there is no lust. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXXVIII: The lock of error shuts the gate, open it with the key of love: Thus
poems.excerpt:
The lock of error shuts the gate, open it with the key of love: Thus, by opening the door, thou shalt wake the Beloved.
Kabîr says: "O brother!  do not pass by such good fortune as this."
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XXXIX: O friend! this body is His lyre; He tightens its strings
poems.excerpt:
O friend! this body is His lyre; He tightens its strings, and draws from it the melody of Brahma.
If the strings snap and the keys slacken, then to dust must this instrument of dust return:
Kabîr says: "None but Brahma can evoke its melodies."
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XL: He is dear to me indeed who can call back the wanderer to his home
poems.excerpt:
He is dear to me indeed who can call back the wanderer to his home.  In the home is the true union, in the home is enjoyment of life: why should I forsake my home and wander in the forest?
If Brahma helps me to realize truth, verily I will find both bondage and deliverance in home.
He is dear to me indeed who has power to dive deep into Brahma; whose mind loses itself with ease in His contemplation. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLI: O sadhu!  the simple union is the best
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLII: There is nothing but water at the holy bathing places
poems.excerpt:
There is nothing but water at the holy bathing places; and I know that they are useless, for I have bathed in them.
The images are all lifeless, they cannot speak; I know, for I have cried aloud to them.
The Purana and the Koran are mere words; lifting up the curtain, I have seen. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLIII: I laugh when I hear that the fish in the water is thirsty:
poems.excerpt:
I laugh when I hear that the fish in the water is thirsty:
You do not see that the Real is in your home, and you wander from forest to forest listlessly!
Here is the truth!  Go where you will, to Benares or to Mathura; if you do not find your soul, the world is unreal to you.
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLIV: The Hidden Banner is planted in the temple of the sky
poems.excerpt:
The Hidden Banner is planted in the temple of the sky; there the blue canopy decked with the moon and set with bright jewels is spread.
There the light of the sun and the moon is shining: still your mind to silence before that splendour.
Kabîr says: "He who has drunk of this nectar, wanders like one who is mad."
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLV: Who are you, and whence do you come?
poems.excerpt:
Who are you, and whence do you come?
Where dwells that Supreme Spirit, and how does He have His sport with all created things?
The fire is in the wood; but who awakens it suddenly?  Then it turns to ashes, and where goes the force of the fire? …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLVI: O sadhu!  purify your body in the simple way.
poems.excerpt:
O sadhu!  purify your body in the simple way.
As the seed is within the banyan tree, and within the seed are the flowers, the fruits, and the shade:
So the germ is within the body, and within that germ is the body again. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLVII: There is a strange tree
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLVIII: I have stilled my restless mind, and my heart is radiant
poems.excerpt:
I have stilled my restless mind, and my heart is radiant: for in Thatness I have seen beyond That-ness.  In company I have seen the Comrade Himself.
Living in bondage, I have set myself free: I have broken away from the clutch of all narrowness.
Kabîr says: "I have attained the unattainable, and my heart is coloured with the colour of love."
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLIX: That which you see is not: and for that which is, you have no words.
poems.excerpt:
That which you see is not: and for that which is, you have no words.
Unless you see, you believe not: what is told you you cannot accept.
He who is discerning knows by the word; and the ignorant stands gaping. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song L: The flute of the Infinite is played without ceasing
poems.excerpt:
The flute of the Infinite is played without ceasing, and its sound is love:
When love renounces all limits, it reaches truth.
How widely the fragrance spreads!  It has no end, nothing stands in its way. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LI: Dear friend, I am eager to meet my Beloved!  My youth has flowered
poems.excerpt:
Dear friend, I am eager to meet my Beloved!  My youth has flowered, and the pain of separation from Him troubles my breast.
I am wandering yet in the alleys of knowledge without purpose, but I have received His news in these alleys of knowledge.
I have a letter from my Beloved: in this letter is an unutterable message, and now my fear of death is done away. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LII: When I am parted from my Beloved, my heart is full of misery
poems.excerpt:
When I am parted from my Beloved, my heart is full of misery: I have no comfort in the day, I have no sleep in the night.  To whom shall I tell my sorrow?
The night is dark; the hours slip by.  Because my Lord is absent, I start up and tremble with fear.
Kabîr says: "Listen, my friend!  there is no other satisfaction, save in the encounter with the Beloved."
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LIII: What is that flute whose music thrills me with joy?
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LIV: Have you not heard the tune which the Unstruck Music is playing
poems.excerpt:
Have you not heard the tune which the Unstruck Music is playing? In the midst of the chamber the harp of joy is gently and sweetly played; and where is the need of going without to hear it?
If you have not drunk of the nectar of that One Love, what boots it though you should purge yourself of all stains?
The Kazi is searching the words of the Koran, and instructing others: but if his heart be not steeped in that love, what does it avail, though he be a teacher of men? …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LV: Subtle is the path of love!
poems.excerpt:
Subtle is the path of love!
Therein there is no asking and no not-asking,
There one loses one's self at His feet, …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LVI: He is the real Sadhu
poems.excerpt:
He is the real Sadhu, who can reveal the form of the Formless to the vision of these eyes:
Who teaches the simple way of attaining Him, that is other than rites or ceremonies:
Who does not make you close the doors, and hold the breath, and renounce the world: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LVII: Receive that Word from which the Universe springeth!
poems.excerpt:
Receive that Word from which the Universe springeth!
That word is the Guru; I have heard it, and become the disciple.
How many are there who know the meaning of that word? …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LVIII: Empty the Cup!  O be drunken!
poems.excerpt:
Empty the Cup!  O be drunken!
Drink the divine nectar of His Name!
Kabîr says: "Listen to me, dear Sadhu! …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LIX: O man, if thou dost not know thine own Lord
poems.excerpt:
O man, if thou dost not know thine own Lord, whereof art thou so proud?
Put thy cleverness away: mere words shall never unite thee to Him.
Do not deceive thyself with the witness of the Scriptures: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LX: The savour of wandering in the ocean of deathless life has rid me of…
poems.excerpt:
The savour of wandering in the ocean of deathless life has rid me of all my asking:
As the tree is in the seed, so all diseases are in this asking.
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXI: When at last you are come to the ocean of happiness
poems.excerpt:
When at last you are come to the ocean of happiness, do not go back thirsty.
Wake, foolish man!  for Death stalks you.  Here is pure water before you; drink it at every breath.
Do not follow the mirage on foot, but thirst for the nectar; …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXII: Who has ever taught the widowed wife to burn herself on the pyre of…
poems.excerpt:
Who has ever taught the widowed wife to burn herself on the pyre of her dead husband?
And who has ever taught love to find bliss in renunciation?
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXIII: Why so impatient, my heart?
poems.excerpt:
Why so impatient, my heart?
He who watches over birds, beasts, and insects,
He who cared for you whilst you were yet in your mother's womb, …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXIV: Now hard it is to meet my Lord!
poems.excerpt:
Now hard it is to meet my Lord!
The rain-bird wails in thirst for the rain: almost she dies of her longing, yet she would have none other water than the rain.
Drawn by the love of music, the deer moves forward: she dies as she listens to the music, yet she shrinks not in fear. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXV: O brother! when I was forgetful, my true Guru showed me the Way.
poems.excerpt:
O brother! when I was forgetful, my true Guru showed me the Way.
Then I left off all rites and ceremonies, I bathed no more in the holy water:
Then I learned that it was I alone who was mad, and the whole world beside me was sane; and I had disturbed these wise people. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXVI: The Yogi dyes his garments
poems.excerpt:
The Yogi dyes his garments, instead of dyeing his mind in the colours of love:
He sits within the temple of the Lord, leaving Brahma to worship a stone.
He pierces holes in his ears, he has a great beard and matted locks, he looks like a goat: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXVII: I do not know what manner of God is mine.
poems.excerpt:
I do not know what manner of God is mine.
The Mullah cries aloud to Him: and why?  Is your Lord deaf?  The subtle anklets that ring on the feet of an insect when it moves are heard of Him.
Tell your beads, paint your forehead with the mark of your God, and wear matted locks long and showy: but a deadly weapon is in your heart, and how shall you have God?
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXVIII: I hear the melody of His flute, and I cannot contain myself:
poems.excerpt:
I hear the melody of His flute, and I cannot contain myself:
The flower blooms, though it is not spring; and already the bee has received its invitation.
The sky roars and the lightning flashes, the waves arise in my heart, …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXIX: If God be within the mosque, then to whom does this world belong?
poems.excerpt:
If God be within the mosque, then to whom does this world belong?
If Ram be within the image which you find upon your pilgrimage, then who is there to know what happens without?
Hari is in the East: Allah is in the West.  Look within your heart, for there you will find both Karim and Ram; …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXX: He who is meek and contented., he who has an equal vision
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXI: Go thou to the company of the good
poems.excerpt:
Go thou to the company of the good, where the Beloved One has His dwelling place:
Take all thy thoughts and love and instruction from thence.
Let that assembly be burnt to ashes where His Name is not spoken! …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXII: The jewel is lost in the mud, and all are seeking for it;
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXIII: The palanquin came to take me away to my husband's home
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXIV: O my heart! you have not known all the secrets of this city of love
poems.excerpt:
O my heart! you have not known all the secrets of this city of love: in ignorance you came, and in ignorance you return.
O my friend, what have you done with this life?  You have taken on your head the burden heavy with stones, and who is to lighten it for you?
Your Friend stands on the other shore, but you never think in your mind how you may meet with Him: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXV: The Vedas say that the Unconditioned stands beyond the world of…
poems.excerpt:
The Vedas say that the Unconditioned stands beyond the world of Conditions.
O woman, what does it avail thee to dispute whether He is beyond all or in all?
See thou everything as thine own dwelling place: the mist of pleasure and pain can never spread there. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXVI: Open your eyes of love
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXVII: O my heart!  let us go to that country where dwells the Beloved
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXVIII: Kabîr says: "O Sadhu! hear my deathless words
poems.excerpt:
Kabîr says: "O Sadhu! hear my deathless words.  If you want your own good, examine and consider them well.
You have estranged yourself from the Creator, of whom you have sprung: you have lost your reason, you have bought death.
All doctrines and all teachings are sprung from Him, from Him they grow: know this for certain, and have no fear. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXIX: I am neither pious nor ungodly, I live neither by law nor by sense,
poems.excerpt:
I am neither pious nor ungodly, I live neither by law nor by sense,
I am neither a speaker nor hearer, I am neither a servant nor master, I am neither bond nor free,
I am neither detached nor attached. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXX: The true Name is like none other name!
poems.excerpt:
The true Name is like none other name!
The distinction of the Conditioned from the Unconditioned is but a word:
The Unconditioned is the seed, the Conditioned is the flower and the fruit. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXI: In the beginning was He alone, sufficient unto Himself: the formless
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXII: Kabîr ponders and says: "He who has neither caste nor country
poems.excerpt:
Kabîr ponders and says: "He who has neither caste nor country, who is formless and without quality, fills all space."
The Creator brought into being the Game of Joy: and from the word Om the Creation sprang.
The earth is His joy; His joy is the sky; …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXIII: The harp gives forth murmurous music
poems.excerpt:
The harp gives forth murmurous music; and the dance goes on without hands and feet.
It is played without fingers, it is heard without ears: for He is the ear, and He is the listener.
The gate is locked, but within there is fragrance: and there the meeting is seen of none. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXIV: The Beggar goes a-begging, but
poems.excerpt:
The Beggar goes a-begging, but
I could not even catch sight of Him:
And what shall I beg of the Beggar He gives without my asking. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXV: My heart cries aloud for the house of my lover
poems.excerpt:
My heart cries aloud for the house of my lover; the open road and the shelter of a roof are all one to her who has lost the city of her husband.
My heart finds no joy in anything: my mind and my body are distraught.
His palace has a million gates, but there is a vast ocean between it and me: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXVI: Serve your God, who has come into this temple of life!
poems.excerpt:
Serve your God, who has come into this temple of life!
Do not act the part of a madman, for the night is thickening fast.
He has awaited me for countless ages, for love of me He has lost His heart: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXVII: Clouds thicken in the sky!  O
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXVIII: This day is dear to me above all other days
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXIX: Is there any wise man who will listen to that solemn music which…
poems.excerpt:
Is there any wise man who will listen to that solemn music which arises in the sky?
For He, the Source of all music, makes all vessels full fraught, and rests in fullness Himself.
He who is in the body is ever athirst, for he pursues that which is in part: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XC: To whom shall I go to learn about my Beloved?
poems.excerpt:
To whom shall I go to learn about my Beloved?

poems.title: I Come, and I Say to Thee
poems.excerpt: I come, and I say to thee. Prince, listen and learn how a noble horse may be known. Active and brisk, see if his nostrils are rapidly swelling and shrinking alternately; whether his slender limbs are like the limbs of the gazelle, ready to commence its course. His haunches must resemble those of a chamois: his tender mouth yields to the slightest motion of the bridle, like the mouth of a young camel. When he eats, his teeth grind the grain, and make them crack like a millstone in motion; and he swallows them like a famished wolf. His back ought to remind you exactly of that of a hare: his mane is soft and silky: his neck is lofty, formed in semblance of the peacock's. The best time to mount him is between his fourth and fifth year. His head, neat and small as the head of the great serpent, chah-maur: his eyes projecting like two apples: his teeth are like so many diamonds. The shape of his mouth ought to approach that of a male camel: his limbs are neatly turned and fashioned; their shape is rather rounded than elongated. When brought out of the stable he is playful and prances. His eyes are like the eyes of the eagle, and he walks along with the restlessness of a hungry wolf. His belly and his ribs ought to fill the girth exactly. A young man of good family lends an obedient ear to the words of his parents: he pays the greatest attention to his horse: he knows by heart its descent and its pure blood; often he tries the vigour of the joints of its knees. In one word, he ought to be what Mirza-Serraf was in his youth.

poems.title: My Prince Has Issued an Order
poems.excerpt: My prince has issued an order that I should be punished. But, by Allah, I know how to defend myself, I shall escape. In vain wouldst thou offer me thy riches and favours, as food is offered to the gluttonous and famished eagle; I will reject them all.

poems.title: I Am Called God in My House
poems.excerpt: I am called God in my house. Yes; I am a God. I shall not bend my neck before a coward like thee. The pitcher has carried water long enough for thee; but that pitcher is broken at last.

poems.title: Enough of This Boasting
poems.excerpt: Enough of this boasting. What are in my eyes thirty, sixty, or a hundred of your warriors? What are your rocks, your precipices, and deserts, under the hoof of my steed? In me you behold the leopard of the mountains and of the valleys.

poems.title: Listen to the Words of Kurroglou
poems.excerpt: Listen to the words of Kurroglou. Life is a burden to me. From this day I yield my head to the chances of fortune, like an autumn leaf abandoned to the wilful breath of the wind. With God's assistance I shall go to Persia, to establish there the worship of Ali, who is venerated in that country.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: The Hour of Departure Has Arrived
poems.excerpt: The hour of departure has arrived. Whoever will follow me into Kurdistan, now let him be ready! The man whose lips are wont to drink in the cup of valour, let him follow me! I will have no cowards. Accursed be their infamous race! Those who can tear to pieces the shroud of death, — let them follow me!
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: My Heart Is Fond of a Youth
poems.excerpt: My heart is fond of a youth whose eyebrows are arched. His waist is slender, his lips like a bud, a smiling rose. Youth, sacrifice thy soul to beauty! Behold in me its victim. Go round the world you will not find a more promising lad. His name is Ayvaz Bally. The meadow of the eighth paradise! His father is by trade a butcher. The son, a mine of precious stones.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: Am I to Confess It, Then?
poems.excerpt: Am I to confess it, then? No, I am a shepherd. The life of created beings must have an end. When I shoot from the bow, my arrow pierces through the rock. O! son of the butcher.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: Thou Sayst I Must Not Weep
poems.excerpt: Thou sayst I must not weep. How can I help my tears, O Kurroglou? Thou tellest me not to torment thee with my grief. How can I help being sad?
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: How Beautiful Thy Head Looks
poems.excerpt: How beautiful thy head looks with this plume; it is like the male crane's head. I shall keep it; I shall watch over it carefully. I sought thee in heaven, and I have found thee on earth; do not weep, my young crane. The arched line of thy eyebrows has been sketched by the pen of the Almighty. Thou art just come of age, thou art fifteen, O my youth. To all these ornaments one only is wanting, and it is that of chivalrous achievements. Thou shalt be the model of a Warrior. I shall cover thy head with a calotte of gold. O my young crane, weep no more.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: O My Steed, Thy Father Was Bedon
poems.excerpt: O my steed, thy father was Bedon; thy mother Koldan. On! on! my worthy Kyrat, carry me to Chamly-bill! Leave me not here amongst unbelievers and foes, in the midst of the brown fog. On! on! my soul, Kyrat, carry me to Chamly-bill!
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: Warrior Reyhan! Thou Art Come with an Army
poems.excerpt: Warrior Reyhan! thou art come with an army against me alone. Where is thy honour, where thy boasted valour? Why dost thou seek to destroy my soul? Warrior Reyhan, thou must be mad!
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: In Thy Breath There Is the Fragrance
poems.excerpt: In thy breath there is the fragrance of the violet and hyacinth; like them thou art blooming in solitude. Thou art an arrow in my heart's core; Heaven will take vengeance on thee, because thou wouldst not listen to my complaints.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: A Mist Is Descending upon the Tops of the High Mountains
poems.excerpt: A mist is descending upon the tops of the high mountains. Darkness, fog, and humidity dwell on them. The snow is coming down, the ravines and mountain passes become inaccessible for a caravan. Bitter and cold blasts are blowing.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: Winter, Winter Is Come
poems.excerpt: Winter, winter is come, wild ducks are flocking on the lakes. The antelopes have descended in herds into the valleys. Thou art alone, foreign warrior, in the midst of men who are strangers to thee; their language is unknown to thee; thou art indeed to be pitied.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: Without Kyrat
poems.excerpt: Without Kyrat, life and the world is but a sin to me. Poor Kurroglou! Now, when Kyrat has left thy hands, thou must strike with sorrow thy head, Kurroglou!
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: O Thou Whom I Got First into My Hands
poems.excerpt: O thou whom I got first into my hands in Turkestan, come Kyrat, come, darling of my life! Thou hast fallen into the hands of a villain; come Kyrat, thou dearest to me of all things in life, come! I had a bit made for thee of fifteen pounds of iron. When thou art angry, thou wilt not touch food for three days. Thou wilt not stumble once in a race of forty farsakhs. O! Kyrat, thou dearest of all things to me in life, come!
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: A Noble Horse Walks Boldly
poems.excerpt: A noble horse walks boldly, as if he were anxious to overthrow his rider. He stirs his ears, and pulls so hard on the reins that the rider must hold him tightly, and let his hand have no rest. The horse of a ram-warrior ought to be as mad as his master.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: The Pregnant Sun Brings Forth the Day
poems.excerpt: The pregnant sun brings forth the day. It gathers a host of rays on its head. From its face comes snow — the frost. What does it signify? Is it a hurricane, or a winter?
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: The Guns Roar, Peal After Peal
poems.excerpt: The guns roar, peal after peal; the bombs shoot out, the treacherous lead whistles; heads drop down like unripe melons; the blood gushes, and, like water, flows in streams.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: O My Gardens!
poems.excerpt: O my gardens! I used to gather your flowers, make nosegays of them, and send them as presents to my sweethearts. My friends standing on the road, cried and remained alone. Kurroglou, put thy confidence in God! He will be a shield against the misfortune that may befal thee unawares. Foe! do not step out before mine eyes, and do not conceal from me the last sight of Chamly-bill, left so far behind me.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: The Spring Comes
poems.excerpt: The spring comes. The snow melts on the mountains. My sisterly mountains unveil their fronts before my eyes. Here my Egyptian sword revelled in blood to satiety! O my mountains! my battles will live eternally in your echoes! How happy I was wandering upon your bosom! Hidden amongst your rocks, I lay in ambush, waiting till a heavy caravan ascended your acclivities. O my mountains, you never betrayed my secrets! Thanks to you! Thanks!
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: Kurroglou Says, I Came into This World
poems.excerpt: Kurroglou says, 'I came into this world. I learned the price of the days gone by. I died the very day my mother brought me forth. I have only two brothers, my sword and my horse. Ye mountains, ye are my sisters.'
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)

poems.title: A True Warrior Must Lose His Life
poems.excerpt: A true warrior must lose his life on the field of battle. The guns and the carbines thunder for him the death-song. O death! whom didst thou spare? The most cunning of all men, Babai-Amir, once run from thee, and endeavoured to escape. Didst thou not catch him, jumping upon him from an ambush? The heart of Kurroglou the ram fears thee not, provided his vows may be agreeable to God. Were even Hassan and Hussein, these footstools of the throne of God, on the seventh heaven (Ersh) spared by thee? No! thou hast made them martyrs at Kerbella.
poems.collection: Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842)
